headline: Most Undervalued Chip Stocks In October 2026: Four Are Cheaper Than The S&P 500
summary: Undervalued chip stocks in October 2026: Micron, NXP, Qualcomm and Nvidia trade below the S&P 500's forward P/E of 20.3.
content_html:
Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) tops the list of the most undervalued chip stocks in October, gaining more than 460% in 12 months.

The memory chip maker trades at 6 times forward earnings. That’s according to TradingView’s latest screener data on the 28 U.S.-listed members of the PHLX Semiconductor Sector index.

The forward price-to-earnings ratio (forward P/E) divides the share price by the profit analysts expect over the next year. A lower number means investors pay less for each dollar of expected profit.

By comparison, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) trades at 20.3 times next-12-month earnings.

Four chip stocks currently trade at cheaper valuations than the broader market: Micron, NXP Semiconductors N.V. (NASDAQ:NXPI), Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM) and Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA). Microchip Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MCHP) sits just above it.

So why is the market paying less than the index for the industry driving U.S. earnings growth?

Undervalued Chip Stocks Start With Micron’s Memory Boom

Micron’s largest business is DRAM (dynamic random-access memory), the short-term memory that servers, PCs and phones use to run programs.

Demand for that memory has outrun supply because of artificial intelligence. As a result, prices have surged.

Micron sold 211% more DRAM in the first nine months of fiscal 2026 than a year earlier, according to its latest quarterly filing.

Average selling prices rose about 140%, while volumes grew about 30%.

Consequently, profitability exploded.

Gross margin, the share of revenue left after the cost of making the product, reached 85% in the fiscal third quarter. A year earlier, it was 38%.

Why The Market Doesn’t Trust Micron’s Earnings Yet

Memory has always been a cyclical business. High prices push manufacturers to build new factories. New factories create too much supply. Then prices fall, and margins shrink.

As a result, investors tend to put low multiples on memory stocks when profits peak. A low forward P/E does not mean the market missed the boom. Instead, it signals doubt that these earnings can last.

The key question now is whether AI has changed the rules for Micron. If memory demand now grows every year, instead of rising and falling with the cycle, a multiple of 6 would be too low.

NXP And Qualcomm Are Cheap For Different Reasons

NXP trades at 14.6 times forward earnings, even as its business accelerates. The Dutch chipmaker reported second-quarter revenue of $3.5 billion, up 19% from a year earlier.

“AI is moving from the cloud into the physical world — into vehicles, factories, and robots,” Chief Executive Rafael Sotomayor said in the results release.

NXP expects third-quarter revenue of $3.75 billion. However, the stock has gained only 4.58% over the past year.

Meanwhile, Qualcomm’s fiscal third-quarter revenue fell 4% to $9.9 billion. Handset chip revenue dropped 20% to $5.1 billion, as Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) shifts to its own modems.

Its automotive revenue, however, jumped 61% to a record $1.6 billion. The company targets $40 billion in non-handset revenue by fiscal 2029.

Read Also: US Economy Kept Growing For 78 Months: These 10 Stocks Top The Leaderboard

Nvidia Is Now Cheaper Than The S&P 500

Nvidia, the world’s largest company by market value, trades at 19.9 times forward earnings — below the multiple of the overall index. Yet its growth is nothing like the index’s.

Nvidia’s second-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue more than doubled to $96.2 billion. Data center revenue rose 117% to $89.0 billion.

“AI has reached its inflection point,” founder and CEO Jensen Huang said in the earnings release. “Now, compute is revenue.”

The stock has risen 27.70% over the past year, while revenue grew 106%. In other words, profits have grown faster than the share price, and the multiple has compressed.

Cheap For A Reason, Or Cheap By Mistake?

A forward P/E is only as good as the estimates behind it. If memory prices fall or AI spending slows, analysts would cut their forecasts, and today’s low multiples would no longer look so low.

On the other hand, if AI demand proves more durable than past chip cycles, the market may be underpricing the companies at the center of the buildout.

For now, the S&P 500 costs more than the chipmakers supplying its biggest growth story.

headline: The Stock Market Is Falling: VIX Says Investors Aren’t Really Scared Yet
summary: Stocks are falling as yields top 5.3%, but the VIX remains below 16. Here's what the calm volatility signal means for investors.
content_html:
Wall Street is pulling back, but the options market isn’t behaving as if investors expect a major breakdown. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq are retreating from record highs as the 10-year Treasury yield climbs above 5.3% and oil moves past $100, yet the CBOE Volatility Index, known as VIX, remains below 16 — suggesting investors see the latest sell-off as a risk to watch, not a panic to flee.

The VIX Isn’t Flashing Panic

The S&P 500 fell roughly 0.6% Wednesday while the Nasdaq declined about 0.8%, as rising Treasury yields and higher oil prices pressured risk assets. The 10-year yield reached roughly 5.3%, its highest level since 2002, while Brent crude moved above $100 a barrel.

Yet the VIX closed Tuesday at 15.01, after falling 3.29% in the previous session, before rising to around 15.76 Wednesday.

That is remarkably subdued given the backdrop. The VIX measures the options market’s expectations for S&P 500 volatility over roughly the next 30 days.

The message is straightforward: investors are selling stocks, but they aren’t aggressively paying for protection against a much bigger move.

The Tail-Risk Signal Matters

The market isn’t completely complacent, though. The CBOE SKEW Index was around 141 Tuesday, suggesting investors were still paying attention to the risk of an unusually sharp market move even as the VIX remained low.

The Cboe SKEW Index measures how much investors are paying for protection against an unusually large move in the S&P 500, particularly a sharp downside move. A SKEW reading of 100 represents a roughly normal distribution of expected S&P 500 returns. As SKEW rises above 100, the market is assigning more weight to the possibility of unusually large moves, particularly on the downside.

That combination suggests investors aren’t expecting broad market chaos, but they are still assigning meaningful odds to an extreme downside event.

For high-growth names such as NVIDIA Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Marvell Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MRVL), that distinction matters. Higher yields put pressure on richly valued future earnings, but a low VIX indicates the market isn’t yet treating that pressure as a systemic threat.

Read Also: Nvidia Stock at New All-Time Highs: Market Expert Says ‘Cusp of a Major Breakout’

Volatility ETFs Are the Trade to Watch

The calm VIX also matters for volatility-linked ETFs.

The iPath Series B S&P 500 VIX Short (BATS:VXX) and the ProShares Ultra VIX Short Term Futures ETF (BATS:UVXY) offer leveraged or futures-based exposure to short-term volatility, while the ProShares Short VIX Short Term Futures ETF (BATS:SVXY) takes the opposite side of short-term VIX futures.

These products don’t simply track the spot VIX, making VIX futures important to their performance. When volatility stays subdued, products positioned for falling volatility can benefit — but that equation can change rapidly if the VIX and its futures spike.

Investment Takeaway

The interesting signal isn’t that stocks are falling. It’s that they are falling without a corresponding surge in fear.

If the VIX stays below 20 while yields remain above 5.3%, this could remain a valuation reset rather than a full-blown risk-off event. But if volatility suddenly breaks higher, investors may discover that today’s calm VIX was less a sign of confidence than complacency.

headline: Fed Minutes Hint to Another Hike This Year: Traders Don't See It Coming In October
summary: Minutes of the Sept. 15-16 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, released Wednesday, show a central bank united on raising rates and leaning toward another hike.
content_html:
Every Federal Reserve policymaker backed last month’s rate hike. Yet traders now see little chance of another hike in October.

Minutes of the Sept. 15-16 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, released Wednesday, show a central bank united on raising rates and leaning toward another hike.

“Most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end,” the minutes said.

Why The Fed Hiked

The minutes describe an economy running hotter than the Fed wants. Inflation, measured by the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, rose to an estimated 3.8% in August.

Core Personal Consumption Expenditures, which excludes food and energy, held at 3.4%. The Fed’s target is 2%.

Officials pointed to three sources of pressure: oil prices pushed up by the Middle East conflict, past tariff increases and the artificial-intelligence buildout.

Some participants warned that the AI buildout “could cause aggregate demand to outpace aggregate supply over the medium term,” the minutes said.

In plain terms, companies are spending on data centers and chips faster than the economy can produce what they need, and that lifts prices.

Others worried about what years of high inflation do to behavior.

After “more than five years of inflation above 2 percent,” some officials said, high price gains could start to shape inflation expectations and wage decisions.

Several participants said they saw the current policy rate as “not restrictive or only mildly restrictive.”

In other words, rates may still be too low to slow the economy.

Read Also: Marvell Stock Is Up 230% This Year: Bank of America Sees a Further 40% Upside

October Hike Odds Have Faded

Markets had been pricing out an October move before the Fed minutes.

According to the CME FedWatch tool, traders now see an 82.8% chance the Fed holds rates at its Oct. 27-28 meeting and a 17.2% chance of a hike.

Those odds had already moved last week after a cooler-than-expected employment report. The minutes do not commit to a date. Officials said they approach “each meeting with an open mind.”

Chances for a hike in December remain as high as 70%.

How Markets Reacted

The 2-year Treasury yield, the one most sensitive to Fed expectations, fell 2.6 basis points to 4.772%.

The 10-year yield was flat at 5.286%. The 30-year yield edged up to 5.668%, near its highest level since May 2002.

The minutes also addressed long-term yields.

Officials said stronger economic data, expectations of heavy AI-related borrowing and geopolitics had pushed them higher. Many said financial conditions still support growth, with stocks up sharply this year and corporate bond spreads narrowing.

The S&P 500 — tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) — slipped 0.2% to 7,803.73, and the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.4%. Gold — tracked by the SPDR Gold Shares (NYSE:GLD) — dropped 1.2% to $4,112 an ounce, while the U.S. dollar index rose 0.4%.

headline: Scott Bessent's Advisor Defends Real Yield Spike, Showcasing 'Trending Lower' Inflation Measures Since Biden's Presidency
summary: Treasury advisor Zervos defends real yield spikes with 'trending lower' inflation data, while critics slam trimmed-mean PCE as 'useless'.
content_html:
David Zervos, counselor to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, published market data showing four key core inflation measures have been “trending LOWER” since the 2024 election, attributing the rise in 10-year Treasury yields to real economic expansion rather than inflation expectations.

Treasury Data on Inflation and Breakevens

One of the charts posted by Zervos tracks Core CPI, Cleveland trimmed-mean CPI, Atlanta sticky core CPI, and Dallas trimmed-mean PCE from January 2017 through August 2026.

A second chart based on U.S. Treasury yield curves from Nov. 5, 2024, to Oct. 6, 2026, indicates that 10-year breakevens traded within a 33-basis-point band between 2.17% and 2.50%, ending at 2.36%.

Zervos highlighted that “long-term inflation expectations have been remarkably STABLE,” while 10-year TIPS real yields drove the borrowing cost increase across a 128-basis-point range, reaching 2.91%.

Read Also: Jim Cramer Says Oil Surge, Higher Rates Are ‘Convenient Excuses’ To Sell Semis as QQQ, SOXX Drop and Investors Question Data Center Spending

Critics Challenge ‘Useless’ Inflation Metrics

However, Zervos’s reliance on modified inflation data has drawn sharp pushback from financial experts. Macro investor Otavio Costa slammed the St. Louis Fed’s promotion of trimmed-mean PCE, calling it a “useless” metric, back in May.

Because the measurement calculates inflation by systematically stripping out the most extreme price changes each month— which often include volatile but essential consumer goods and broad commodity spikes — critics argue it masks surging living costs to artificially justify central bank policy decisions.

Bessent Links Yields to Economic Growth

Zervos published the charts to support comments made by Bessent on Oct. 8, during an Oval Office gathering with President Donald Trump, Senator Ted Cruz, and Michael Dell and Susan Dell regarding child investment accounts.

Addressing rising borrowing costs and mortgage rates tied to the 10-year yield, Bessent termed the rise a “global phenomenon” and characterized the domestic market movement as a “real rate issue.”

“Growth here is strong,” Bessent said, noting that elevated headline readings stem from an “energy shock” while core inflation moves toward central bank goals. Bessent projected that following the conflict, “mortgage rates and the tenure will come back down.”

White House Projections on Energy Prices

President Trump reinforced Bessent’s outlook by predicting a reduction in energy costs once military operations end.

“Oil will drop like a rock as soon as we’re finished with the war, which will be very soon. It’s going to be very soon. One way or the other we’ll be finished with it. But oil will come down to levels that were, I think, maybe even lower than they were before the war,” said President Donald Trump.

At the last check, Brent Oil Futures for December 2026 rose over 4.39% to $104.60 per barrel. Similarly, Crude Oil WTI Futures for November 2026 climbed to $92.21, a gain of 4.45%.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) has about 8.45% in Nvidia, 7.30% in Apple, and 5.76% in Microsoft. Together, the three stocks account for roughly 21.5% of the fund.

The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:VOO) has a similarly concentrated portfolio, with Nvidia at 8.08%, Apple at 7.03% and Microsoft at 5.70%.

That means investors buying broad-market ETFs are making a substantial bet on a handful of mega-cap companies, whether they intend to or not.

QQQ And VGT Amplify The AI Trade

The concentration becomes even more pronounced in technology-focused ETFs.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, has roughly 8.5% in Nvidia, 7.2% in Apple and 5.8% in Microsoft. Together, the three represent more than 21% of the fund.

The Vanguard Information Technology ETF (NYSE:VGT) takes the concentration much further. Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft together account for approximately 45% of the portfolio, giving investors substantially greater exposure to the mega-cap technology trade.

RSP Offers a Different Approach

For investors concerned about a potential AI-led unwind, the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP) provides a stark contrast. Rather than letting the largest companies to dominate the portfolio, RSP assigns roughly equal weights to S&P 500 constituents.

That could make equal-weight exposure particularly interesting if leadership broadens beyond mega-cap technology.

The bottom line is that Dalio’s warning isn’t just a call on individual AI stocks. For ETF investors, the bigger question is how much of their supposedly diversified portfolio is ultimately riding on the same handful of mega-cap winners.

headline: ‘Dean of Valuation’ Warns of AI Cash Drain: 4 Ways to Play the Shift
summary: Aswath Damodaran breaks down 2026 AI capex: rising cash burn, tech shifting to heavy assets, and 4 paths for stock investors.
content_html:
NYU Stern School of Business professor Aswath ‘The Dean of Valuation’ Damodaran sees a basic split across corporate America in 2026. Soaring headline earnings have kept stock indexes buoyant despite surging yields.

At the same time, massive artificial intelligence spending is draining free cash flow and turning capital-light technology giants into heavy infrastructure plays.

How Capex Moves Through the Books

In the latest market reflection, Damodaran notes that capital spending at U.S. public companies reached $507.4 billion in the second quarter, up 35.66% from a year earlier.

Technology led the gains, up 79.88%, followed by communication services at 62.01%. Invested capital climbed $3.69 trillion, or 13.24%, as debt rose $1.91 trillion and book equity $1.77 trillion.

This capital boom operates through an asymmetric accounting loop between builders and suppliers. Hyperscaler "builders" such as Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), and Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) capitalize outlays directly onto balance sheets, while longer amortization schedules being used by many of them are reducing the current hit to earnings.

“There is no way the year that you do capex that your earnings are going to go up,” Damodaran said.

But that spending becomes revenue for suppliers such as NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE:TSM) and Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO), and their rich margins carry it through to profit.

“That’s why AI capex will increase earnings,” he said. “It’s not at the hyperscalers, but it’s collectively across companies.”

See More: Top Value Stocks

Payout Ratios at 20-Year Lows

Since capex represents a direct, upfront cash deduction, aggregate cash burn among builders dwarfs net cash generation by suppliers.

“No matter how much you downplay the amortization effect on earnings, capex is capex,” Damodaran said. Over 12 months, dividends rose about 5% and gross buybacks about 9%, or roughly 7% net of share issuance.

Both trailed far behind a 49% surge in net income. S&P 500 companies returned about 63% of earnings to shareholders, the lowest since 2004, compared with a historical 80% to more than 100%.

Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and Amazon are becoming asset-heavy companies. Their returns must now clear a much higher cost-of-capital hurdle to avoid market repricing. A decade ago, Damodaran said, several of them were “capital light, high growth businesses.”

Four Paths for Investors

Going forward, Damodaran sees four actionable paths, none of which lets investors sit out the debate.

  • The Maximum Bull (All-In Disruption): Investors can pursue the thesis articulated by Leopold Aschenbrenner by going long AI architecture builders and suppliers while shorting vulnerable legacy industries. Investors must strictly avoid leverage, as excessive debt triggers forced liquidation long before secular cash flows materialize.
  • The Passive Realist (Market Consensus): Maintaining broad equity exposure via holdings like the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY). Yet, passive indexing assumes aggregate corporate AI investments will generate returns that clear the cost of capital.
  • The Defensive Skeptic (Capital Reallocation): Pivoting toward insulated niches like food processing and leisure – or allocating into regulatory-shielded regions like Europe or labor-competitive Asia. Damodaran advises preserving liquidity in short-term Treasuries yielding above 4% to withstand extended market exuberance.
  • The Direct Contrarian (Crash Out / Reversal): Investors expecting imminent failure can liquidate equities into cash or even short overextended AI darlings while buying disrupted incumbents – the reverse of Aschenbrenner’s playbook. However, this approach demands strict discipline against market momentum.

headline: Tanker Rates Hit $1.3M a Day As 9 Shipping Stocks Double in 2026
summary: Nine of 13 U.S.-listed tanker stocks have more than doubled this year. For comparison, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust is up 13.5%.
content_html:
The cost of shipping crude oil by sea has hit a record. The Breakwave Tanker Shipping ETF (NYSE:BWET), which tracks tanker freight futures, closed Thursday at $1,012.75.

It ended 2025 at $19.26. That is a gain of 5,157%.

Meanwhile, nine of 13 U.S.-listed tanker stocks have more than doubled this year. For comparison, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) is up 13.5%.

So why have tanker stocks gained so much less than the freight rates that drive their profits?

Why Tanker Freight Rates Hit a Record

A very large crude carrier, or VLCC, is a supertanker that carries about 2 million barrels of oil.

At the start of the year, a VLCC sailing from the Middle East to Asia earned around $30,000 a day, according to shipbroker Poten & Partners.

The rate has since reached $1.3 million a day, the firm said in its Tanker Opinion of Oct. 2.

That is 43 times as much.

Per barrel, the cost rose from $1.73 to almost $33. Freight now equals 27% of the delivered cost of the crude, up from 3% in January, according to Poten.

For this reason, its price follows expected freight rates directly.

The mechanism works in steps. First, the war with Iran disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has targeted nine vessels there in recent days, according to United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations data cited by Barchart.

As a result, owners demand more money to send ships into the Gulf.

In addition, voyages are getting longer.

Frontline plc (NYSE:FRO) said it expects average VLCC voyage length to stay elevated as Asian buyers source crude more widely.

Longer voyages keep each ship busy longer. As a result, fewer ships are available to take new cargoes, and rates rise.

“The entire energy complex is being challenged,” creating inefficiencies that support tanker utilization, Frontline CEO Lars H. Barstad said in the company’s second-quarter results release.

9 Tanker Stocks That Have More Than Doubled

Why Tanker Stocks Trail the Freight Rally

BWET does not own ships. Instead, it holds freight futures with an average maturity of about 50 to 70 days, and roughly 90% of them are tied to VLCC rates.

For this reason, its price closely tracks expected freight rates.

By contrast, shipowners book vessels weeks in advance, and some lease them at fixed rates for a year or more.

Frontline shows the gap. The company reported a record second-quarter profit of $659.2 million.

Yet its VLCCs earned an average of $152,700 per day that quarter. For the third quarter, Frontline had booked 86% of its VLCC days at $156,900 a day.

Both figures are a fraction of the current spot rate.

The gap suggests investors continue to value these companies on the profits they expect over several years, not on this month’s freight rate.

content_html:
American consumers are the gloomiest they’ve been in more than seven decades. That’s according to the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index, which fell to 46.3 in the preliminary October reading, from 48.1 in September.

Economists expected 47.6. Only May’s 44.8 was lower.

Before this year, the record low was 50.0 in June 2022, and before that 51.7 in May 1980.

Consumers now expect prices to rise 4.7% over the next year, up from 4.6% in September. That is the highest reading since May. However, the households that own the most stock have barely changed their mind this year.

Why is Consumer Sentiment Falling So Unevenly?

The current conditions index—which measures how consumers judge their finances and buying conditions today—dropped 12.2% in a month to 44.7, a record low, versus a consensus of 50.5.

In contrast, the expectations index rose to 47.3 from 46.3.

"Buying conditions for durables plummeted amid high prices and borrowing costs," Surveys of Consumers Director Joanne Hsu said.

The split by wealth is wide. Since January, sentiment has fallen roughly 25% among consumers who own no stock and roughly 27% among those with the smallest portfolios, according to a chart published with the release.

For the top third of stockholders, the decline is roughly 7%.

The same survey shows a drop of about 23% among independents, 14% among Republicans and 9% among Democrats.

"Frustration over cost-of-living continues to mount, as consumers across the political spectrum believe that the trajectory of the economy has weakened since the beginning of the year," Hsu said.

Read Also: Memory Chip Sales on Track to Top $2 Trillion By 2030: The Numbers Micron Bulls Need to Know

Gasoline Drives Inflation Expectations Higher

Year-ahead inflation expectations stood at 3.4% in February, before the Iran conflict began. They have not returned to that level since. Long-run expectations also rose, from 3.4% to 3.5%.

Gasoline averaged about $2.93 a gallon before the conflict, according to a report the University of Michigan published Friday. It rose above $4.50 in May and approached that level again in September.

The AAA national average was $4.37 on Friday, 40.5% higher than a year ago.

As a result, most households plan to change how they spend. Only 31% of consumers expect to keep buying as usual the items with large price increases. Another 54% plan to cut back, and 16% plan to stop buying them.

The share planning to stop was 8% in 2022, near the peak of post-pandemic inflation.

Half Of The Wealthiest Stockholders Plan To Spend As Usual

For example, half of the wealthiest stockholders expect to spend as usual, up from 39% in 2025. Among consumers with no stock, the share is 18%.

The 16% who plan to stop buying have a sentiment reading of 27.5 and expect inflation of 5.3%. They also expect unemployment to rise.

"These expectations are largely stagflationary," Hsu said in the report.

In addition, the survey tracks how many consumers want to buy early to avoid future price increases.

That share has climbed modestly since February. In the 1960s and 1970s, sharp increases in this measure came before each new wave of inflation.

"It is likely that the risks of inflationary psychology have yet to pass," Hsu said.

Read Also: Forget the AI Bubble: Jordi Visser Says the 'Bankpocalypse' Has Begun

Bond Yields Moved Higher After the Release

The 10-year Treasury yield rose 3 basis points to 5.27% at 10:14 a.m. ET. The 2-year yield rose 5 basis points to 4.81%, and the 30-year yield rose 2 basis points to 5.63%.

Fed funds futures priced a 21% chance of a rate increase at the Oct. 28 meeting, up from 18% on Thursday.

Stocks were little moved. The S&P 500 — tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) — gained 0.3% to 7,788 and the Nasdaq 100 added 0.2% to 30,795.

The State Street Consumer Discretionary Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLY) rose 0.6% to $112.43. However, the State Street SPDR S&P Retail ETF (NYSE:XRT) slipped 0.3% to $83.63.

Gold futures rose 1.3% to $4,211.60 an ounce, and Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) gained 1.3% to $82,745.

headline: S&P 500 Earnings Preview: Will Strong Profits Fuel the Next Rally?
summary: In this S&P 500 Index earnings preview, we look at whether the expected profits growth will fuel the next rally.
content_html:
The S&P 500 Index is hovering near its all-time high as investors turn their attention to the upcoming earnings season, which kicks off on October 13, when the biggest U.S. banks report their results. It has jumped by 13.5% this year, with the technology and energy sectors driving most of this growth.

Wall Street Expects Strong Earnings Growth

Top Wall Street analysts expect American companies to publish strong financial results in the upcoming earnings season. 

FactSet (NYSE:FDS) data shows that the expected earnings growth is 29.6%. If this is the final figure, it will mark the third consecutive quarter of earnings growth above 25%.

Historically, actual earnings growth has come in well above analyst estimates, so the final figure is likely to be higher. FactSet expects third-quarter growth to end up above 35%. That would still be strong, even though it would mark a slowdown from the second quarter, when many companies booked tariff refunds.

Most of the earnings growth is being driven by several important catalysts. American banks like Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and JPMorgan are benefiting from the ongoing investment banking boom. Technology companies like Micron, SanDisk, Dell, and HP Enterprise are seeing strong demand as the data center buildup accelerates. 

Read Also: Disney Stock Falls Into a Correction, but Goldman Sachs Calls It Highly Compelling

Further, energy companies like ExxonMobil, Chevron, and Marathon Petroleum are benefiting from the rising oil prices because of the ongoing US-Iran, Saudi Arabia-Houthi, and Ukraine-Russia wars. Brent and the West Texas Intermediate benchmarks are much higher than where they were last year. FactSet estimates that this sector will report an earnings growth rate of 121%.

Utilities are also benefiting from the rising demand for power amid the AI boom. It is expected to report an earnings growth of 7%, with most of this figure coming from independent power and renewable energy producers.

S&P 500 is Trading at Bargain Levels

The upcoming earnings season is coming at a time when the S&P 500 Index is trading at bargain levels. It has a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 19.1, lower than the five- and ten-year averages. 

Some of its biggest companies are trading with valuation multiples that are lower than their historical averages. For example, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has a forward multiple of 23, lower than the five-year average of 42. This is one reason why it decided to boost its share buyback by $150 billion. 

Micron, a company whose revenue jumped by over 300% last quarter, has a forward multiple of less than 10. Other top companies like SanDisk and Western Digital are trading at significantly lower multiples.

A key risk for the index is that US bond yields continue rising, with the ten-year soaring to the highest point in over two decades. In a statement this week, Ray Dalio warned that the rising interest rates may lead to the bursting of the AI bubble.

content_html:
The Dow Jones, S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 have held steady in recent weeks as investors have focused on rising US bond yields and the escalating situation in the Middle East. Their resilience will be tested in the coming weeks as major US companies report earnings and key economic data is released.

Dow Jones, S&P 500, and Nasdaq 100 to React to Earnings Season

The main catalyst for the US stock market this week will be the upcoming earnings season, which will kick off on Tuesday. Top US banks, including popular names like Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan, will release their numbers. Other non-bank companies that will release their numbers are Johnson & Johnson, UnitedHealth Group and Kinder Morgan.

Analysts are optimistic about this earnings season. FactSet (NYSE:FDS) data shows that the estimate among analysts is that earnings growth will be 29.5%. Historically, the real earnings growth tends to be 7% above the estimate. As such, there is a likelihood that the growth will be over 40%. 

The earnings growth comes at a time when American stocks are trading at discount levels. For example, the forward price-to-earnings ratio for the S&P 500 Index is 19.1, lower than the five and ten-year averages.

Read Also: Why Micron Stock is Struggling Despite Revenue Growth and a Low Valuation

US Consumer Inflation Report and US Bond Yields

The stock market will also react to the upcoming US consumer price index (CPI) report on Wednesday. Economists expect the data to show that the headline and core CPI numbers rose last month as gasoline and diesel prices jumped. 

The average estimate among analysts is that the headline CPI rose from 3.4% in August to 3.6% in September. Core inflation, which excludes the volatile food and energy prices, is expected to come in at 2.5%, up slightly from the previous 2.4%.

These numbers will provide more hints about what to expect from the Federal Reserve. Economists expect the bank to leave rates unchanged in this meeting and then hike in December. 

The stock market will also react to the bond market, where the ten-year and five-year yields have pulled back in the past few days. 

Middle East Crisis

The US stock market will also react to the ongoing crisis in the Middle East, which is escalating. For example, Yemen’s Houthis launched a major attack against Saudi Arabia’s main airport, with President Donald Trump hinting that the US will intervene. 

Iran has also continued striking ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz. There is also fear that the crisis will escalate. If this happens, it means that crude oil prices will continue rising in the coming weeks. This, in turn, will lead to higher inflation, pushing the Fed to hike interest rates, which may affect the stock market.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent labeled Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.)an “inflationista” while releasing the “Trump Affordability Tracker” to counter her economic claims. Bessent published the data to directly contrast economic and cost-of-living metrics between the Donald Trump and Joe Biden administrations.

‘Statistical Sleight of Hand’

Bessent took to X to criticize Warren’s “Trumpflation” tracker, stating he was providing “Another day, another Econ 101 lesson for Professor Warren.” He argued her tracker “conveniently ignores the Bidenflation tidal wave that crushed American families” and “cherry-picks wage growth by refusing to acknowledge positive real wage gains” under President Trump.

He also accused her of swapping “official medical-care CPI data for premium projections when it suits her narrative.” Bessent dismissed her claims by writing, “The Harvard Square inflationista is offering a statistical sleight of hand, not a serious assessment of today’s U.S. economy.”

Read Also: Elizabeth Warren Says Trump Made '28,000+' Trades, More Than Congress Combined: ‘Stock Trading…Should Be Illegal’

The Affordability Tracker Data

To provide what he called an “apples-to-apples comparison,” Bessent shared the “Trump Tracker: The Full Picture,” updated as of Oct. 9, 2026.

The graphic reports annualized core inflation at 2.5% under Trump, compared to 4.7% under Biden. The data show cumulative real weekly wages grew 1.5% during the Trump administration, compared with a 3.9% decrease under Biden.

The document also highlights a “Record Real Median Household Income” of $87,460 and cites the “Lowest Poverty Rate in History” at 10.2%.

Employment and Living Costs

Regarding the workforce, the tracker displays an increase of 1 million private sector jobs alongside a 328,000 reduction in the federal workforce.

A section titled “Cost Of Living Reality Check” outlines lower annualized price changes under Trump versus Biden for everyday expenses. According to the graphic, grocery inflation was 2.1% under Trump compared to 5.3% under Biden, while rent inflation stood at 3.0% under Trump versus 5.6% under Biden.

Furthermore, the chart notes that prescription drug prices dropped by 2.5% under Trump but rose by 2.2% under Biden, ultimately claiming a “Bidenflation Cost To Households” of over $30,000.

headline: SpaceX Shares Up 22% in 2 Months, Crushing S&P 500’s 1% Gain
summary: SpaceX shares are up 22% from their Aug. 11 closing price. For comparison, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust is up only 1% over the same period.
content_html:
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) went public on June 12 and, amid investor anticipation, debuted above its IPO price, surging 19% on day one. About a month later, the stock fell about 30% from its debut price. SpaceX stock has rebounded significantly over the last two months, rewarding patient investors.

SpaceX Stock Rallies

Fueled by multiple catalysts and continued strong investor demand, SpaceX stock has rallied over the last two months, helping CEO Elon Musk once again become a trillionaire.

The stock’s up-and-down price since its June 12 debut could be a good lesson in timing and patience for investors, particularly around a highly anticipated IPO.

SpaceX stock was priced at $135 for its IPO and opened trading at $150. On the first day of trading, shares were up 19%.

By the end of July, the stock price had crashed over 30% and hit a 52-week low of $104.83.

Recent launches, Musk’s optimism, and a new spectrum deal for the Starlink unit have fueled optimism in the stock price once again.

SpaceX shares closed Friday at $162.57, up 22% from their Aug. 11 close.

For comparison, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), which tracks the S&P 500, is up only 1% over the same period: Aug. 11 to Oct. 9.

That’s a 22-to-1 outperformance for SpaceX stock over the last two months.

Read Also: EXCLUSIVE: Top 12 Most-Searched Tickers in September on Benzinga Pro – Meta Rises, SpaceX Falls, Dell & Bloom Energy Join List

Patience Pays Off

Investors who bought in on the SpaceX IPO are up from the initial IPO price. Those who bought in on the first day of trading may be up only slightly now, at the closing price of the first day, if they chose to wait and buy shares on the first day of trading.

Others, like some members of Congress, bought SpaceX stock in the days after the market debut, when shares hit their highest levels. Those investors are holding a loss today.

The smartest investors may have been the traders who sat out the IPO entirely, waited for the dust to settle, and then bought SpaceX stock two months after the offering.

Those traders avoided periods of high volatility and are now up over 20% in two months.

With SpaceX recently securing spectrum needed for a full mobile launch and quarterly earnings expected next month, upcoming catalysts could keep the stock in the spotlight and reward the patient investors even more.

headline: Steve Eisman Warns S&P 500 Is One Giant AI Bet: 'I Own NVDA and I Worry'
summary: Steve Eisman says more than 65% of the S&P 500 is tied to AI, yet he still owns Nvidia and GE Vernova.
content_html:
Steve Eisman warns that more than 65% of the S&P 500 is now tied to artificial intelligence, leaving investors far less diversified than they might think.

Yet the investor famous for The Big Short says he owns Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and GE Vernova Inc. (NYSE:GEV), two major beneficiaries of the AI infrastructure boom.

“I own Nvidia, for example, and I watch and I worry,” he said in an interview with In the Money’s Amber Kanwar.

Suppliers Are Collecting the AI Cash

Eisman favors companies receiving AI infrastructure spending over those financing the buildout.

“I would be looking at the companies that are getting that cash flow,” he said in an interview on Oct. 8.

Nvidia supplies the chips powering data centers. Its revenue rose 106% from a year earlier to $96.2 billion in the quarter ended July 26.

GE Vernova sells gas turbines and electrical equipment needed to power AI data centers. Its companywide backlog reached $176 billion at the end of June, while data-center orders in its Electrification business topped $5 billion in the first half of 2026, more than double its full-year 2025 total.

But Eisman is taking precautions. He has partially hedged four unnamed AI-related holdings while remaining mostly long.

He worries that OpenAI and Anthropic could struggle to finance their enormous commitments, potentially slowing spending throughout the supply chain.

The S&P 500’s Hidden AI Exposure

Eisman has long recommended buying the S&P 500 and leaving it alone. He now warns the index, tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), provides limited protection against an AI downturn.

Information technology represents roughly 40% of the index by his count. Add Alphabet, Amazon and other technology-related companies, and the figure exceeds 50%.

Include utilities and industrial firms supplying AI infrastructure, and Eisman estimates exposure rises above 65%.

“It’s mostly all one trade. And to be perfectly frank, that makes me nervous,” he said in his podcast on Oct. 9.

The warning comes amid broader market pain. More than 40% of S&P 500 stocks have fallen in 2026, despite the index gaining roughly 14%, Reuters reported Monday.

Even bonds may offer limited shelter. Eisman estimates more than half of this year’s corporate bond issuance is AI-related, exposing lenders to the same investment cycle.

For investors seeking to avoid AI exposure, his preference is clear.

“I would just buy short-term treasuries,” he said.

On Polymarket, traders assign approximately 6% odds to a qualifying AI industry downturn by year-end. The contract requires at least three specified stress events within a 90-day period, rather than an ordinary market correction.

Eisman isn’t predicting a collapse, and he’s still long Nvidia and GE Vernova.

content_html:
Bitmine Immersion Technologies (NYSE:BMNR) bought 12,532 more Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) last week, inching closer to Chairman Tom Lee‘s 5% supply cap that will trigger a full stop on purchases.

Holdings Near the Finish Line

Bitmine announced Monday that its crypto holdings, cash and marketable securities now total $16.2 billion. 

As of Oct. 11, the company held 6,028,946 ETH, worth $2,544 per token, equal to 4.9% of the total 122.1 million ETH supply.

As Benzinga reported last week, Lee said at Token2049 that Bitmine will stop buying once it reaches 5%, needing only about 100,000 more ETH to get there. 

At last week’s pace, that puts the company roughly six to seven weeks from hitting its target.

Why Lee Calls This the Start of a Bigger Bull Run

Bitmine released its October Chairman’s Message on Oct. 7, titled “Crypto Bull Underway—This Cycle Likely the Largest.” 

Lee pointed to four forces he expects to drive the next cycle: tokenization, wealth transfer, digital asset treasuries absorbing supply, and crypto’s role as a downstream AI story.

On wealth transfer specifically, Lee cited Robinhood (NASDAQ:HOOD) CEO Vlad Tenev’s recent comment that $100 trillion in wealth is changing hands, with IRS and Fundstrat data estimating $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion of that shifting between 2026 and 2028. 

Moreover, Lee argued younger heirs tend to carry higher risk appetite for crypto, making this wealth transfer a stronger tailwind than the one seen in the 2019-2021 cycle.

He also flagged digital asset treasuries like Bitmine as a structural difference from prior cycles, since these companies remove supply from circulation permanently rather than trading it.

BMNP Preferred Stock Outperforms Comparable Yields

Bitmine’s preferred stock, BMNP (NYSE:BMNP), issued at $80 in June, has gained 24% since launch and last closed at $99.53. 

Lee said BMNP’s 9.56% yield sits 256 basis points below Strategy’s (NASDAQ:MSTR) comparable Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) credit yield and 515 basis points below Solana’s (CRYPTO: SOL) CHAD yield, which he called evidence of ETH’s stronger yield and stability profile.

ETH’s Quarterly Performance Against Stocks

Lee also highlighted that ETH outperformed the S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY) by 6,832 basis points in the third quarter, despite a hawkish Fed, rising oil prices, and tightening global financial conditions.

BMNR stock also outperformed ETH itself during the 2025-2026 bear market, falling just 3% over the first nine months of 2026 compared to ETH’s 10% decline.

Where BMNR Stands Technically

BMNR is consolidating after pulling back from September’s $29 high.

Price sits below its 20-day EMA near $25 but above its 50-day, 100-day, and 200-day EMAs, currently testing trendline support from July’s $13 low.

headline: S&P 500—What Happens In Q4 After A Negative September?
summary:
The final four months of the year are a particularly interesting period for stock markets, often associated with recognizable seasonal patterns.



In this article, we’ll analyze market performance in September,
content_html:
The final four months of the year are a particularly interesting period for stock markets, often associated with recognizable seasonal patterns.

In this article, we’ll analyze market performance in September, October, November, and December, comparing two major stock indexes: the S&P 500 for the U.S. market and the DAX as a European benchmark.

Our goal is to determine whether the final four months of the year have historically shown recurring patterns and whether those patterns have been similar or different across the two markets. We’ll also examine fourth-quarter returns following a positive or negative September.

S&P 500 and DAX: Comparing US and European Stock Markets

To represent the two markets, we selected the S&P 500 for the United States and the DAX for Europe. The S&P 500 includes 500 leading U.S. companies and covers a substantial share of U.S. stock market capitalization, making it one of the most widely used benchmarks for U.S. equity performance.

The DAX, meanwhile, includes 40 leading German-listed companies and represents one of Europe’s most important stock markets. It’s worth emphasizing that the DAX specifically represents the German market, rather than Europe as a whole. Nevertheless, its size and significance make it a useful benchmark for comparing a major European stock market with its U.S. counterpart.

The two indexes also differ in their sector composition. At current weights, technology plays a particularly prominent role in the S&P 500, while industrials account for the largest share of the DAX, followed by financial services.

These weights are a snapshot of the indexes’ current composition and should not be treated as constant over time. Sector exposure has shifted over the years, as have the companies included in each index and their relative weights.

September Through December: What Average Returns Show

Let’s start by examining the average return for each of the final four months of the year, using data beginning in 1998. As Figure 1 shows, September is the only one of these months with a negative average return in both markets: approximately -1.06% for the DAX and -0.62% for the S&P 500.

The picture changes considerably in October, which posts an average positive return of approximately 1.55% for the DAX and 1.18% for the S&P 500. The two markets show even more similar results in November, with average returns of 1.54% and 1.50%, respectively.

December also shows positive average returns, although the gap between the two indexes is wider: the DAX averages approximately 1.45%, while the S&P 500 averages 0.68%.

Overall, Figure 1 reveals a broadly similar seasonal pattern across the U.S. and German markets.

Figure 1. Average monthly returns for the DAX and S&P 500 from September through December, based on the sample beginning in 1998.

A Long Strategy From October to January

The initial analysis shows that both the S&P 500 and the DAX have historically posted positive average returns in each of the final three months of the year. Based on this finding, we can construct a very simple strategy: open a long position at the beginning of October and hold it until the beginning of January.

We can then introduce another variable. As we’ve seen, September is the only month in the final four months of the year with a negative average return in both markets. We therefore divided the trades into two groups: those following a positive September and those following a negative September. This allows us to examine whether the previous month’s performance is associated with differences in returns over the following three months.

Average Q4 Returns Are Higher After a Negative September

Looking at Figure 2, the first notable feature is the strong similarity between the equity curves of the strategies applied to the DAX and the S&P 500. The curves follow broadly similar paths over time, further highlighting similarities in the seasonal patterns observed in the two markets.

It’s also important to remember that these strategies are deliberately simple and include no risk management rules. Positions are opened at the beginning of October and held until January, regardless of what happens in between. This is particularly evident in 2008, when the sharp stock market decline caused a significant drawdown in the equity curves.

The most interesting finding, however, concerns performance following September. Although the number of trades is nearly identical in the two groups, the strategies that enter the market after a negative September show substantially higher average returns. For the DAX, the average return per October-to-January trade rises from approximately 3.73% after a positive September to 5.80% after a negative September. A similar pattern emerges in the S&P 500, where the average return increases from approximately 2.37% to 4.63%.

In both markets, September weakness does not necessarily persist into the following months. On the contrary, within the sample analyzed, the final three months of the year delivered better average results when September had ended in negative territory.

Figure 2. Equity curves for the October-to-January long strategy on the DAX and S&P 500, separating trades following a positive September (dashed lines) from those following a negative September (solid lines).

From Seasonality to a Trading Strategy: Limitations and Further Research

The analysis of the final four months of the year reveals broadly similar seasonal patterns in the S&P 500 and the DAX. An even more interesting finding emerges when September’s performance is introduced as a filter: for both indexes, the average October-to-January return was substantially higher following a negative September.

One possible explanation is mean reversion, or a recovery following a decline. If the conditions behind the selloff do not develop into a deeper crisis, some of that decline may subsequently be reversed.

Once again, the analysis presented here should primarily be viewed as a starting point for further research. The simple strategy used does not include stop losses, early exit criteria, or other forms of risk management. The pattern could be explored further by introducing filters based on the size of September’s decline, the longer-term trend, or different entry and exit rules.

Until next time, happy trading!

headline: S&P 500 Dominated by AI Stocks, Adding SpaceX Would Create History Last Seen in 1880s
summary: AI stocks are reaching unprecedented territory when it comes to their inclusion in a major US stock market index.
content_html:
Many investors know that the S&P 500 is heavily weighted to companies with exposure to the artificial intelligence sector. Data shows that the market capitalization of AI pure plays in the index is now reaching record levels last seen in the 19th century.

AI Dominance in the S&P 500

AI stocks make up 49% of the S&P 500, which is tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), which could explain some of the fears of an AI bubble popping.

Data from Bianco Research shared on social media shows that along with making up 49% of the S&P 500, the 41 companies named as AI pure plays in the index make up around two-thirds of the S&P 500’s year-to-date market cap changes.

Bianco Research’s Jim Bianco takes things a step further, with just how concentrated in AI the S&P 500 could be had rules been changed or could become in the future.

"If SpaceX was in the $SPX now, AI-related stocks would be 51% of the index. With Anthropic and OpenAI coming public, add them to the $SPX in 2027 and AI would be ~55% of the $SPX," Bianco tweeted.

The S&P 500 declined to change its rules to include SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) stock early, instead holding to the normal principles that a company needs profitability and has sufficient float.

Bianco shares that the precedent of AI stocks making up this much of the U.S. stock market dates back more than 100 years.

"The last time a single theme was >50% of the $SPX was the railroads in the 19th century."

Bianco shared the list of AI pure plays in the S&P 500, which includes all of the top 10 holdings in the SPY:

  • NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA)
  • Apple Inc (NASDAQ:AAPL)
  • Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)
  • Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN)
  • Alphabet Inc Class A (NASDAQ:GOOGL)
  • Broadcom Inc (NASDAQ:AVGO)
  • Alphabet Class C (NASDAQ:GOOG)
  • Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META)
  • Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU)
  • Tesla Inc (NASDAQ:TSLA)

While all the Magnificent Seven stocks are included in the index, the list also includes AI utilities, AI capital equipment companies and a list of AI direct companies across software, cybersecurity and other technology fields.

Read Also: EXCLUSIVE: Top 12 Most-Searched Tickers in September on Benzinga Pro – Meta Rises, SpaceX Falls, Dell & Bloom Energy Join List

Going Back to the Railroads

The S&P 500 was launched in 1957, so it hasn’t been around long enough to be dominated by the railroad sector.

The 1880s did see the overall U.S. stock market capitalization dominated by the sector, which emerged as the top sector and dominated the country.

In 1881, railroad companies made up 63% of U.S. stock market capitalization, according to Bank of America data.

Today, railroads make up less than 1%. The railroad sector has been a strong performer, though, beating the overall U.S. stock market since 1900.

A newsletter from BeBusiness Smart notes that sectors have dominated the S&P 500 or the overall U.S. stock market index at other times, but never near the 63% seen from the late 1880s to 1900. Here were some standout time periods of sector dominance:

  • Railroad, 1900: 63%
  • Energy, 1980: 28%
  • Technology, March 1980: 33% to 35%
  • Financials, before 2008: 20% to 22%
  • Technology, October 2026: 40%+

Railroads led to one of the greatest expansions of the U.S. economy, lowering freight and transportation costs and connecting many areas across the country.

AI is viewed as a technology that could change and impact multiple sectors in similar ways. The question is whether AI representing more than 50% of the U.S. stock market would be good or raise even more questions about a potential bubble.

headline: Institutional Confidence in Banks Has Collapsed Ahead of Earnings
summary: U.S. bank stocks lag the market as rising bond yields and tight deposit margins squeeze earnings. Discover key insights as big banks report.
content_html:
The banking sector has diverged from the broader equity rally. While the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY) is up about 14% for the year, the five largest U.S. banks, measured by the Invesco KBW Bank ETF (NASDAQ:KBWB), have collectively dipped around $270 billion from summer peaks.

Institutional investors have retreated – with only 35% expecting banks to beat the broader market, the Truist Securities survey showed, according to BigGo Finance. Compared with about 82% in December 2025, the decline reflects the repricing of bond yields.

Earnings season starts today, with JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM), Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (NYSE:GS), Wells Fargo & Co. (NYSE:WFC), and Citigroup Inc. (NYSE:C) reporting before the market opens.

The Yield Shock

Net interest margin is the gap between what banks earn on their assets and what they pay to fund them. That margin is now under pressure. Since the Fed raised its benchmark rate in September, deposit and wholesale funding costs have climbed as lenders fight to hold on to cash.

“Loan growth is easier to find than deposit growth, and so it’s putting pressure on deposit dynamics of raising funds,” said Brendan Coughlin, president of Citizens Financial Group.

The 10-year Treasury yield is trading around 5.24%, and the 30-year around 5.55%. Higher rates make borrowing harder for corporate clients and increase the risk of trouble with floating-rate debt and commercial real estate loans coming up for renewal.

Not everyone sees a squeeze coming. “Banks are asset-sensitive still,”  Matt Stucky, chief portfolio manager for equities at Northwestern Mutual, said according to MarketWatch.

Stucky notes that bank loans reprice faster than deposits. FactSet consensus shows net interest income rising across several big lenders, led by JPMorgan Chase, which is projected to grow 5.4% from the prior quarter and 12.2% from a year earlier.

See More: Top Value Stocks

The Dealmaking Drag

After a blockbuster second quarter, profit expectations have been subdued. Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s (NASDAQ:SPCX) record $85 billion IPO in June boosted that quarter.

Since then, high financing costs have slowed merger announcements. NVIDIA-backed Firmus Grid shelved its listing this week after investors pushed back on its valuation.

“A great deal of the recent underperformance for banks has been driven by the dramatic rise in long-term rates,” UBS analyst Erika Najarian told clients. Deutsche Bank research puts the specially serviced rate on securitized commercial real estate loans at 12%.

Others think the selloff has gone too far. Chris Grisanti of MAI Capital Management called the pullback “more of an opportunity than a harbinger of a downturn.” RBC Capital Markets‘ Gerard Cassidy said “underlying fundamentals remain strong” and the economy is “nowhere near a recession.”

“The No. 1 credit input is unemployment, which has been under 5% for 61 consecutive quarters,” said Macrae Sykes, portfolio manager of the actively-managed Gabelli Financial Services Opportunities ETF (NYSE:GABF).

Citigroup’s global co-head of M&A Guillermo Baygual sees demand holding up. 

“Yes, the interest rate environment is not helpful, but as a topic in the boardroom, M&A hasn’t slowed down,” he said.

Four-Year Cyclical Bull Market Milestone

Q3 Earnings and Seasonal Window Focus

“Let’s see if that momentum combined with the start of a bullish seasonal window could be enough to push the S&P 500 index above 8k,” Timmer wrote.

Valuation Pressures and Profit Margins

Timmer highlighted structural divergence underneath headline index performance. High yield credit spreads have widened, and only half of market components remain in uptrends as financial conditions tighten.

Investors currently pay 19 times forward earnings for 30% to 40% growth rates. However, corporate profit margins have climbed to a historic peak of 17.4%, driven by technological breakthroughs rather than COVID recession-era base effects.

Portfolio Positioning Strategy

Evaluating historical cycles since 1950, Timmer observed that the current 48-month bull market duration exceeds the 39-month average, while price gains of 119% (monthly basis) compare to the historical 101% average.

Timmer confirmed maintaining a 60/20/20 asset allocation framework, citing commodities and 1-5 year TIPS as key diversifiers, while noting Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) may be initiating a new 4-year cycle.

summary: Goldman Sachs stock jumps 4.5% after equities trading revenue soared 72% to $6.44 billion. JPMorgan and Wells Fargo show the same split with bond desks.
content_html:
Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (NYSE:GS) stock traders generated $6.44 billion of revenue in the third quarter, 72% more than a year earlier. Its bond traders generated $3.47 billion, unchanged from a year ago and below Wall Street’s estimate.

The same split appeared at JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM) and Wells Fargo & Co. (NYSE:WFC), which also reported before the open on Tuesday.

Investors rewarded the bank most exposed to stock trading.

Goldman shares rose 4.5% in premarket trading. JPMorgan was little changed after missing profit estimates. Wells Fargo fell 1.4% despite beating them.

Goldman’s Equities Desk Topped Estimates by $1.35 Billion

Goldman’s equities revenue of $6.44 billion compared with the $5.09 billion analysts expected. The firm cited derivatives and prime financing, which is lending to hedge funds.

Fixed-income desks trade bonds, currencies and commodities. Goldman’s brought in $3.47 billion, below the $3.72 billion estimate. The firm cited lower revenue in mortgages, credit and interest-rate products.

Investment banking fees rose 21% to $3.22 billion.

As a result, Goldman earned $17.01 per share, up from $12.25 a year earlier and above the $13.08 consensus.

Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS), which reports on Wednesday, rose 2.1%.

Equities revenue rose 72% at Goldman, 49% at JPMorgan and 21% at Wells Fargo. Equities produced about 34% of Goldman’s revenue, against about 10% at JPMorgan and 2% at Wells Fargo.

Fixed-income revenue was flat at Goldman, fell 4% at JPMorgan and fell 7% at Wells Fargo.

Read Also: Micron, SanDisk Look Cheaper by the Day: Here’s the Catch

JPMorgan Missed Estimates but Raised Its Outlook

JPMorgan earned $15.3 billion, or $5.57 per share, up 6% from a year earlier.

The result included $658 million of net losses on investment securities, which cut earnings by 18 cents per share. Excluding that item, earnings were $5.75 per share, below the $5.90 consensus.

Equities revenue of $4.95 billion beat the $4.47 billion estimate. Yet, fixed-income revenue of $5.37 billion missed the $6 billion estimate.

Chief Executive Jamie Dimon said client activity "did moderate somewhat during the quarter."

Meanwhile, the bank raised its outlook. It now expects about $106.2 billion of net interest income in 2026.

For 2027, its central case is about $107 billion excluding its markets unit, up from about $97.2 billion this year.

Wells Fargo Beat on Profit and Missed on Revenue

Wells Fargo earned $1.87 per share, up 13% from a year earlier and 2 cents above consensus.

However, revenue of $21.87 billion missed the $22.31 billion estimate. Net interest income of $12.52 billion came in below the $12.59 billion expected.

Chief Executive Charlie Scharf said growth was "partially offset by lower revenue from our venture capital investments" and by lower lease income after the sale of its rail car leasing business.

headline: Paul Tudor Jones Says Oil Can Rally Another $25, Warns 2027 Will Be 'Really Challenging' for Stocks
summary: Paul Tudor Jones sees oil rising another $20 to $25 a barrel and warns 2027 could be a difficult year for stocks.
content_html:
Billionaire investor Paul Tudor Jones is betting oil could rise another $25 a barrel and warning that 2027 could be a “really, really challenging” year for stocks.

“Long oil, bullish on oil, I think it can rally another 20 or 25 bucks,” the Tudor Investment Corp. founder told CNBC Tuesday.

Asked how stocks would react, he replied: “Well, it’ll hate it. Absolutely totally hate it.”

Why Jones Is Bullish on Oil

Jones suspects President Donald Trump could take a tougher approach to Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. If a softer solution existed, he argued, it would likely have emerged by now.

“It’s kind of like the sword of Damocles sitting over the oil market post the midterms,” Jones said, acknowledging he had no inside knowledge of Trump’s plans.

Trump said last Thursday the U.S. would not attack Iran before the elections, while Tehran has been preparing for renewed hostilities.

WTI crude traded near $94 Tuesday. A $20-to-$25 increase would take it to roughly $114-$119, although Jones did not specify a benchmark or deadline.

On Kalshi, traders put the chance of WTI settling above $115 before December 31 at around 33%, and above $120 at 26%.

Kalshi and Benzinga have an existing data collaboration agreement.

A Strong Fourth Quarter Before a Tough 2027?

Jones sees a strong fourth-quarter rally as “very possible” based on historical midterm-election patterns, which often see stocks bottom in late October or early November.

But he compared today’s AI-driven, “two-speed” market to 1999, when technology stocks surged before the dot-com crash.

“2027 is going to be really, really challenging for the stock market,” he warned.

His concern is less about valuations than about the supply of shares. Buybacks and acquisitions have supported stocks for years by reducing available shares, but IPOs and insider sales could reverse that trend.

“You’ve probably got the most negative flow picture for the U.S. stock market that we’ve had say since 2002,” Jones said.

Jones cited SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), which went public in June but still has billions of shares held by insiders and early investors restricted from sale until 2027.

He also pointed to potential IPOs from Anthropic and OpenAI. Jones fears the combination of new listings and insider share sales could overwhelm investor demand, pushing stock prices lower.

Goldman Sachs forecasts $600 billion in new stock issuance next year, while another $1.7 trillion in previously restricted shares could become eligible for sale. The bank says the resulting increase in stock supply could be the largest since 2000.

However, Goldman expects $1.7 trillion in corporate buybacks and believes many newly unlocked shares won’t actually be sold. Unlike Jones, the bank expects the stock market rally to continue.

The United States Oil Fund (NYSE:USO) rose about 0.7% late Tuesday morning, while SpaceX shares fell nearly 4% and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) edged lower.

headline: Ray Dalio Warns US Debt Crisis Could Deepen as $2.1T in New Treasury Supply Hits Market: 'Credit Market Players Call That a Death Spiral'
summary: Ray Dalio warns US debt faces a 'death spiral' as Treasury supply overwhelms demand, spiking bond yields despite $6B in government buybacks.
content_html:
Investor Ray Dalio warned that the United States faces a “death spiral” due to an oversupply of government debt. This structural imbalance is materializing as the U.S. Treasury struggles to contain rising yields despite escalating its bond buyback operations.

Supply Overwhelms Demand

Dalio outlined that countries go broke when the supply of debt surpasses demand and when debt service payments rise enough to “painfully squeeze out other spending.” He noted that both conditions are currently occurring in the U.S.

According to Dalio, increased debt pushes yields higher, which raises interest expenses and deficits, directly requiring even more debt issuance. Credit market participants refer to this compounding cycle as a “death spiral.”

Read Also: Scott Bessent Says ‘I Am the House Now’ and Dares Traders to Bet Against Him — Wall Street Fires Back With ‘Activist Treasury’ Label

The Bond Market Fights the Treasury

Dalio’s warnings align with recent Treasury market friction. In September, the U.S. Treasury tripled its long-term bond buyback operations to a $6 billion maximum to support market liquidity.

Despite this intervention, the 10-year Treasury yields climbed to multi-year highs. Market commentators like The Kobeissi Letter noted that “the bond market is quite literally fighting the US Treasury,” warning that consumers and borrowers are “in for a rude awakening” if yields continue their ascent past 5%.

Corporate Debt and Equities Face Pressure

Dalio projects that the federal government will issue $2.1 trillion in net new marketable debt over the full year of 2026. Furthermore, corporate debt and equity issuance are surging simultaneously, driven largely by artificial intelligence capital expenditures.

Dalio expects this combined wave of government and corporate issuance to create “too much supply of financial assets (both debt and equity) relative to the demand for it.”

While the economy is currently in a “mid-cycle” phase where rates have not yet crashed asset prices, Dalio anticipates that these sustained supply imbalances will eventually lead to economic weakness and negatively impact equity markets.

How Have the Stock and Bond Markets Performed?

At the last check, the 10-year Treasury bond yielded 5.20%, the 2-year Treasury bond yielded 4.78%, and the 30-year Treasury yielded 5.55%.

On long-term equity returns, Siegel wrote that with the S&P 500 trading around 19 times earnings, the inverse P/E suggests roughly a 5.5% long-term real return, and he raised his estimate of long-term real equity returns to approximately 5.5%–6.5%. He said, “Higher rates are not necessarily bearish for stocks if those rates reflect stronger productivity and economic growth.”

Siegel said equities can continue to move higher if yields stabilize and growth expectations remain intact, and he flagged a risk he is monitoring: “The real danger would be a sudden technological breakthrough that makes a large portion of the current spending on data centers and compute obsolete.” He added, “But there is no evidence of that today.”

headline: Wall Street’s ‘Last Men Standing’: The Mag 7 Are Propping Up the S&P 500, Then Why Are Your ETFs at Risk?
summary: The Mag 7 are propping up the S&P 500 as market breadth weakens. Here’s why SPY and QQQ investors may face hidden concentration risks.
content_html:
The S&P 500 has gained approximately 14% in 2026, yet more than 40% of its constituent stocks have declined this year, according to Reuters.

The median S&P 500 stock has gained just 4%, while fewer than half of its constituents are trading above their 200-day moving averages, masking growing weakness beneath the surface.

As more index constituents struggle, the Magnificent Seven — a small group of U.S. mega-cap technology companies — remains the critical pillar of support, raising questions about how diversified investors really are when they own broad-market ETFs.

Read Also: S&P 500—What Happens In Q4 After A Negative September?

BTIG Warns Mag 7 Is The Market’s ‘Last Man Standing’

In a warning highlighted by ZeroHedge, BTIG chief market technician Jonathan Krinsky, in his technical note named “Last Man Standing,” cautioned that the Magnificent Seven’s continued strength has become a key support for the broader market.

That concentration extends directly into ETF portfolios. The Magnificent Seven accounted for approximately 34.8% of the S&P 500’s market capitalization as of Oct. 13, according to historical index-weight data.

That means investors in market-cap-weighted funds already have substantial exposure to Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA), Apple Inc (NASDAQ:AAPL), Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon.com, Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Meta Platforms, Inc (NASDAQ:META) and Tesla, Inc (NASDAQ:TSLA), even without buying a dedicated technology or AI fund.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) provides broad exposure to the index, but its market-cap-weighting methodology gives the largest companies disproportionate influence over returns. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) offers another route into mega-cap growth stocks, potentially adding to concentration when held alongside an S&P 500 fund. Meanwhile, the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (BATS:MAGS) provides more direct exposure to the group.

Can Equal-Weight ETFs Offer an Alternative?

Investors seeking to reduce their dependence on mega-cap leaders could consider the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP). By assigning approximately equal weights to S&P 500 constituents at rebalancing, RSP spreads out the influence of the largest companies and increases exposure to smaller index members.

However, equal weighting is not automatically a safer bet. RSP can lag when mega-cap leaders continue outperforming and carries different sector-allocation and rebalancing risks.

Why Market Breadth Matters For ETF Investors

The bigger question is whether the S&P 500’s resilience reflects broad corporate strength or the performance of a handful of dominant companies. If the Magnificent Seven lose momentum before the rest of the market recovers, index funds could come under pressure despite their apparent diversification.

With market breadth weakening, investors may need to look beyond headline index returns to understand the concentration risk embedded in their ETF portfolios.

headline: Hot Inflation Flips Fed’s October Rate Odds: Economists Warn About ‘Debasement’ Risk
summary: Hot September CPI flipped Fed October hike odds to 54%. Economists Robin Brooks, LPL and Oxford Economics warn of debasement risk if the Fed waits.
content_html:
On Tuesday, the script for the Federal Reserve’s October meeting looked settled. Policymakers would hold rates, wait for more data and let the midterm elections pass.

On Wednesday morning, a hotter-than-expected September consumer price index rewrote it.

Traders now see a 54% chance that the Fed raises rates at its Oct. 28 meeting.

A day earlier the chance was 20.7%, and a week ago it was 24.1%, according to 30-day fed funds futures tracked by CME FedWatch tool.

The economists reacting to the report are warning about more than one meeting.

They are talking about debasement. That is the relentless loss of the dollar’s purchasing power when a central bank lets inflation run.

The September CPI Report Beat Forecasts Where It Matters

The consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.6% in September after 0.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. That matched forecasts.

The annual rate climbed to 3.7% from 3.4%, above the 3.6% economists expected.

Gasoline did much of the work.

Pump prices rose 9.1% in the month and accounted for more than half of the overall increase. The energy index gained 5.2%.

However, the number that moved markets was core inflation.

Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% in September against a 0.2% forecast.

The annual core rate rose to 2.6% from 2.4%, above the 2.5% consensus.

The gains were spread widely.

Recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, medical care and apparel all rose in the month, according to the BLS.

Why Economists Are Talking About Debasement

The debasement argument works in steps.

Prices rise faster than the Fed’s 2% target. If the central bank holds rates anyway, real interest rates (interest rates minus inflation) fall.

Savers then earn less, in real terms, for holding dollars. Some of that money moves into assets that cannot be printed, such as gold and other precious metals.

Robin Brooks, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, put it bluntly on X.

"Not a good CPI number," Brooks wrote. He noted that a spike in wireless services had driven last month’s core reading, which gave the Fed "a reasonable excuse" to pause.

"But today’s reading puts an October hike back on the table. If the Fed doesn’t hike, debasement wins."

In a second post, Brooks pointed to the political calendar. The odds of a hike would be higher, he wrote, if the October meeting were not "right before the midterms." The elections take place on Nov. 3.

"If the Fed doesn’t hike, it’ll be a big catalyst for gold and precious metals to take off," Brooks added.

Inflation Is No Longer Just an Energy Story

Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial, said the report shows price pressures moving beyond fuel.

"Inflation pressures are broadening beyond energy and are now filtering into other categories, including apparel and autos," Roach said.

He noted that new and used vehicle prices have now risen for three straight months, reversing the trend from earlier this year.

"As the Middle East conflict continues, inflation pressures are becoming more widespread across other categories," he added.

Nancy Vanden Houten, lead U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, pointed to an unusual source of pressure: technology.

Core prices rose with "widespread gains, including in sectors like computers and smartphones, as price pressures related to the AI building spillover to consumer goods," she said.

Oxford Economics expects a hike this month.

"The larger than expected increase in the core CPI in September increases the odds that the Federal Reserve raises rates at its meeting later this month, which is our forecast," Vanden Houten said.

Bond Traders Moved First

Treasury yields rose across the curve on Wednesday.

The two-year yield, the maturity most sensitive to Fed policy, climbed 10 basis points to 4.90%.

The 10-year yield rose about 7 basis points to 5.29%. That is still below the 5.34% it touched earlier this month, its highest level since 2002. The 30-year yield added 4 basis points to 5.60%.

The U.S. Dollar Index, which measures the dollar against six major currencies, gained 0.5% to 102.73.

Gold – as tracked by SPDR Gold Shares (NYSE:GLD) – fell 1.5% to about $4,100 an ounce, and silver dropped 3.7% to $56.95.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) slipped 0.2% to around $82,870.

The S&P 500 – tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) – sunk 0.7%, minutes after the open in New York.

headline: Top Economist Warns Recession Odds Are ‘Over 50-50’ as AI Bubble and Tightening Financial Conditions Raise Alarm: ‘Bubble Is Never in the Technology, But in the…’
summary: Economist David Rosenberg warns of a market bubble and puts recession odds at over 50-50 as financial conditions tighten.
content_html:
Rosenberg Research Founder and President David Rosenberg stated the probability of a recession in the next year is greater than 50%, attributing the risk to tightening financial conditions, declining real wages, and a market bubble driven by investors rather than technology.

Market Bubble and Tightening Conditions

Speaking on CNBC, Rosenberg warned of building momentum in current market narratives. “I believe that we are in a bubble,” Rosenberg said, clarifying that “the bubble is never in the technology, but it’s in investor behavior.”

He noted that market stresses typically originate in the credit market. Rosenberg highlighted that broader financial conditions—including the dollar, credit spreads, equity and debt cost of capital, and the general level of interest rates—have “tightened 140 basis points just in the past three months.”

When asked directly to make a call on an impending economic downturn, Rosenberg said, “I put the odds of recession at over 50-50, and I’ll leave it at that.”

Read Also: BofA's Brian Moynihan Downplays Inflation Concerns on US Economy, Says it is 'Resilient and Growing' — Here’s What Clients Are Doing

Inflation and the Labor Market

Rosenberg’s comments coincided with the release of the September 2026 Consumer Price Index (CPI) report, which showed the all-items index increased 0.6% over the month and 3.7% over the last 12 months.

Rosenberg called the data “not a good CPI number,” while pointing to a 0.5% monthly decline in real average hourly earnings, arguing that price shocks were "hitting a wall" in the labor market.

He warned that this dynamic will result in “negative real wages,” which will sequentially lead to “negative real consumer spending.”

Federal Reserve Policy and Recession Risks

According to Rosenberg, current inflation is not a “homegrown demand-led” issue, and the economy is not in a state where the Federal Reserve “can just adjust the temperature and get to a soft landing.”

He cautioned that the Federal Reserve’s ongoing tightening policy to fight a supply shock “won’t be able to do that without generating recession,” an outcome he believes is not currently on the market’s mind.
