headline: Billionaire John Arnold Warns Fed Rate Hikes ‘May Be Counterproductive,’ Says ‘Will Do Little to Lower Inflation’
summary: Billionaire John Arnold warns Fed rate hikes may be 'counterproductive' in fighting inflation, arguing higher borrowing costs choke supply.
content_html:
Billionaire and former hedge fund manager John Arnold said that Federal Reserve interest rate increases do little to lower inflation and act as a counterproductive economic measure.

The Supply-Side Argument

Arnold outlined his macroeconomic view in a social media post, writing that he is “increasingly partial to the argument that increases in the fed funds rate will do little to lower inflation, and may be counterproductive.”

He argued that higher borrowing costs raise business operating expenses, some of which is subsequently passed along to consumers.

Furthermore, Arnold noted that higher rates hurt “supply-side solutions in housing, energy, autos, and other capital-intensive industries.” He added that an economy heavily dominated by services is less sensitive to rate changes, while energy markets remain “highly inelastic and rate changes can’t alleviate the current supply shock.”

Arnold characterized the central bank’s approach as a “blunt interest rate policy” that has repeatedly demonstrated flaws in both stimulating and suppressing inflation.

Read Also: BofA's Brian Moynihan Downplays Inflation Concerns on US Economy, Says it is 'Resilient and Growing' — Here’s What Clients Are Doing

Housing Shortages and Inflation

Economist Jason Furman challenged Arnold’s thesis, arguing that higher interest rates reduce consumer demand long before they reduce supply, which acts as a deflationary force.

Arnold responded that while he agreed on the concept of a time lag, the current state of the real estate market illustrates his concern. He noted that a recent boom in multifamily construction caused rents to stagnate or decline due to an influx of new supply.

However, Arnold warned that multifamily development is “frozen right now because of rates,” adding that this halt in construction will “fuel higher inflation in the future.”

Wall Street Perspectives

Arnold’s concerns regarding borrowing costs intersect with broader capital market observations from major banking executives. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink recently noted that the U.S. faces “structurally higher interest rates for longer” due to record federal deficit financing and private infrastructure capital demands.

Similarly, Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf stated during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that inflation and higher interest rates continue to act as headwinds. Scharf noted that the longer these elevated rates persist, the more pressure they place on commercial clients attempting to finance capital-intensive projects.

summary: Mike Novogratz said an AI catastrophe would send the Nasdaq down 30%, and that stopping the data center buildout would slow the economy.
content_html:
Galaxy Digital Inc. (NASDAQ:GLXY) CEO Mike Novogratz warned that stopping the artificial intelligence data-center buildout would slow the U.S. economy, while saying a hypothetical "AI catastrophe" could send the Nasdaq crashing.

Data Centers Are Holding Up the Economy

Speaking on the ‘All Things Markets’ podcast with SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci, released on Thursday, Novogratz was asked about BlackRock Inc. (NYSE:BLK) CEO Larry Fink’s warning that a data center moratorium could spark a recession.

Novogratz agreed the economy leans heavily on AI spending, but said he isn’t sure that stopping the buildout would bring a recession.

He doesn’t expect the buildout to stop, but said that if it did, “you’re going to see a slowdown” in the economy.

Novogratz also warned of the downside: “I think if there was a catastrophe, an AI catastrophe, Nasdaq would be down 30%.”

Read Also: Anthropic IPO Could Come in ‘Weeks, Not Months’ — Top Hedge Fund Manager Sees $500 Billion Demand, Draws Parallels With SpaceX

AI Financing Is Pressuring Yields

Fink estimated that the U.S. would need “$7 to $9 trillion over the course of a number of years” for power and data centers.

Competition between private capital and record government borrowing, he said, means “structurally higher interest rates for longer.”

The biggest spenders are already borrowing heavily.

Five of the biggest hyperscalers issued roughly $200 billion of investment-grade debt in the first half of 2026, almost twice that of all of 2025, according to iShares.

Novogratz said a hotter-than-expected “ugly” inflation print, the Federal Reserve’s interest rate hikes, and heavy hyperscaler funding have left fixed income uncertain, and “it looks like that’s finally kicked the equity market in the stomach.”

A Chip Rout Brings Bonds Relief

headline: AI Bubble Worries Hand Long-Term Treasuries Their Best Week Since March 2025
summary: AI bubble worries lifted the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF 2.55% this week, its best week since April 2025, despite hot inflation data.
content_html:
Wall Street spent the week watching inflation. The bond market saw a bigger shark.

Two inflation reports came in hotter than expected. That is normally the signal for bond investors to sell.

Instead, they bought long-dated Treasuries at the fastest pace in a year and a half.

The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:TLT) rose 2.55% this week to $79.97 by Friday morning.

It is on pace for its best week since March 2025. Just nine days ago, on Oct. 7, the fund traded at $76.43, the lowest price in its history going back to 2002.

So why buy bonds when inflation is heating up? The answer is artificial intelligence.

Hot Inflation Should Have Sunk Long-Term Treasuries

On Wednesday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said consumer prices rose 0.6% in September. That pushed annual inflation to 3.7% from 3.4%, above the 3.6% economists expected.

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, rose to 2.6% annually, still topping the Fed’s 2% target.

Thursday’s producer price report was hotter still. Headline producer inflation soared to 6.3% year over year, the highest print since December 2022.

On a monthly basis, prices jumped 1.3%, more than double economists’ 0.5% forecast.

The first reaction followed the script. The 10-year Treasury yield briefly climbed above 5.32% after the consumer price report.

Then it reversed.

By Friday, the 10-year yield was at 5.10%, down 14 basis points from last Friday. The 30-year yield fell 16 basis points to 5.44%, after touching 5.73% last week, its highest level since 2001.

Bond prices move opposite to yields, which is why TLT rises when long-term yields fall.

Read Also: Chip Meltdown Hits Micron, SanDisk and SK Hynix: $1 Trillion Vanishes From Memory Makers

The Bond Market Is Pricing a Slower AI Boom

The selling that mattered this week hit AI debt, not Treasuries.

On Thursday, CoreWeave Inc.’s (NASDAQ:CRWV) bonds due 2032 fell below 80 cents on the dollar, with yields above 15%.

CoreWeave’s five-year credit default swaps rose to 1,194.5 basis points, a record intraday high, according to ICE Data Services data reported by Bloomberg.

At that level, the swaps imply a more than 60% chance of default within five years.

Read Also: CoreWeave’s Bonds Hit 15% Yield: This Analyst Still Sees 105% Upside for the Stock

On Wednesday, Gartner, one of the world’s largest technology research and advisory firms, estimated that AI data center operators need $8.5 trillion in cumulative revenue through 2030 to cover their spending, financing costs and a 12% return on invested capital. It forecasts no more than $3.6 trillion.

As a result, Gartner said more than $3.5 trillion of planned AI infrastructure spending is exposed to write-downs.

The chain works in steps:

  • The AI buildout has become a major engine of U.S. growth.
  • If lenders demand more to fund it, some projects get delayed.
  • Less investment means slower growth.
  • Slower growth means lower long-term yields.

"When expected activity in AI declines, yields decline," Dennis DeBusschere, analyst at 22V Research, said in a note Thursday.

Tech stocks felt it.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq 100, is down 3.1% this week.

The Long End Is Doing the Work, Not the Fed

The rally was concentrated in long-dated bonds. The 2-year yield, which tracks expectations for Federal Reserve policy, slipped only 2 basis points to 4.74%.

Meanwhile, traders have stepped back from an immediate rate hike.

Fed funds futures price in a 14.9% chance that the Fed will raise rates at its Oct. 28 meeting, down from 19.5% a week ago, according to CME FedWatch.

In other words, the bond rally bets on slower growth, not cheaper money.

One Good Week After a Long Slide

Not everyone is ready to call the AI spending cycle over.

"We are nowhere near ready to write off the AI investment boom," Ed Yardeni said in a note.

He noted that Amazon.com Inc., Alphabet Inc., Meta Platforms Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Oracle Corp. are expected to spend a combined $892 billion this year and $1.1 trillion next year.

TLT is still down 8.5% since January.

One strong week does not reverse a slide in long-term bonds that began in the fall of 2024. For now, it shows bond investors fear an AI slowdown more than inflation.

headline: October Rate-Hike Odds Collapse as Warsh Keeps His Cards Close but AI Transition Looms
summary: October Fed hike odds fell to 14% after Kevin Warsh avoided signaling another increase and emphasized AI-driven growth
content_html:
Despite surging inflation, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh offered no hint of another interest-rate hike at an IMF event Friday, sending October hike odds tumbling as he talked up artificial intelligence’s potential to transform the economy.

Wednesday’s hot inflation report had sent CME FedWatch’s October hike odds soaring from 21% to 54%, making another increase more likely than not.

But those expectations quickly faded. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said Wednesday that further hikes were likely, but there was no urgency to act in October.

By the time Warsh spoke Friday, the odds had already retreated to around 28%. His refusal to signal another increase helped push them down to approximately 15%.

On Polymarket, traders now give an October quarter-point hike just 14% odds, compared with 87% for no change. The market has attracted $43.5 million in trading volume.

But traders aren’t ruling out another hike altogether. Polymarket’s December market puts the probability of a quarter-point increase at 79%, suggesting investors expect the Fed to delay its next move rather than abandon it.

The Fed’s Inflation Dilemma

“I don’t prejudge meetings,” Warsh said Friday during a discussion with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva in Bangkok.

He refused to preview the Fed’s remaining decisions this year, saying economic developments had broadly matched policymakers’ expectations since September’s rate increase.

Consumer prices rose 3.7% annually in September, while producer prices jumped 1.3% during the month, the largest increase since March 2022.

The Fed raised its benchmark rate to 3.75%–4.00% last month, but September’s weak jobs report, showing just 29,000 positions added, complicates the case for another immediate increase.

S&P 500 futures rose around 0.2% following Warsh’s remarks, pointing to a firmer open for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY).

Chang Wei Liang, a macro strategist at DBS Bank, said Warsh’s optimism about AI-driven productivity could help ease inflation expectations and “temper fears of back-to-back Fed rate hikes.”

AI Boom Pushes Up Tech Prices

Warsh described AI as “probably the most consequential change” to the US and global economies in his lifetime.

He expects the technology to deliver substantial productivity gains and create wealth, but acknowledged that spending is boosting economic demand before those benefits materialize.

He warned the transition could be “very bumpy,” with employment effects over the next 12 to 18 months uncertain.

A San Francisco Fed report published Thursday found annual inflation in information-processing equipment reached 13% in August, its highest reading since records began in the 1960s.

Researchers linked the increase to AI-driven demand for chips, pushing up computer and smartphone prices, although they found little evidence of inflation spilling into other sectors.

Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) raised MacBook prices by as much as $300 in June and increased iPad prices amid AI-driven memory shortages.

headline: S&P 500 Index Outlook: Strong Earnings Meet AI Rout, $110 Oil Prices
summary: The S&P 500 Index is in a tight range as the ongoing earnings season fails to offset the AI rout and the soaring oil prices.
content_html:
The S&P 500 (SPX) has pulled back this month after hitting key resistance at 7,817, as investors weigh a strong earnings season, rising crude oil prices, and elevated US Treasury yields. The index is now 2.45% below its all-time high.

Earnings Season Has Started Well, But Risks Remain

The S&P 500 Index retreated even as major American companies posted strong results. FactSet (NYSE:FDS) data shows that 9% of index constituents have reported so far, with average earnings growth of 29%. If that rate holds, it will mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%.

The final growth figure will likely come in higher, since most technology companies have yet to report. Companies due to release results in the coming weeks include SpaceX, GE Aerospace, Netflix, Meta Platforms, and T-Mobile. For comparison, S&P 500 earnings growth topped 50% in the second quarter.

The challenge, however, is that the index is facing other challenges, including the rising oil prices as the crisis in the Middle East escalates. Brent has jumped to $110, while the West Texas Intermediate has crossed the $100 level. Gasoline and diesel prices have continued rising. 

Read Also: CoreWeave Stock Crashes 20% This Week, but JPMorgan Says Wall Street Is Overreacting

These numbers mean that consumer and producer inflation will remain elevated. Data released this week showed that consumer inflation jumped 3.7% in September, moving further from the Fed’s target of 2.0%. 

Higher inflation means that the Fed may be forced to hike interest rates later this year. All this is happening as US bond yields remain at an elevated level, with the five-year hovering at its highest level in nearly two decades.

The index is also confronting the rising fears that the AI bubble may burst soon. Anthropic’s valuation has been slashed after the company’s third-quarter revenue growth came short of expectations. OpenAI’s annualized revenue was about $20 billion lower than expected. In a report this week, Gartner estimated that AI infrastructure companies will have substantial impairments in the next few years.

S&P 500 Index Has Hit a Crucial Resistance

SPX Index chart | Source: TradingView

Technically, the SPX Index has hit a major barrier at 7,817, its highest point on August 13 and on October 8. It has formed a double-top pattern and a neckline at 7,512, its lowest level on September 16. This pattern often leads to a bearish reversal.

The two lines of the MACD indicator have formed a bearish crossover and are pointing downwards. These technicals suggest that it may drop further in the near term. If this happens, it may drop to the neckline of 7,512 points followed by the 200-day moving average of 7,312.

The Fear Is ‘Overdone’

The Kobeissi Letter took the opposite approach to the calls for a Black Monday crash, posting on X a chart that tracks every time the term has trended since May 2025.

In an analysis published last week, the firm argued that the S&P 500 is in a “stealth” bear market “within a bull market.”

It said that 84% of the index’s stocks trade at least 10% below their record highs, while just 10 stocks have driven 70% of its gain since the March low.

Without the Iran war, the index could, it contends, be above 9,000.

headline: Michael Burry Warns Stocks Could Face 15-20 Years of Poor Real Returns: ‘Speculation Has Overrun Investing’
summary: Michael Burry warns stocks could face a 15-20 year period of poor returns. What history reveals about the last three prolonged bear markets.
content_html:
Investor Michael Burry states that stock indices are overstretched and warns investors to prepare for a potential 15- to 20-year span of low or negative real returns. He bases this assessment on historical market data, inflation metrics, and comparisons to three past market cycles.

Market Speculation and Overstretched Indices

Burry, writing in an X article on Oct. 18, noted that the S&P 500 reached a record high on Oct. 6 without significant trading volume. He contrasts the modern investing environment, where trades are free and information is ubiquitous, with the 1980s when stock quotes were found in newspapers and brokers charged high fees.

Today, Burry observes that the current market mantras are “Stonks go UP!” and “Buy the Dip, or BTFD.” However, he counters this optimism, stating, “Speculation has overrun investing, stock indices appear overstretched, and inflation is rearing its head again.” Consequently, he warns that “another 15-20 year period of negative or little real returns in stocks is in the offing.”

Read Also: Michael Burry Warns Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac Could Become ‘Worthless’ as Trump-Era Gains Collapse Under Fresh Pressure

Three Historical Bear Markets

While modern algorithmic traders excel at technical analysis, Burry notes that “what they do not generally do is history.” He outlines three prolonged periods of poor inflation-adjusted returns to demonstrate what a long-term bear market looks like.

From 1966 to 1982, the S&P 500’s inflation-adjusted price fell about 53%, excluding dividends. During the Great Depression era from 1929 to 1949, the real price return was negative 58%. More recently, from the 2000 market top through the 2011 trough, the S&P 500’s real price return was roughly negative 40%.

A ‘Very Long Wait’

Burry acknowledges that reinvesting dividends softens these declines. With dividends reinvested, the 1966 to 1982 loss shrinks to roughly 10%, the 2000 to 2011 loss drops to 25%, and a 1929 investor would be ahead by 1949.

However, he cautions that typical holding periods and life stages often prevent perfect dividend compounding. He concludes that “it has always been, one way or another, a very long wait rather than a wipeout for the patient holder through these three real bear markets.”

headline: Kevin Warsh Says 'I Have Failed,' Admitting That He Neglected Bank Supervision in First 148 Days
summary: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh admits he neglected bank supervision in his 148 days, promising to shift focus to regulation in his next 100 days.
content_html:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh stated that he failed to adequately focus on non-monetary policy functions, including bank supervision, during his first 148 days in office.

Warsh Admits Neglect

Speaking at a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva during the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings on Oct. 16, Warsh admitted that his initial tenure disproportionately favored monetary policy over other mandates.

“I’d say where I would say I’ve failed in my first 148 days is mostly because of all of you and the people that are on the end of this camera. They’re all focused on monetary policy,” Warsh stated.

Warsh highlighted that “75% of the people at the Federal Reserve” do not work directly on monetary policy, according to his remarks. Instead, these employees manage functions given to the central bank by Congress, including “supervision and regulation, payment systems, consumer and community affairs,” he said.

Read Also: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh Keeps October Rate Hike in Limbo, Warns AI Could Trigger a ‘Very Bumpy’ Transition: ‘No Free Riders’

Prioritizing Institutional Credibility

Warsh confessed that he had not communicated his support effectively to those operational divisions. “I haven’t been as good as I need to be to make sure they know I care about their issues everybody as much as I care about the conduct of monetary policy,” Warsh noted.

The Fed Chairman emphasized that “the head of the Fed needs to be the head of all parts of the Fed.” He warned that the central bank’s true power derives from its institutional credibility rather than just monetary tools.

“And so whatever any part of the Federal Reserve does, if they slip up, if they stumble on supervision or on payments, that reflects on our institutional credibility,” he explained.

The Next Hundred Days

To correct this imbalance, Warsh outlined a shift in his upcoming leadership agenda. “So my next hundred days I’m going to try to give equal focus those other parts of the business because they matter too,” he declared.

Warsh concluded that leading the central bank requires questioning the status quo across all departments. “When you take over a position like this you need to lead all of it and you need to love the institution enough across everything they do to go back and ask first principles instead of will we do it this way because that’s how we’ve always done it,” he stated.

headline: Top Economist Warns US Is Headed for a ‘Fiscal Reckoning’ as $1.99 Trillion Deficit Pushes Interest Payments Above Defense Spending
summary: The United States government recorded a budget deficit of $1.992 trillion for fiscal year 2026, with federal interest payments exceeding defense spending. Moody’s Analytics Chief Economist Mark Zandi stated this
content_html:
The United States government recorded a budget deficit of $1.992 trillion for fiscal year 2026, with federal interest payments exceeding defense spending. Moody’s Analytics Chief Economist Mark Zandi stated this trajectory moves the country toward a “fiscal reckoning.”

Budget and Outlay Data

The Treasury Department reported that the $1.992 trillion deficit for the period ending Sept. 30 resulted from $7.396 trillion in total outlays and $5.403 trillion in total receipts. Zandi noted the deficit represents more than 6% of the Gross Domestic Product. The government spent $1.052 trillion on net interest during the fiscal year. This outpaced the $965 billion spent on national defense.

The primary budget deficit, which excludes interest payments, reached nearly 3% of GDP. Zandi called this figure “eye-popping.” He stated that because unemployment remains low, the primary budget should be in surplus or balanced. He attributed the $1 trillion in interest payments to the “ballooning debt load.”

Read Also: BlackRock CEO Larry Fink Says $40 Trillion US Debt ‘Will Not Be as Consequential’ If AI Drives 3% GDP Growth

Treasury Yields and Market Reaction

Zandi observed that global investors “appear to be demanding a higher rate to compensate for the mounting risk.” The 10-year Treasury yield rose by about one percentage point this year. Zandi stated this increase is among the largest of any major economy. He noted that nations with the heaviest interest burdens experienced the biggest yield increases.

Cycle of Debt

Zandi cautioned that a “vicious cycle threatens to take hold” within the economy. He explained that higher rates add to the debt load and interest payments, which subsequently pushes rates higher.

He acknowledged that other countries face similar issues, but he emphasized the U.S. is the most important because U.S. Treasuries act as the global benchmark.

How Have the Bond and Stock Markets Performed?

At the last check, the 30-year Treasury bond yielded 5.41%, the 10-year Treasury bond was at 5.07%, and the two-year bond was at 4.73%.

headline: 'Of Course' Bitcoin Could Grow to $50 Trillion, Jordi Visser Says: But How?
summary: Jordi Visser says Bitcoin could reach a $50 trillion valuation as fund leverage unwinds and asset tokenization expands.
content_html:
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) could eventually reach a $50 trillion valuation, macro investor Jordi Visser says, as hedge funds unwind leverage while Bitcoin quietly outperforms every major asset class.

Why Visser Says Hedge Funds Are Blowing Up, Not AI

Visser said on Anthony Pompliano‘s podcast Saturday that the market selloff tied to AI stocks has nothing to do with AI itself failing.

He compared it instead to 1998’s Long-Term Capital Management collapse, arguing leveraged hedge funds, not the AI buildout, are the real source of stress.

His evidence: Lone Pine Capital was up more than 40% through September before giving back the entire gain, proof in Visser’s view that something structural is breaking in how funds use leverage rather than any flaw in AI’s growth story.

Visser also pushed back on dot-com comparisons for AI infrastructure companies.

CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), he said, differs fundamentally from that era since its revenue comes from Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Meta (NASDAQ:META) and OpenAI rather than speculative telecom debt. 

He argued AI’s eventual earnings remain inevitable because demand for compute keeps outpacing supply, even when individual stock valuations overshoot in the short term.

Why Bitcoin Keeps Holding While Everything Else Wobbles

Visser said Bitcoin has traded between $82,000 and $85,000 for four months while the S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY) and Nasdaq sat flat and bonds declined, a sign he reads as Bitcoin acting as a safe landing spot as capital flees riskier, leveraged trades. 

He called this “good Sharpe ratio” behavior standing out precisely because so few other assets are generating clean returns right now.

Asked whether Bitcoin could realistically reach a $50 trillion valuation, Visser said “of course it could,” pointing to roughly $900 trillion in largely illiquid global assets that tokenization could eventually unlock into liquid, tradable form. 

He argued the same logic applies to Bitcoin that Elon Musk has floated for SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX): as a much larger pool of capital turns liquid, a single asset’s value can scale right alongside it.

Why Visser Flags November and December as Key Windows

Visser said he expects the next major move higher in both AI stocks and Bitcoin to come around two specific windows: right after hyperscaler earnings reports later this month, and again in December, when many funds stop taking risk for the year. 

He noted that AI-linked long-short positioning on Morgan Stanley’s (NYSE:MS) prime brokerage desk has fallen to the seventh percentile of the past year, suggesting most leveraged risk has already been pulled from the trade.

He downplayed September’s hotter-than-expected CPI print entirely, arguing that inflation readings between 2% and 3.5% have little bearing on markets unless they coincide with actual job losses, which he said remain near historic lows.

headline: You Could Be Right About Valuations But Wrong About Prices
summary:
Five years ago, on October 14, I launched TKer, the newsletter that tells the story of how the stock market usually goes up.



That first year was highlighted by a bear market as the Federal Reserve went to war against
content_html:
Five years ago, on October 14, I launched TKer, the newsletter that tells the story of how the stock market usually goes up.

That first year was highlighted by a bear market as the Federal Reserve went to war against inflation. The S&P 500 fell 19%.

Year two brought an impressive stock market rebound. It began two days after the current bull market started. That year, the S&P ended up 21% higher despite lingering uncertainty.

Year three extended the rally, with the S&P surging an incredible 35%. Interestingly, the average annualized return since TKer’s launch up to that point was an extraordinarily average 9%.

Year four brought political upheaval after the U.S. presidential election, trade wars sparked by new tariffs, volatility in interest rates and currency markets, heightened geopolitical tensions, threats to Federal Reserve independence, and a government shutdown, which added to concerns about the quality of economic data. Yet the stock market repeatedly set new all-time highs, climbing 14% during the period — arguably because earnings were resilient.

📈 Year five saw many of year four’s challenges linger. But one key difference was that the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio was unusually elevated at close to 23x, the highest level since 2020.

In other words, stocks looked expensive when I published my previous annual update.

But as we’ve discussed for years, elevated valuations don’t mean prices are likely to fall soon. We were reminded of this in TKer’s fifth year as the S&P 500 climbed 16%.

TKer Stock Market Truth No. 6 📜

About a year ago, some of Wall Street’s most prominent strategists made a bold prediction: High valuations were justified, and they’ll remain elevated in 2026 as stock prices go higher.

Others argued valuations were a headwind and at risk of contracting, capping price returns.

I’ve written before that P/E ratio forecasts are where Wall Street’s year-end price target calculations often go wrong, mostly because the direction of the ratio is hard to predict over short periods.

But ten months into 2026, P/E ratios have been contracting. Does that mean the bulls were wrong and the skeptics were right?

Sort of, but also not really.

One of this year’s defining market stories has been the aggressive, ongoing upward revisions to earnings forecasts, which have pulled P/E ratios down. This occurred even as stock prices trended higher. Fractions 101: If the denominator (E) rises faster than the numerator (P), then the P/E falls.

This brings us to TKer Stock Market Truth No. 6:

6. Valuations won’t tell you much about next year

There are many valuation methods that’ll help you estimate whether a stock or stock market is cheap or expensive. We won’t go through all of those here.

While valuation methods may tell you something about long-term returns, most tell you almost nothing about where prices are headed in the next 12 months. Over short periods like this, expensive things can get more expensive and cheap things can get cheaper.

It’s worth noting that prices can be cheap or expensive for extended periods of time. In fact, some folks would argue valuations are not mean-reverting.

Expensive stocks often get more expensive. Cheap stocks often get cheaper.

And sometimes prices fall as stocks get more expensive, and prices rise as they get cheaper.

Trading the stock market can be hard. You could’ve been absolutely right if you predicted P/E ratios would contract. But if you used that information to sell stocks, you might’ve made a huge mistake.

headline: Homebuilder Sentiment Hits 2012 Lows As Stocks Trade Like They Did During COVID-19 Pandemic
summary: Builder confidence fell to 29, lowest since 2012, while the XHB/SPY ratio sits near its weakest level since April 2020 as rates top 7%.
content_html:
In April 2020, with most of America locked indoors, the country’s home builders recorded their darkest mood in eight years.

Six years later, with no virus and no lockdown, they feel even worse.

The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI), a monthly survey tracking builder confidence in the market for newly built single-family homes, fell three points to 29 in October.

That is the lowest reading since June 2012, below the 30 recorded in April 2020, and short of the 32 economists expected.

All three components of the main index fell.

Current sales conditions dropped two points to 33, sales expectations for the next six months slid five points to 32, and prospective buyer traffic plunged five points to 18.

The main trigger is the cost of money.

The 30-year fixed mortgage rate averaged 7.40% last week, the highest in nearly three years, according to Freddie Mac.

"Mortgage rates have climbed well above 7% in recent weeks, and higher gas prices and inflation have further weakened buyer traffic across much of the country," NAHB Chairman Bill Owens said.

Chart: Homebuilder Sentiment Sinks Below 2020 Lows, Hitting June 2012 Levels

Builders Are Paying To Keep Buyers

To keep sales moving, builders are giving up margin. In October, 43% of builders cut prices, the highest share during the 2020-2026 period, according to NAHB.

The average cut held at 6% for a seventh straight month.

Meanwhile, 65% of builders used sales incentives, such as mortgage rate buydowns.

It was the 19th straight month that at least 60% of builders have done so.

Labor is a second pressure point. More than one-third of builders reported immigration enforcement activity in their market areas in the past month, according to Owens, causing construction delays.

"Housing remains squeezed by supply-side constraints and significant affordability challenges," NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz said.

"Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines," he added.

Read Also: Chip Stocks Repeated a Lehman-Era Losing Streak: Is The Bottom Now In?

Economists See Little Relief Ahead

Pantheon Macroeconomics’ Oliver Allen said the typical 30-year mortgage rate has jumped to around 7.5%, from roughly 6.6% in early July.

He warned that "if anything—confidence is likely to fall much further over the next month or two, given the recent trends in rates."

Oxford Economics cut its forecasts for housing starts, home sales and home price growth on Monday.

"A median-income household now earns less than three-quarters of what it needs to afford a median-priced home, and the rise in rates this year alone has put homeownership out of reach for another 5 million households," Lead US Economist Nancy Vanden Houten said.

"We don’t expect a meaningful improvement in housing activity until around the end of 2027, when we look for mortgage rates to decline," she added.

XHB/SPY: Back To Pandemic Levels

Wall Street has priced the slowdown in for months.

The SPDR S&P Homebuilders ETF (NYSE:XHB) relative to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) traded at 0.1229 Monday.

That’s slightly above last week’s lows, but the ratio remains at levels last seen during the pandemic crisis.

On Oct. 14, it closed at 0.1206, its lowest level since April 2020.

At its late-September 2024 peak, the same ratio was close to 0.218. Builders have lost roughly 43% of their value relative to the S&P 500 in two years.

Over that stretch, XHB is down 24% while SPY has gained 34%.

This year, the homebuilder ETF is down almost 9% while the S&P 500 tracker is up nearly 12%.

Why Homebuilders Could Become An AI Hedge

One scenario could change that quickly, and it has little to do with housing.

22V Research analyst Dennis DeBusschere said in a Friday note that the artificial intelligence investment boom has crowded out housing.

"Real Private Residential Fixed investment has not contributed to GDP in 4 years as private fixed investment (AI capex) has accelerated," DeBusschere said.

In his view, consumer spending and AI capital spending have pushed U.S. growth well above trend. That has kept 10-year yields high, and high yields are what keep buyers away from new homes.

The logic also works in reverse.

Housing would contribute to economic growth if AI capex suddenly fell. The Fed would cut rates aggressively and 10-year yields would decline, DeBusschere said.

"Long Homebuilders is an interesting AI capex decline hedge,” he added.

headline: TIPS Now Pay 2.8% Above Inflation. Here's The Hurdle That Sets For S&P 500 Investors
summary:
Key Takeaways




The 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) yield closed at 2.78% on Oct. 15, up from 1.71% a year earlier, yet the S&P 500 gained 16.8% in that span.



The index’s forward P/E fell
content_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) yield closed at 2.78% on Oct. 15, up from 1.71% a year earlier, yet the S&P 500 gained 16.8% in that span.
  • The index’s forward P/E fell to 19.0 from 22.4 while forward earnings estimates rose about 38%. Earnings carried the gain.
  • With the earnings yield about 2.5 points above TIPS, each quarter-point rise in real yields is worth roughly 4.5% of index value if estimates stay flat.

On Sept. 17, the morning after the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate for the first time since 2023, the Treasury sold $19 billion of 10-year TIPS at a real yield of 2.653%, the highest for that maturity at auction since October 2008. In theory, that should make stocks harder to own.

But the S&P 500 closed at 7,744.06 on Oct. 15, up 16.8% from a year earlier per FRED index data, even as the 10-year real yield rose from 1.71% to 2.78%, near its highest level since the 2008 financial crisis. Did stock investors ignore the bond market? The arithmetic says no.

The Multiple Shrank 15% And The Index Still Rose 17%

An index price is two numbers multiplied together. One is expected earnings per share; the other is the multiple investors pay for them, and separating them shows a textbook repricing that earnings outran.

FactSet’s Oct. 17, 2025 report put the S&P 500’s forward 12-month P/E at 22.4. Its latest Earnings Insight, dated Oct. 16, 2026, puts it at 19.0, below its five-year average of 19.8.

Dividing price by multiple implies forward earnings of about $296 a share a year ago and $408 now, and a 15% smaller multiple applied to 38% more earnings produces almost exactly the 17% price gain. Rates did bite. The earnings boom bit harder.

Chris Carpentier, a senior investment strategist at State Street Investment Management, reached the same conclusion in a Sept. 21 note. “Markets are still responding to higher discount rates in a manner broadly consistent with financial theory,” he wrote.

Two Measures Of The Cushion Point Different Ways

The equity risk premium (ERP) is the extra annual return investors demand for holding stocks instead of a risk-free bond, and when it runs thin, a modest rate shock can erase months of gains. Nobody observes it directly.

The simplest estimate subtracts the real yield from the forward earnings yield, the inverse of the P/E. At 19.0 times earnings, that yield is 5.26%, or 2.48 percentage points above the TIPS yield, compared with 2.75 points a year earlier, when real yields were more than a full point lower. The cushion narrowed by 0.27.

Aswath Damodaran, a finance professor at NYU Stern, gets a different reading from his cash-flow model. His implied ERP series rose to 4.20% on Oct. 1 from 3.78% a year earlier, even as the Treasury rate he uses climbed to 5.29% from 4.16%. His trailing cash-yield version slipped to 3.70% from 4.01%, closer to Carpentier’s view that the premium “has compressed and remains at lows.”

Forward-earnings measures depend on analysts being right, and cash-yield measures assume the past year repeats; neither shows stocks as cheap relative to TIPS. The method decides the answer.

Two Chipmakers Carry 9 Points Of Earnings Growth

The earnings lift is narrow. FactSet’s blended third-quarter growth rate is 29.0%, but exclude Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) and NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and it falls to 20.0%.

Growth should slow. FactSet consensus projects 16.0% for calendar 2027 but only 2.8% for the second quarter of 2027 as year-ago comparisons stiffen, while sector multiples range from 13.3 times forward earnings for Energy to 23.4 for Consumer Discretionary.

The sensitivity is steep. Hold the 2.48-point cushion constant and leave earnings estimates flat, and a quarter-point rise in the real yield implies a P/E near 18.1, or about 4.5% lower prices. A half-point rise implies roughly 17.4 times earnings, an 8.7% decline, while a half-point drop supports about 21 times.

A Quarter-Point Hike Does Not Reopen Hormuz

CBS reporter Richard Escobedo put the problem plainly at the Sept. 16 press conference. A quarter-point hike, he told Chair Kevin Warsh, “does not reopen the Strait of Hormuz.” Warsh replied that the Fed “cannot affect any individual price” but can keep relative price changes from broadening, the official transcript shows.

The September CPI report shows the gap. Headline inflation hit 3.7%, with gasoline up 34.2% over 12 months, while core ran at 2.6%. Regular gasoline averaged $4.33 a gallon in the week of Oct. 12, up from $3.06 a year earlier, EIA weekly data show, and the CPI print briefly lifted rate-hike bets, Benzinga reported.

The bond market is pricing the shock as temporary. The 10-year breakeven rate, the inflation rate at which TIPS and ordinary Treasuries of the same maturity return the same, stood at 2.35% on Oct. 16, next to the Fed’s median projection of 2.3% inflation for 2027 on its preferred PCE gauge.

Warsh listed this among the Fed’s aims: ensuring “that inflation compensation in market prices stays low.” For investors, that sets the bar. TIPS beat nominal 10-year Treasuries only if inflation averages more than about 2.35% over the decade, and Warsh noted that inflation has run above target for more than five years.

Inflation protection is not price protection. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF (NYSE:TIP) shows a 2.81% real yield and a 6.19-year effective duration, yet its net asset value total return was negative 0.95% year to date as of Oct. 15. Real yields rose 0.84 points this year, and that duration implies roughly a 6% price loss per full point.

What The 2.8% Hurdle Means For A Portfolio

A risk-free real return near 2.8% now sets the bar for every risk asset, and stocks clear it by a narrower margin than a year ago.

  • Measure stocks against the real yield. The forward earnings yield minus the 10-year TIPS yield, now 2.48 points, is a workable cushion gauge; FactSet’s weekly revisions show which way it is moving.
  • Match the instrument to the date. Individual TIPS held to maturity lock in their real yield; a fund such as TIP never matures, so its price moves with real yields. Under TreasuryDirect rules, principal changes may affect federal taxes yearly, so account location matters.
  • Check allocation drift. A stock-and-TIPS mix set a year ago, such as one built with the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and TIP, has likely drifted toward stocks. Written rebalancing bands decide when drift becomes a trade.
  • Watch the next catalysts. FactSet lists Oct. 21 for the first “Magnificent 7” reports, and the Federal Open Market Committee meets Oct. 27-28. Prediction-market traders put October hike odds at 14%.

Equities absorbed higher real yields because earnings grew faster than the discount rate rose; if that reverses, the earnings line will show it first. Stocks now compete with a specific number.

At the Oct. 15 real yield, $100,000 placed in a 10-year TIPS and held to maturity compounds to about $131,500 in today’s purchasing power, before taxes.

headline: Tom Lee Predicts S&P 500 At 8,400 By Year-End, Says Midterm Elections Could Trigger ‘Risk-On’ Rally in Tech Stocks and Crypto: ‘We Are in an Unprecedented Time’
summary: Tom Lee predicts S&P 500 will hit 8,400 by year-end, dismissing pessimism. He calls the market a 'coiled spring' ready to lift tech & crypto.
content_html:
Fundstrat head of research Tom Lee expects the S&P 500 to reach 8,400 by year-end, dismissing market fears as “excessive pessimism.” He predicts the upcoming midterm elections will serve as a “clearing event” that propels technology and cryptocurrency stocks upward.

‘Coiled Spring’ Market Ready to Jump

Despite recent market drawdowns, Lee believes the current environment is primed for a rally, agreeing with the S&P 500 target of “maybe 8,200, maybe 8,400” before year-end, 9.22% higher from the current levels.

Affirming the characterization of the market as a “coiled spring” poised to go “much higher,” Lee told CNBC this potential is largely driven by fundamentals that many investors are overlooking.

“We are in an unprecedented time because earnings growth is accelerating,” Lee said, projecting that third-quarter earnings could see nearly 30% growth. He added that valuations have compressed, noting that “EPS revisions from the start of this year to now for 2027 earnings are up more than 20%, and the S&P is not even up 20%.”

Read Also: Tom Lee vs. AI Debt Trap: What Happens When 10-Year Bonds Fund 2-Year Microchips?

Midterms as a ‘Clearing Event’

With midterm elections approaching, Lee anticipates the political outcome will reduce uncertainty and act as a catalyst for risk assets. He referred to the midterms as an expiration date for a correction and a “clearing event” that will likely be “a very big risk-on signal for markets regardless of outcome.”

Lee presented a contrarian view on how a potential Democratic sweep might affect the market. If Democrats control Congress, it “would be viewed as gridlock,” which markets tend to favor. He also predicted that post-midterms, Democrats will begin supporting data centers and the Clarity Act, providing a tailwind for AI and crypto stocks.

Easing Financial Conditions

A softening labor market and the rolling off of one-time inflationary pressures could allow the Federal Reserve to step back from its hawkish stance. Lee expects “softer readings on inflation” over the next six months, which will “allow bond yields to actually sort of normalize.”

He pointed to the recent strength in certain sectors as an indicator of this shift. “Tech stocks making new highs and crypto doing so well, these can’t do well in the face of tightening conditions,” Lee stated. “They’re anticipating easier financial conditions ahead.”

How Has the Stock Market Performed?

The S&P 500 index has advanced 12.35% year-to-date. Similarly, the Nasdaq Composite index is up 13.72%, and the Dow Jones has gained 8.12% during this period.

headline: Bank Stocks Are On Their Longest Losing Streak Since 2008: Rates Aren't The Only Problem
summary: Bank stocks are on their longest losing streak since 2008 as Treasury yields rise and Bank of America's fine weighs on big lenders.
content_html:
The KBW Nasdaq Bank Index, which tracks 24 of the largest U.S. lenders, has fallen for six straight weeks — its longest losing run since July 2008. It slipped another 1.1% on Monday, putting it on track for a seventh.

The index closed Monday at 167.15 points. That is 11.8% below where it stood when the streak began in early September, and 13.8% below its Aug. 14 record close of 193.91.

Bank stocks are now up just 1.8% this year, against an 11.8% gain for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY).

Read Also: Chip Stocks Repeated a Lehman-Era Losing Streak: Is The Bottom Now In?

Memories of 2008

In the spring and summer of 2008, U.S. bank stocks fell for 10 weeks in a row. Bear Stearns had already been rescued. Lehman Brothers would file for bankruptcy two months after the streak ended.

In the 18 years since, bank stocks have never lost more than five weeks in a row. That record has now been broken.

Last month, the Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time since 2023 to 3.75% to 4.00%.

Long-term yields followed. The 10-year Treasury yield stands at 5.12%, the 30-year at 5.45% and the 2-year at 4.77%.

Higher rates can help banks earn more on loans. When they rise quickly, however, they cut the value of the bonds banks already own and raise the risk that borrowers fall behind on payments.

Investors appear to be trading bank stocks against the direction of rates, treating a rapid climb as a clear negative, according to a Bank of America Global Research report led by analyst Ebrahim Poonawala.

Bank Of America Takes The Biggest Hit

Bank of America Corp. (NYSE:BAC) reported a few days after the Treasury Department hit it with a $1.2 billion penalty. Regulators found the bank failed to properly report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions.

Third-quarter net income fell to $6.9 billion from $8.3 billion a year earlier. Trading revenue dropped 5% and investment banking fees 11%.

The stock trades at $50.39, about 23% below its 2026 high.

Citigroup Inc. (NYSE:C) sits 18% below its June peak. Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS) has lost 11.7% over the past month.

Bank of America does not read the selloff as a verdict on profits.

“Positioning, not fundamentals or EPS revisions, drove post-earnings stock reactions,” Poonawala said in the report.

The bank saw no material change to 2027 earnings estimates. Large U.S. banks trade at about 10 times expected 2027 earnings, according to the report.

Read Also: Nasdaq 100 Stocks Add Nearly $500 Billion As Chips Battle To Snap 2008-Style Rout

Not One Bank In The Index Is Above Its 50-Day Average

None of the 24 stocks in the KBW index trades above its 50-day moving average, the average closing price of the past 50 sessions, Jonathan Roque of 22V Research said in a note on Monday. Only 29% are above their 200-day average.

Roque flagged six names that together make up half of the index’s market value: Bank of America, Capital One Financial Corp. (NYSE:COF), Citigroup, Wells Fargo & Co. (NYSE:WFC), Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (NYSE:GS).

All six trade below both averages.

Rouge sees the index risking a drop to its March low, near 146 to 147 points.

“The market cannot go up when banks go down,” Roque said.

Regional lenders have held up better. The State Street SPDR S&P Regional Banking ETF (NYSE:KRE) is up 6.7% this year.

The comparison with 2008 has limits. Back then, the streak reflected mounting losses on mortgage assets.

This time, Bank of America links the pressure to rising rates and investor positioning, not to the banks’ earnings.

headline: Michael Burry Sees a 2000-Style Rotation Out of the Market's Winners
summary: Michael Burry predicts an AI-driven market decline such as in 2000, when major winners plunge while beaten-down stocks rise.
content_html:
Michael Burry expects the next phase of the stock market to resemble the months after the dot-com peak in 2000, when the biggest winners fell hard and the stocks investors had abandoned climbed.

In an Oct. 17 post on his "Cassandra Unchained" Substack, the investor best known for his bet against the housing market laid out a base case built on four decades of market breadth data.

The market, he wrote, will fail in a way that lifts the median broken stock.

  • PLTR stock is moving. See the real-time price action here.

Burry sees prices drifting lower rather than collapsing in one crash, with some violent stretches along the way, as fundamental news makes its way into the AI narrative.

The AI trade has been a recurring target on his Substack.

In an Oct. 7 post, Burry wrote that the tech giants, other than Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL), are spending as if their lives depended on it. 

The heaviest AI spenders include Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) and Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META). Burry has also published lengthy critiques of Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR).

The March 2000 Template

Burry studied every S&P 500 record close since 1985 that came just before a bear market or a near miss. He split each index into leaders and broken stocks, the latter being names already 20% or more below their 10-year highs when the index peaked.

Only one top produced a clean split. After March 24, 2000, the leaders lost 33% in a year and 50% in 18 months. Two-thirds of them sat more than 20% lower a year after the peak, a share that rose to 79% after 18 months.

The broken stocks went the other way. The median name gained 14% over the first year and held an 8% gain at 18 months. Strength among the laggards pulled the median index member up 5% a year after the top, even as the S&P 500 headed toward a roughly 50% decline over two and a half years.

Burry called the numbers "incredible and unique." No other top in his data saw leaders fall while broken stocks rose at both the 12- and 18-month marks.

Read Also: CoreWeave Stock Down 56% From its Peak — HSBC Sees More Pain Ahead

How Other Tops Played Out

The rest of the record followed different scripts. In 1987 and 2022, everything fell, with leaders doing slightly worse. In 1990, 2007, 2011, 2015 and 2018, broken stocks fell further over the following year as weakness spread outward from the weakest names.

The 2020 and 2025 sell-offs took both groups down together. Both were higher a year later.

Burry noted one partial echo. During the DeepSeek scare in early 2025, which hit AI leaders such as NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), broken stocks outperformed the leaders before April’s tariff shock dragged everything down.

See More: Top Growth Stocks

Why Today Looks Like 2000

Burry’s case rests on breadth. When the S&P 500 closed at a record on Oct. 6, 55% of its members sat at least 20% below their 10-year highs. Among the tops he studied, only March 2000 ranked higher, at 71%. Ordinary tops ran between 20% and 31%.

Just 15 stocks closed at new highs with the index that day, and 97 were within 10% of one. In March 2000, the figures were 15 and 87.

He also flagged a structural difference. A constant mechanical bid from passive and systematic money has kept the deepest losers from piling up the way they did in 2000, he argued. Burry expects that bid to lose steam over the next two years.

Burry describes the bid as pushing more dollars toward fewer of the largest companies in market-cap-weighted indices. 

A rotation like the one he expects would show up in the gap between the cap-weighted SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP), which gives every member the same weight.

Timing Remains Open

Burry cautioned the setup typically takes six to nine months to play out. Nobody knows where the clock stands, he wrote, and the market could be at the start, several months in or close to the end.

The bigger worry comes afterward. Burry questioned what could lift stocks again, given a federal government he sees as too stretched to support a private debt bubble when it bursts.

He describes the market as stuck in denial, the first stage of grief. "Denial is a hell of a drug," Burry wrote, "and I will be watching."

headline: Larry Fink Warns Data Center Slowdown Could Push US Into ‘Recession’ as Trump Orders Facilities to Generate Their Own Power and ‘Make Deals’
summary: Trump mandates AI data centers produce their own electricity, as BlackRock's Larry Fink warns construction delays could trigger inflation.
content_html:
President Donald Trump mandated that new data centers generate their own electricity, as BlackRock Inc. (NYSE:BLK) CEO Larry Fink stated that slowing data center construction will increase inflation.

Trump’s Power Generation Mandate

On Wednesday, President Trump said on Truth Social that he wants data center developers to produce their own power. “New and large, in some cases gigantic, data centers are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid,” Trump stated.

To counter local opposition to these facilities, Trump suggested companies offer financial incentives to residents. “If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a dividend,” Trump noted.

He added that facilities facing opposition become popular when financial agreements are reached, concluding, “Make Deals, and get them built!”

Read Also: Trump Says Communities Hosting AI Data Centers Could Get a ‘Dividend' From Teacher Bonuses to Payments: 'People are Going to Benefit Directly'

Fink’s Economic Warnings

Simultaneously, BlackRock CEO Fink warned that obstructing artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure expansion carries economic risks.

Speaking to Bloomberg Television, Fink linked construction delays directly to rising prices. “If we don’t build out these data centers, it is actually more inflationary because the cost of compute is so high right now,” Fink said.

He added that a slowdown in the build-out of this technology could “jeopardize the economy.”

Fink also addressed the broader economic impact in a separate CNBC interview. “If we have a moratorium of some sort in this country, we will be in a recession,” Fink said.

Wall Street analysts estimate that total AI capital expenditures could exceed $5 trillion by 2030, according to CNBC.

Fink noted that local opposition is often based on “misinformation” and emphasized the economic benefits of the industry.

“Data centers are not the problem. They’re creating more new jobs than ever before,” Fink stated, adding that the investment creates demand for construction workers and energy infrastructure.

How Has the Stock Market Performed?

The S&P 500 index has advanced 12.45% year-to-date. Similarly, the Nasdaq Composite index was up 13.73%, and the Dow Jones gained 8.50% YTD.

On Tuesday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (NASDAQ:QQQ), which track the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, respectively, closed mixed. SPY rose 0.34% to $769.05, while QQQ declined 0.10% to $717.63. Meanwhile, the Dow tracker, State Street SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (NYSE:DIA), ended 1.05% higher at $524.36.

In premarket trading on Wednesday, SPY was up 0.25%, QQQ rose 0.62%, and DIA advanced by 0.44%.

headline: Bitcoin Bulls Get ‘Trapped’ on Dump to $82,000: 4 Reasons Why BTC Sold Off
summary: Bitcoin falls after a failed $84,300 breakout traps bulls, even as US spot ETFs attract $528 million in inflows.
content_html:
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) sold off sharply during Asian trading hours after failing to hold a breakout above $84,300, leaving bulls who bought the move trapped as prices reversed lower.

Why Bitcoin’s Breakout Attempt Failed

Widely-followed cryptocurrency trader JDK Analysis posted on X that Bitcoin pushed strongly above its monthly value-weighted average price and local value area high during New York trading, backed by spot buying and fresh long positions. 

That momentum stalled near $84,300 as passive sellers absorbed large market buy orders and prevented the price from moving higher.

When Asian trading began, price retreated back toward that same breakout zone, and buyers failed to defend it. 

JDK compared the setup to a football team pushing too many players forward, losing possession and leaving itself exposed to a counterattack.

If the breakout fails, those committed buyers are now trapped, and their exits fuel the move down,” JDK wrote. 

“That’s exactly what we saw: longs and spot buyers committed to the attack, then found themselves trapped as it stalled,” he added.

Four Reasons Asian Markets Bled $600 Billion

Widely-followed market commentator Bull Theory posted on X that Asian stock markets lost more than $600 billion in value during the same stretch, pointing to four factors behind the move:

  • US futures weakness: S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY) futures fell 0.8% and Nasdaq futures dropped 1.6%, dragging Asian markets lower.
  • Iran tensions: President Donald Trump said the U.S. is “not negotiating” with Iran, adding fresh geopolitical uncertainty.
  • AI stock concerns: semiconductor and AI-linked stocks fell across Asia as investors question returns on massive AI spending.
  • Oil prices: crude climbing above $100 per barrel revived inflation fears and concerns that central banks keep rates higher for longer.

Why ETF Flows Stayed Positive Despite the Selloff

Even as Bitcoin’s price reversed, demand through regulated channels held up. SoSoValue data showed U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $528.40 million on October 21, led by BlackRock’s (NYSE:BLK) IBIT (NASDAQ:IBIT) at $234.99 million and Fidelity’s FBTC (BATS:FBTC) at $212.71 million.

The divergence between falling spot prices and rising ETF inflows suggests institutional buyers kept accumulating while the Asian session selloff flushed leveraged traders out of the market.

headline: Bitcoin ‘Goes to Zero’ After a Hack, Chamath Palihapitiya Predicts
summary: Chamath Palihapitiya says Bitcoin is capped and warns an AI-driven hack could drain wallets and send BTC to zero.
content_html:
Billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya says Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) has a ceiling on its value and believes a future hack could eventually send it to zero.

Why Palihapitiya Thinks Bitcoin Is Capped

Palihapitiya told the Moonshots podcast that traditional crypto lacks the fungibility needed to attract the full range of potential buyers. 

Retail and institutional investors can hold it, he said, but central banks largely can’t.

He flagged two additional risks beyond that limited buyer pool:

  • Privacy exposure: citing France, where forced publication of crypto holdings led to a wave of kidnappings
  • AI-driven hacking: He argued that recursively self-improving AI models could eventually target Bitcoin’s SHA-256 security and potentially crack Satoshi Nakamoto’s wallet.

On that second risk, Palihapitiya noted an attacker could profit twice, first by draining the wallet, then by shorting Bitcoin after revealing the hack publicly. 

“I just think it’s capped, and then I think eventually it gets hacked, and then it goes to zero,” he said, adding that migrating to quantum-resistant cryptography is “basically impossible” given how divided the Bitcoin community already is on basic coordination.

Palihapitiya also said he no longer holds Bitcoin directly. He moved his exposure into equity through Digital Currency Group years ago specifically to avoid storage and security risk.

Why He Still Sees Opportunity Elsewhere

Despite his Bitcoin call, Palihapitiya said he remains bullish on power and energy infrastructure as the defining investment theme of the next decade, pointing to roughly six gigawatts of capacity he has personally accumulated.

He argued that the U.S. faces a structural electricity shortfall even if developers complete every planned power project on time, making solar and natural gas the fastest and most practical options to close the gap.

He also pushed back on traditional index investing, arguing the S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY) no longer offers the diversification it once did because gains concentrate in a small handful of mega-cap names. 

His alternative: rank companies across the S&P 500 and global indexes by free cash flow yield, then buy the top performers instead of the index itself.

On his own portfolio, Palihapitiya called himself the least invested he’s been in 15 years. “I’m in this schizophrenia about pivoting towards cash flow,” he admitted, pointing to uncertainty over how artificial general intelligence could reshape markets and asset values in the years ahead.

He said he still favors cash flow-generating businesses, power infrastructure, and alternative ways to deploy capital outside traditional financial systems.

headline: Warren Buffett Who? Berkshire Stock Hits Records as These Holdings Drive Gains Under Greg Abel
summary: Warren Buffett is no longer in charge of Berkshire Hathaway, but that hasn't stopped the conglomerate from hitting new all-time highs in 2026.
content_html:
Shares of Berkshire Hathaway Inc (NYSE:BRK)(NYSE:BRK) hit an all-time high on Wednesday, which may come as a surprise to those expecting lower returns after Warren Buffett stepped down as CEO and chairman of the conglomerate.

What’s Leading the Gains?

Berkshire Hathaway trailed the S&P 500, tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), in 2025, closing out Buffett’s final year leading the company as CEO with a decline relative to the broader market.

There could be multiple reasons why investors are warming up to the Berkshire stock in a post-Buffett scenario.

The stock sold off earlier this year on his CEO exit and again on news that he was stepping down as chairman. Those declines came with the underlying businesses and investments still performing solidly.

The conglomerate’s second-quarter net earnings were $25.67 billion, more than double the $12.37 billion posted in the year-earlier period. Operating earnings, which include the underlying businesses, were up 16% year-over-year in the same quarter.

Along with the business strength, Berkshire Hathaway also bought back $4.5 billion of its own shares in the second quarter, a sign that the stock could be undervalued. The company also has a large cash balance, which could be put to work for more buybacks, acquisitions or to buy more stocks for the investment portfolio.

The firm’s investment portfolio could also be fueling investor enthusiasm, with its holdings offering a potential source of untapped value.

Here are the top 10 holdings as of the end of the second quarter and their year-to-date returns:

  • Apple Inc (NASDAQ:AAPL): +26.9%
  • American Express (NYSE:AXP): -13.2%
  • Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO): +32.6%
  • Alphabet Class A (NASDAQ:GOOGL): +6.2%
  • Bank of America (NYSE:BAC): -9.2%
  • Chevron Corporation (NYSE:CVX): +45.5%
  • Occidental Petroleum (NYSE:OXY): +48.0%
  • Chubb Limited (NYSE:CB): +13.7%
  • Moody’s Corporation (NYSE:MCO): -3.6%
  • Alphabet Class C (NASDAQ:GOOG): +5.0%

Of the 10 positions, three are down and seven are up. Of the ones that are up, five are up double-digit percentages. Of the top 10 positions, the average return is a gain of 15.2% year-to-date.

That beats the current 13.1% year-to-date gain for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust, meaning the top 10 stocks in the Berkshire Hathaway portfolio are outperforming the S&P 500 in 2026.

Read Also: If You Invested $1,000 In Berkshire Hathaway Stock When Warren Buffett First Did, Here's How Much You'd Have Today

Changing of the Guard

With the change of CEO comes a learning curve and some uncertainties from long-time investors who were in Berkshire Hathaway due to Buffett.

New CEO Greg Abel has already begun reshaping Berkshire’s portfolio, with its first-quarter 13F filing showing the number of stock holdings fell from 42 to 29.

This included cutting long-time holdings like Visa and Mastercard and also exiting newer positions in UnitedHealth and Constellation Brands.

Not all of Abel’s stock picks will pay off, but his early portfolio changes and gains in retained holdings are rewarding investors who stayed the course.

Next up will be beating the S&P 500, which Buffett did in 13 of his last 25 years at the helm of Berkshire Hathaway and even more if you go back the decades before that.

Berkshire Hathaway stock is currently up 8.5% year-to-date, compared to the 13.1% gain for the SPY. Last year, the SPY outperformed Berkshire Hathaway with gains of 16.6% compared to 11.5%.

summary: SOXL dropped to a six-month low as chip stocks came under pressure. Nvidia CEO's warning and a surge in oil prices may hold clues to what spooked investors.
content_html:
The Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares (NYSE:SOXL) plunged almost 20% on Thursday, hitting a six-month low as surging oil prices, concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) financing and a broader technology selloff rattled semiconductor investors.

Read Also: Dell Stock Drops in Tech Sell-Off: Profit-Taking Hits AI Server Giant

SOXL was among the most actively traded ETFs during midday trading Thursday, with shares falling to levels last seen in April. The selloff extended across the semiconductor sector, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH) dropping around 5.8% and the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) tumbling more than 6.5%. Both funds hit fresh three-month lows.

Why SOXL’s Losses Are So Severe

Unlike traditional semiconductor ETFs, SOXL targets 300% of the daily performance of its benchmark index before fees and expenses. That leverage can magnify both gains and losses. The fund’s objective applies to a single trading day, not longer holding periods.

Consequently, a broad sector selloff can translate into a substantially larger decline for SOXL, making it particularly vulnerable when semiconductor stocks face simultaneous macroeconomic and AI-related headwinds.

Thursday’s plunge puts the spotlight on whether investors will treat the selloff as a buying opportunity or continue reducing exposure to one of the market’s most volatile AI-linked trades.

Technical Talk

SOXL shares were down 19.76% at $82.83 at the time of publication on Thursday, according to Benzinga Pro data. The significant decline reflects broader market pressures impacting the semiconductor sector, which has faced volatility amid changing economic conditions and investor sentiment.

The current price is notably below both key moving averages, indicating a bearish trend that suggests a lack of upward momentum in the short to medium term. The substantial gap from these averages highlights the challenges the ETF faces in regaining investor confidence and establishing a more stable price trajectory.

Trading volume on Thursday reached 140.3 million shares, suggesting heightened activity as investors reacted to market developments. SOXL was also the most actively traded fund on Thursday.

Read Also: Marvell Feels Supply Chain Bottlenecks Pressure, Stock Drops Amid Tech Sell-Off

Oil Shock Fans Wall Street’s Worries

President Donald Trump blamed Iran for the surge in oil prices, alleging in a Truth Social post that Tehran was fabricating attacks and deliberately pushing prices higher ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Brent crude futures expiring in December rose 2.3% to above $111 per barrel, while December West Texas Intermediate futures gained 1.4%.

The broader market weakened as investors assessed the implications of higher energy prices. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY) fell more than 1%, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, lost around 3%.

For semiconductor stocks, persistent energy-price pressures could add to concerns about inflation, interest rates and the cost of financing capital-intensive AI infrastructure.

Jensen Huang’s Funding Warning Hits AI Stocks

Fresh concerns about AI investment added to the pressure.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC that demand for neocloud computing providers was exceptionally strong, but access to working capital was becoming a bottleneck.

Nvidia shares fell more than 4.3% in midday trading. Meanwhile, semiconductor companies Coherent Corp (NYSE:COHR), Entegris Inc (NASDAQ:ENTG), Lam Research Corp (NASDAQ:LRCX) and Lattice Semiconductor Corp (NASDAQ:LSCC) recorded double-digit declines.

The pressure also spread to AI infrastructure providers. CoreWeave Inc (NASDAQ:CRWV) dropped nearly 9%, hitting a fresh 17-month low and falling below $60 for the second time that week. IREN Ltd. (NASDAQ:IREN) slid below $25 to a fresh 13-month low.

headline: Walmart’s Best Month Since 1999 Leads a Record Staples Rally: Is This a Warning Sign?
summary: Walmart is on track for its best month since 1999 as XLP heads for a record October. Past staples surges like this often came before weaker markets.
content_html:
Walmart Inc. (NASDAQ:WMT) is up 16.2% in October, on track for its best month since 1999.

And it is not alone.

Toothpaste, laundry detergent and soda are beating artificial intelligence on Wall Street this month.

By a wide margin.

The Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLP) is up 11.3% in October, heading for its best month since it launched in December 1998.

Meanwhile, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) is roughly flat, and the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLK) has lost 6.9%. Chipmakers, as tracked by the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX), have tumbled over 15%.

That puts staples about 11 percentage points ahead of the S&P 500 in a single month. In the fund’s 27-year history, only April 2022 produced a gap that wide.

So why are investors loading up on shampoo and cereal? And more importantly, are they seeing trouble coming?

Walmart Inc. monthly price change. Source: TradingView

The AI Trade Is Losing Its Grip

On Thursday, Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) fell about 8% on worries about its artificial intelligence spending. As a result, XLK dropped 3.4%, while XLP rallied 2.7%.

The 10-year Treasury yield fell about 17 basis points to 4.95%, its biggest one-day drop since Aug. 2, 2024.

Read Also: Meta Tumbles 6% on AI Spending Fears, 10-Year Yield Falls Below 5%: Stock Market Today

The exit started earlier.

Bank of America clients sold a record $14.8 billion of individual U.S. stocks in the week through Oct. 16.

“Clients sold stocks in 8 of 11 sectors led by Tech (2nd biggest outflows ever),” Bank of America equity quant strategist Jill Carey Hall said in a Bank of America Global Research report.

Staples were among the few sectors clients bought.

Defensives Can Get Crowded Too

Bank of America’s equity derivatives team, which includes strategist Abhinandan Deb, does not see the start of a tech crash.

The strategists described the AI selloff as “a largely positioning-driven hiccup on the fringes of the AI trade rather than evidence of secular weakness in the core,” in a report this week.

“US equities continue to rotate sharply in times of stress rather than rupture, with the recent outperformance of defensives vs tech historically extreme,” they said.

That rotation has its own risks.

“While seemingly paradoxical, defensives like healthcare and staples now sit among the highest BRI pockets of the market,” analysts added, referring to the bank’s Bubble Risk Indicator.

The buying among staples has been across the board.

Procter & Gamble Has Not Had a Month Like This Since 1998

Procter & Gamble Co. (NYSE:PG) rose 5.9% on Thursday after its fiscal first-quarter results.

The maker of Tide and Gillette is up 14.6% in October, on pace for its best month since October 1998, when it jumped 24.7%.

Core earnings rose 1% to $2.00 per share, net sales climbed 4% to $23.28 billion, and volumes grew 2.4%. The company also kept its fiscal 2027 core earnings outlook.

Still, P&G expects about $1.4 billion in after-tax commodity cost headwinds this fiscal year. Its chief financial officer said those pressures will be materially higher in the second quarter and second half because of oil prices.

Read Also: QUICK SPARK: Procter & Gamble Stock Eyes Best Day Since 2020 – The Rally Is Hiding Something Bigger

What Happened the Last Times Staples Ran This Far Ahead

Five of the seven earlier months came in 2000 and 2001, as investors fled the dot-com winners before a recession that began in March 2001.

The S&P 500 was lower a year later in five of the seven cases.

However, there is one key difference.

In every earlier case, the S&P 500 itself fell, by 1.6% to 9.5%. This October, SPY is flat and sits about 2.5% below the record intraday high it hit this month. In other words, money is rotating inside a market near its peak.

The closest match is recent. In February 2026, XLP gained 7.8% while SPY slipped 0.9%. Six months later, SPY was up 11.8%.

Prediction Markets Do Not See a Recession Yet

Polymarket traders see a 7.5% chance of a U.S. recession by the end of 2026 and a 35% chance by the end of 2027.

What the record month does show is how much investors want protection from the AI trade. The last time that urge was this strong, in 2000 and 2001, a bear market and a recession followed.

headline: Peter Schiff Warns Stock Market Crash Before Midterms 'Is Not Outside the Realm of Possibility' — 'This Is October'

content_html:
Veteran investor Peter Schiff warned Thursday that there was a possibility of a stock market crash before the midterm elections, citing rising inflation, a weak economy and an AI boom that is getting harder to finance.

An October Crash

“Remember, this is October,” Schiff said in a post on X, adding that treasury bond yields have risen sharply, rising inflation, a softer job market and a weak economy could potentially lead to a market crash.

“A stock market crash before the midterms is not outside the realm of possibility,” the investor said.

October has a reputation for market turmoil, known as the ‘October Effect,’ and it rests on some of the worst crashes in market history.

Schiff also added that investors are worried about a slowdown in AI spending as borrowing to finance the buildout gets more expensive and scarce.

“AI capex is all that’s keeping GDP positive, the impending recession is very bullish for gold and the miners,” he said.

The Bear Case and Market Outlook

While geopolitical tensions and high energy costs weigh heavily on traditional equities, the AI sector remains a massive focal point for valuations. Valuation expert Aswath Damodaran highlighted the upcoming Anthropic IPO, noting that the AI firm could price between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

Damodaran cautioned that young AI companies are currently being priced on unconventional metrics like annualized revenue run rates (ARR)—similar to how dot-com era stocks were priced on “eyeballs”—making them incredibly difficult to evaluate through traditional intrinsic valuation methods.

headline: AI Stocks Are Getting Crushed, But This Strategist Says the Pullback Could Keep the Boom Alive: 'Restraint Prevents Excess'
summary: James Thorne argued Thursday that the market is misreading the AI stock slide, a pullback that may help the boom last longer.
content_html:
James Thorne, Chief Market Strategist at Wellington Altus, argued Thursday that investors may be misreading the pullback in artificial intelligence stocks, saying the correction could ultimately help extend the AI boom.

Why a Pullback Could Help

AI-linked stocks led Thursday’s tech selloff, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 falling 2.90%.

In a post on X, Thorne said it was a “natural, healthy correction” that was overdue and argued that a short-term downturn could keep the boom from “collapsing under its own weight.”

Lower valuations, tougher credit scrutiny and slower construction impose discipline, he said, stretching investment over more years and easing the inflationary pressure of a concentrated spending surge.

Falling share prices, he pointed out, are “not falling demand for computing power,” and slower capital expenditure growth is not shrinking investment.

The market sees friction as a threat, Thorne contended, but “restraint prevents excess, cools the inflationary impulse and gives the AI boom more time to run.”

Read Also: Trump Asked Google’s Sundar Pichai to Rename Atlantic Ocean After America, But the CEO Wasn’t Having It: ‘Please Don’t Ask Us to Do That’

Friction Builds From Communities to Credit Markets

The friction he described is already visible. About 157 U.S. data center projects have been paused, severely delayed or canceled since 2024, according to a Politico report, citing S&P Global’s 451 Research.

San Francisco recently imposed a 45-day moratorium on data center development, and President Donald Trump has urged developers to pay host communities a “dividend” to ease local opposition.

Credit markets are also getting choosier, Thorne argued.

Meta Platforms Inc.‘s (NASDAQ:META) five-year credit default swaps hit a record 114.79 basis points on Thursday, according to Markit data cited by Reuters.

CoreWeave Inc.‘s (NASDAQ:CRWV) 2031 bond yield reached a record 15.8%, according to TradingView.

More Years to Build, Less Strain

Spreading construction over more years, Thorne reasoned, eases the strain on equipment, labor and electricity infrastructure, giving suppliers time to expand and power systems time to catch up.
