headline: The Average Stock Is Beating the S&P 500 by the Most Since April 2009: Is the Rotation Now Over?
summary: The equal-weight S&P 500 ETF (RSP) is beating SPY by the most since April 2009 as money exits AI stocks. Analysts weigh whether the rotation can last.
content_html:
The typical S&P 500 company is having its best month against the index in more than 17 years. The index itself, however, has barely moved.

That gap is the clearest sign yet that money is leaving the artificial intelligence trade and spreading across the rest of the market.

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP), which gives every company in the index the same weight, has gained 4.9% in October through Thursday’s close. Meanwhile, the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY), dominated by the largest technology names, is up just 0.2%.

As a result, the ratio between the two funds has climbed 4.7% this month. That is the biggest relative monthly jump since April 2009, when stocks were rebounding from the financial crisis lows.

The rotation has also flipped the year-to-date scoreboard. The equal-weight ETF is now up 13.5% in 2026, ahead of the 11.4% gain for SPY.

Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF relative to the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF, monthly change. Source: TradingView

Thursday showed the shift in a single session.

The equal-weight ETF rose 0.7%, while the S&P 500 fell 1.2% as Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) tumbled 7% on concerns about its AI spending. Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) lost 4.4%.

The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLK) dropped 3.3%. By contrast, the State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLP) jumped 3.3% and the State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLU) added 2.1%.

Read Also: Walmart Stock Eyes Best Monthly Rally Since 2014: Is This an Early Recession Warning?

Investors Are Questioning Who Pays for the AI Build-Out

Bank of America Global Research strategist Sebastian Raedler said in a report Friday that there are “mounting signs of markets becoming increasingly unwilling to fund the AI infrastructure build-out.”

In Europe, according to Raedler, cyclical sectors have trailed defensive ones by 11%, the sharpest rotation since the COVID-19 shock of March 2020.

He also pointed to Ramp data showing that AI spending by U.S. businesses has stopped rising in recent months as token prices decline.

At 22V Research, Dennis DeBusschere said the market’s reflex on days when AI capex worries flare has been to buy banks, retailers, small caps, housing and transport stocks.

However, he drew a line between near-term and long-term risk.

“AI capex concerns are about 2028 and beyond. NOT 2027,” DeBusschere said, adding that investors remain highly confident 2027 spending plans will be met.

Is the Rotation Now Over? This Year’s Spikes Faded Fast

History offers two very different answers.

After April 2009, the equal-weight ETF kept going. Over the following 12 months, the RSP-to-SPY ratio rose another 9.4%.

This year, the pattern has been the opposite. In February, the ratio jumped 4.4% in a single month, then gave back 7.6% over the next three months.

A 3.2% gain in June was followed by a 4.3% decline through September.

There is also a key difference with 2009.

Back then, the average stock led because almost everything was rising. In October 2026, it is leading largely because the giants are falling, with defensive sectors doing much of the heavy lifting.

Read Also: QUICK SPARK: Procter & Gamble Stock Eyes Best Day Since 2020 – The Rally Is Hiding Something Bigger

John Roque, also of 22V Research, sees that as a warning rather than a green light. As of Thursday morning, new lows had outnumbered new highs on the NYSE and Nasdaq for 37 and 38 straight sessions, respectively, even though the S&P 500 was only a little more than 1% below its record.

According to Roque, Nasdaq data going back to 2015 shows nine prior streaks of at least 33 days of net new lows. In seven of them, the Nasdaq went on to fall at least 18%.

He also noted that most major U.S. banks are trading below their 200-day moving averages, warning that “when banks / financials are not strong, you cannot have a strong market.”

With six trading sessions left in October, the equal-weight fund is on track for a historic month.

Whether it marks the start of a broader advance, as in 2009, or a defensive retreat from AI will depend on whether the rest of the market can keep rising once the selling in megacaps stops.

headline: China Wields ETFs Against Market Rout: Could America Copy The Strategy?
summary: China is buying $2.5 billion in equity ETFs daily. Investors are wondering: Could the Fed follow suit during the next stock market crash?
content_html:
China’s reported $2.5 billion-a-day equity ETF buying spree is raising a bigger question for investors: Could the U.S. Federal Reserve eventually use ETFs to stabilize stocks during the next major market selloff?

Eric Balchunas, senior ETF analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said China’s government has been buying roughly $2.5 billion in equity ETFs daily since July, following an artificial intelligence-driven market slump. That is about 11.5 times the typical daily ETF flow of $218 million cited by Balchunas. He likened the scale to the U.S. Treasury buying $100 billion of ETFs every day.

Balchunas has previously argued that the Federal Reserve could eventually follow a similar approach, with China and Japan helping normalize government-backed equity purchases. He believes such intervention could become more common over the next five to 10 years.

China’s ETF Purchases Are More Than a Market Signal

China’s state-backed investor Central Huijin Investment has been a key player in the country’s market-support efforts, using ETFs to channel capital into domestic equities.

Bloomberg Intelligence estimates that Central Huijin redeployed $43 billion into equities after purchases resumed in July 2026. It had about $188 billion in available funds remaining, according to Livemint. The buying has included broad-market exposure through funds tracking the CSI 300 Index, alongside greater allocations to technology-focused benchmarks.

However, state buying does not guarantee a sustained recovery. Bloomberg Intelligence has cautioned that intervention may slow a selloff without reversing it when investor sentiment and underlying fundamentals remain weak.

Japan Has Already Crossed That Line

The Bank of Japan built substantial equity ETF holdings through a 2010 program and expanded them during its monetary-easing campaign. In March 2024, it discontinued new ETF purchases.

In September 2025, it announced plans to gradually dispose of its holdings, showing that central-bank equity ownership can become a long-term policy and balance-sheet issue.

Could the Fed Become an Equity ETF Buyer?

A future U.S. intervention would represent a significant departure from conventional Federal Reserve operations. The Fed’s statutory mandate centers on maximum employment and stable prices, not directly supporting stock valuations.

Any move toward equity ETF purchases would raise questions about its legal authority, financial independence, market distortions and the distribution of gains among investors.

For ETF investors, the implication is not that a U.S. rescue is imminent. Instead, China and Japan provide precedents for how governments and central banks might use ETFs to stabilize markets during severe downturns.

The next major bear market could test whether that approach remains largely an Asian policy tool or becomes part of a broader global debate.

summary: IYZ telecom ETF lagged SPY for 12 sessions, its longest run since 2000, as SpaceX moves into U.S. wireless. AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile slide premarket.
content_html:
Gone are the days when telecom stocks were the quiet corner of Wall Street with steady bills, steady dividends and few surprises. Over the past two weeks, they have become the market’s most reliable losers.

The iShares U.S. Telecommunications ETF (BATS:IYZ) has underperformed the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) for 12 straight sessions through Thursday.

That is the longest such run since the fund launched in May 2000.

From Oct. 7 to Oct. 22, IYZ fell 12.9%. Meanwhile, SPY slipped 1.9%.

The company standing over the streak is Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX), better known as SpaceX.

iShares U.S. Telecommunications ETF relative performance against the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust and consecutive underperformance count. Source: TradingView

SpaceX: America’s New Carrier?

SpaceX reported third-quarter results on Tuesday, with revenue up 161% from a year earlier to $14.58 billion.

On the earnings call, CEO Elon Musk reaffirmed the plan to build a U.S. wireless business.

SpaceX “will be building out our terrestrial networks” wherever Starlink is allowed to operate, he said.

The company also said S-band airwaves should carry most Starlink Mobile traffic, while newly acquired 800 MHz spectrum will bring the signal inside buildings.

Starlink Mobile ended the quarter with 22 million monthly users, up 37% from the prior quarter.

Then, on Thursday evening, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is in talks with tower owners, including Crown Castle Inc. (NYSE:CCI), for access to at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites.

That is roughly half of the 158,500 purpose-built towers the Wireless Infrastructure Association counted in the U.S. last year.

Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant was asked about leases with SpaceX on the tower company’s earnings call this week. “You can assume that we’re talking to all parties,” he said.

Read Also: SpaceX Jumps 10%, Nasdaq 100 Rises as AI Trade Returns: Stock Market Today

The Day The Carriers Broke

The streak turned on Oct. 8.

After the close, SpaceX agreed to buy Grain Management’s nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission. The deal would help Starlink Mobile “become a major mobile carrier in the US.”

The next day, AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) fell 10.8%, Verizon Communications Inc. (NYSE:VZ) lost 10.1% and T-Mobile US Inc. (NASDAQ:TMUS) sank 13.3%.

AT&T traded about 150 million shares that session, nearly four times its average over the prior four days.

The carriers clawed back part of those losses. On Thursday, all three rose between 3.3% and 3.8%.

The relief did not last.

In premarket trading Friday, AT&T fell 4.4% to $21.75, Verizon dropped 3.8% to $43.50 and T-Mobile slid 4.8% to $151.20, according to Benzinga Pro data.

Tower owners, by contrast, are being priced as SpaceX’s landlords. Crown Castle jumped 10.3% premarket, while American Tower Corp. (NYSE:AMT) rose 7.3%.

Why IYZ Fell Harder Than The Carriers

IYZ is half a telecom fund and half a networking-hardware fund. Cisco Systems Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) and Arista Networks Inc. (NYSE:ANET) made up about a third of its assets at the end of June, according to the fund’s latest SEC holdings filing.

Since Oct. 6, Arista has dropped 20.6% and Cisco has lost 11.1%. Over the same stretch, AT&T fell 6.9%, T-Mobile 4.3% and Verizon 1.7%.

Thursday showed the split clearly. While the carriers bounced, IYZ fell 2.5% as AI networking stocks sold off with the broader tech sector.

In addition, AST SpaceMobile Inc. (NASDAQ:ASTS), an IYZ holding that is building its own satellite-to-phone network, has lost 37% over the past month.

As a result, the fund was hit from two sides at once: a new competitor for its carriers and an unwind in AI networking hardware.

headline: Michael Burry Warns Washington Has Little Room Left to Fight the Next Crisis
summary: Michael Burry warns high debt may limit Washington’s ability to rescue markets, citing weak breadth and AI-driven bubble risks.
content_html:
Investor Michael Burry, famous for betting against the housing bubble, says the federal government may be in no shape to rescue markets the next time a bubble bursts.

  • AAPL stock is moving. See the chart and price action here. 

In a recent post on his Substack, "Cassandra Unchained", Burry argued Washington has used real crises as cover to abandon fiscal caution and then kept it abandoned. The result, in his view, leaves policymakers in a weak position to support what he describes as a private debt bubble once it breaks.

He called the decision to take on so much debt while repeatedly cutting short the market’s natural recovery process "unconscionable." 

Consequences will follow, he wrote. They may have started already.

Breadth Flashing Red

The warning capped a lengthy study of market breadth built on decades of historical index membership data.

Burry tracked what he calls the Bear Market Ratio, the share of S&P 500 members trading more than 20% below their 10-year highs. When the index, tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY), closed at a record on Oct. 6, the ratio stood at 55%. At the Aug. 13 record, it was 47%.

Only one record high in four decades came with a worse reading. In March 2000, at the peak of the dot-com bubble, 71.2% of index members sat in their own bear markets. Ordinary market tops since 1985 registered between roughly 20% and 31%.

Read Also: Michael Burry Shares Chilling Song on AI: 'Watching Trillion-Dollar Monuments Become Obsolete'

Thin Leadership

Other measures look thin as well. Just 15 S&P 500 stocks closed at a new high alongside the index on Oct. 6, and only 97 traded within 10% of one. In March 2000, the figures were 15 and 87.

The median stock in the index now sits 22% below its high. At the 2000 peak, the median was 31% below.

Burry also built a narrower gauge, the Fresh Drawdown Ratio, to filter out stocks still weighed down by peaks from years earlier. Ordinary tops produced readings between 6% and 13%. The current reading is 27%, about half the 2000 level.

"More like 2000 than any time since, but not 2000 yet," he wrote.

See More: Top Value Stocks

A Slow Grind Lower

His base case calls for a market decline in which the leaders fall while the median beaten-down stock rises, a pattern seen only after the 2000 top. Burry does not necessarily expect one big crash. He sees stocks drifting lower, at times violently, as weak fundamental news works its way into the artificial intelligence story.

Burry credited the “plunge protection team” with skill at handling sudden selloffs. A market deteriorating on both fundamental and technical grounds, with shrinking participation, poses a harder problem. Cheerleading will not fix it, he suggested.

Burry has questioned AI spending for weeks. In an earlier post, he wrote the largest tech companies, with the exception of Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL), are spending as if their survival depended on it.

"Denial is a hell of a drug," he wrote, "and I will be watching."

headline: S&P 500 Near Record Highs, But 60% of Stocks Are in a Bear Market. Is SPY Hiding a Bigger Problem?
summary: The S&P 500 is near record highs, but 60% of its stocks are in a bear market. What do SPY, VOO and RSP reveal about Wall Street’s rally?
content_html:
The S&P 500 is hovering near record highs, but weakness beneath the surface is raising questions about the sustainability of Wall Street’s rally.

Read Also: Wall Street’s ‘Last Men Standing’: The Mag 7 Are Propping Up the S&P 500, Then Why Are Your ETFs at Risk?

According to an analysis by The Kobeissi Letter, 59% of S&P 500 constituents are down at least 20% from their all-time highs, while 84% have fallen at least 10%. Yet just 10 stocks have contributed 70% of the benchmark’s gains since the March 30 market bottom.

The divergence highlights how gains concentrated in a handful of large technology and semiconductor companies can mask widespread weakness across the broader market.

SPY and VOO: Same Index, Similar Exposure

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:VOO) both track the market-cap-weighted S&P 500. Consequently, their returns tend to move closely together, with the largest companies exerting the greatest influence on performance.

Their primary difference is cost. VOO charges an annual expense ratio of 0.03%, compared with approximately 0.0945% for SPY, making VOO the cheaper option for investors seeking long-term S&P 500 exposure.

Neither ETF eliminates the concentration risk inherent in the benchmark. If a small group of mega-cap stocks continues to outperform, both funds can remain strong even as many constituents struggle.

Could RSP Benefit if Market Leadership Broadens?

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP) offers a different way to invest in the same 500 companies. Unlike SPY and VOO, which allocate more money to companies with larger market capitalizations, RSP gives each constituent roughly the same weight and periodically rebalances its portfolio.

This distinction matters when market performance is concentrated in a handful of mega-cap stocks. In SPY and VOO, gains in the largest companies can offset losses across dozens of smaller constituents. RSP reduces that dominance, giving weaker-performing companies a greater influence on the fund’s overall returns.

The concentration gap is substantial. Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) accounts for 7.88% of SPY, Apple, Inc (NASDAQ:AAPL) for 7.45% and Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) for 5.94%. Together, these three stocks represented more than 21% of SPY’s portfolio. RSP’s equal-weight methodology limits any individual constituent to roughly 0.2%–0.3% of the fund, depending on market movements.

Recent performance, however, does not yet show a decisive advantage for equal weighting. SPY has gained 11.8% year to date, while RSP had advanced 12.3% — a minor difference.

VOO provides almost the same market-cap-weighted exposure as SPY but at a lower annual expense ratio. RSP charges 0.20%. On a $10,000 investment, those expense ratios translate to roughly $3, $9.45 and $20 annually, respectively.

If more S&P 500 stocks recover and participate in the rally, RSP could benefit from broader market participation. However, if mega-cap technology stocks continue to lead, SPY and VOO could outperform. RSP’s equal-weighting approach also means it is not automatically safer during a widespread selloff.

Opportunity or Warning?

The breadth data raises the possibility that beaten-down stocks could recover if earnings and market sentiment improve. But a steep drawdown does not automatically make a stock undervalued.

Investors should watch earnings revisions, constituent participation and whether gains spread beyond the largest companies before treating the so-called "stealth bear market" as a buying opportunity.

summary: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 indices pulled back as investors focused on the strong earnings season amid the AI bubble.
content_html:
Major US indices pulled back this week, even as earnings season pointed to strong performance by American companies. The S&P 500 dropped to 7,623, its lowest level since October 1 and 2.8% below its peak for the year. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 tumbled to 28,957, down 7.5% from its year-to-date high.

Earnings Season Shows Companies Are Doing Well

Hundreds of American companies have published strong financial results this month, a sign that consumers and companies are spending. 

FactSet (NYSE:FDS) data shows that 24% of all companies in the S&P 500 Index have already released their earnings. The blended earnings growth is 29.5%. If this is the final number, it will mark the third quarter in which growth has been above 25%. 

Chances are that the final earnings growth figure will be higher than this since many technology and energy companies are yet to publish their numbers. Top technology companies like Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Micron (NASDAQ:MU) are reporting some of their best numbers as demand for GPUs and memory rises. 

The earnings season will intensify in the coming weeks. Top Magnificent Seven companies like Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG), and Amazon (NASDAQ:MSFT) will publish their results next week. Meta Platforms and Tesla have already released their Q3 results. 

Other large companies that will release their numbers next week are Visa, Mastercard, AbbVie, Coca-Cola, Verizon, and SK Hynix. 

Read Also: Jensen Huang Downplays Memory Glut Fears: Will Micron Rebound Next?

AI Bubble Fears and Soaring Crude Oil Prices

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 indices have struggled because of the ongoing AI bubble fears. Ken Griffin, the billionaire founder of Citadel, warned that we are in a bubble, joining other top experts like Ray Dalio and Michael Burry in sounding the alarm. As a result, the biggest companies in the AI space, like Micron, CoreWeave, and Nebius, were among the top laggards this week.

On the positive side, some other experts believe that the AI fears are not justified. In a statement, Stephen Schwarzman, the founder of Blackstone (NYSE:BX), said that the AI boom was real, pointing to the rising demand from consumers. FundStrat’s Tom Lee believes that the AI correction is nearing its end. 

US stocks are also weighed by rising oil prices, with Brent and the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) rising to $117 and $103, respectively. The rising oil prices mean that inflation will remain at elevated levels, pushing the Federal Reserve to maintain high interest rates for longer.

content_html:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sunday that a trade dispute with Canada will resolve shortly, asserting that tariffs were implemented because Canada “has been ripping off” the United States.

Campaign Rhetoric in Michigan

According to Reuters, speaking at a political rally in Port Huron, Michigan, to support Republican candidates ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Trump predicted an imminent end to the trade standoff.

“I had to do it,” Trump told the crowd in reference to his tariff policies. “We’ll have that settled pretty soon,” Trump stated, adding, “They’re willing to give us anything at this moment.”

Local Economic Impact and Reactions

The U.S.-Canada tariff dispute has impacted the Detroit-based U.S. auto industry and the broader Michigan border region economy. Republican Congressman Mike Rogers, who is running against Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, has attempted to distance himself from the president’s auto sector tariff policy.

While Rogers credited the tariffs for securing Michigan manufacturing investments from Chevrolet and Detroit Diesel, he told “Meet the Press” that “the automobile portion of these Canadian tariffs worries me a little bit.”

Rogers further stated, “There’s some good and there’s some things we have to work on.”

Recent Tariff Adjustments

The rally follows a Friday executive order by Trump easing 50% tariffs on select Canadian imports, including plywood sheets, machinery, and fresh seaweed, which takes effect on Oct. 30. Simultaneously, Trump added other Canadian products, including carpets and air conditioners, to the 50% tariff list.

The exemptions offer potential relief to businesses in states like Maine, where Republican Senator Susan Collins faces a closely contested reelection campaign. White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton stated that the latest changes refine existing tariffs while addressing Canada’s treatment of U.S. commerce.

Regarding the trade changes, Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc stated that Ottawa was assessing the adjustments and remained open to constructive negotiations. Additionally, Trump announced Thursday that Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier Inc. (OTC:BDRBF) will invest $270 million in the U.S., following previous administration threats to impose a 50% tariff on the company’s jets.

How Has the Stock Market Performed?

summary: Mohamed El-Erian warns crude oil could hit $150 if Middle East conflict widens, despite Trump halting an immediate U.S. strike on Iran.
content_html:
Oil prices face the risk of surging to $150 per barrel if Middle East conflicts widen, according to Mohamed El-Erian, despite President Donald Trump ruling out an immediate U.S. military strike against Iran.

The Path to $150 Crude

During a recent podcast interview with Mario Nafwal, El-Erian stated that if a broader war breaks out and disrupts tanker flows in the Straits and the Red Sea, prices will climb significantly. “This is not oil at 120. This is oil at 150 because we don’t have these two other things that we had before,” El-Erian said.

He explained that the market previously avoided $150 oil because China cut its imports by 40% and relied heavily on both sovereign and company inventories. With those global inventories now drawn down, El-Erian stated that the market lacks its prior buffers.

Read Also: Oil Jumps to Nearly 6-Month High as Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia Stoke Supply Fears, While Trump Faces Fuel-Price Headwinds Ahead of Midterms

Trump Rules Out Immediate Strike

El-Erian’s warning comes amid short-term market relief following recent comments from President Trump. Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Sunday, Oct. 25, Trump stated that the U.S. would not immediately attack Iran.

“The answer is no,” Trump said. “There will not be a strike today.”

Following Trump’s remarks, oil prices retreated. However, tensions remain high, as U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have tightened security due to intelligence warnings of Iranian plots, and the Pentagon has reportedly prepared options for follow-up strikes.

Economic Tipping Points

Despite the immediate drop in oil prices, El-Erian cautioned that a prolonged conflict would serve as a “major headwind” for the global economy, particularly as borrowing costs remain elevated.

El-Erian noted that recent market stability has been built on “borrowed resilience,” as nations drew down existing inventories and financial wealth. “You can’t keep on borrowing from inventories all the time,” El-Erian stated.

If these buffers fail during a prolonged military conflict, El-Erian concluded that the resulting energy shock would deliver a “significant blow” to the global economy and “undermine the marketplace.”

Oil Prices Ease

At the last check, WTI crude oil futures were trading lower in the early New York session by 2.06% to hover around $101.14 per barrel. Meanwhile, the ETF tracking this, United States Oil Fund LP (NYSE:USO), fell by 2.51% in premarket trading on Monday.

headline: Nvidia Is Now Cheaper Than the Average S&P 500 Stock: Wall Street Still Sees Record Profits
summary: Nvidia stock trades at an 11% discount to the S&P 500, the widest since April 2015, even as its expected profits have grown 30-fold since 2022.
content_html:
In April 2015, Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) was a $12 billion maker of graphics cards for video gamers.

Today, it is worth more than $5 trillion and powers the artificial intelligence boom.

Yet, Nvidia’s stock has just hit its biggest discount to the market since then.

Wall Street expects Nvidia to earn $12.03 per share over the next 12 months. At the end of 2022, that estimate was roughly 40 cents.

At around $215, the stock trades at about 18 times those expected earnings. The S&P 500, tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), trades at 19 times.

So why is the market paying less for a company that keeps earning more?

Nvidia weekly chart, next-12-month EPS estimate and forward P/E ratio. Source: TradingView

Nvidia Stock Trades at an 11% Discount to the Market

When OpenAI launched ChatGPT in November 2022, Nvidia traded at more than 40 times forward earnings.

Since then, profits have risen far faster than the share price.

As a result, the multiple fell to 18 at Friday’s close, less than half its 2022 level and near the lowest reading in eight years.

The comparison with the broader market is even more striking.

At Friday’s close, Nvidia traded at an 11% discount to the average company in the S&P 500. The gap had not been this wide since April 2015, when the company’s biggest customers were still gamers rather than hyperscalers.

Two Fears Are Weighing on Nvidia Stock

The first concern is how long its biggest customers can keep spending.

Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) and Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) are on track to invest $930 billion this year. Estimates point to $1.35 trillion next year.

After that, however, the curve flattens. Projections show $1.45 trillion the following year and $1.415 trillion the year after.

For this reason, if spending stops growing, Nvidia’s growth faces the same ceiling.

Read Also: Meta Just Burned Cash for the First Time Since Its IPO Year: Wall Street Raised Its Targets Anyway

The second fear is the neoclouds.

Companies such as CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) and Nebius Group N.V. (NASDAQ:NBIS) borrow money to buy Nvidia chips, then rent that computing power to AI developers.

The model works as long as demand stays high and money stays cheap. Lately, both conditions are being tested.

Investors now demand more than 16% to lend to CoreWeave, and its shares have lost 42% over the past month. Nebius is down 38% over the same stretch, and both fell more than 3% in early trading Monday.

Even Jensen Huang acknowledged the problem on Oct. 22, saying demand for computing far exceeds the capital available to finance it. Nvidia fell 4.4% that day.

The financing question resurfaced Monday. Meta, which plans a $95 billion funding push for its AI ambitions, said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) and Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) had each indicated interest in buying up to $5 billion of shares in its stock offering.

In other words, the chipmakers are now helping fund one of their biggest customers.

Read Also: CoreWeave Bonds Stop Bleeding After SpaceX Results, But Investors Still Demand 3x Treasury Yields

Wall Street Still Sees the Discount as an Opportunity

Analysts, however, are not backing away.

Nvidia has a consensus Buy rating from the 29 analysts tracked by Benzinga Analyst Ratings. Their average price target of $343 implies about 59% upside. Over the past three months, targets have ranged from $300 to $515, the high end set by Raymond James.

The most recent call came on Oct. 22, when Needham analyst N. Quinn Bolton maintained a Buy rating and a $300 target.

Cantor Fitzgerald analyst C.J. Muse reiterated an Overweight rating and a $350 target after attending Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote.

Muse said Nvidia’s guidance for more than 70% revenue growth in calendar 2027 looks very conservative.

He highlighted demand that still supports well above 100% growth, and supply deals that should expand Nvidia’s substrate capacity 2.5 times over three years.

With shares trading at less than 10 times Cantor’s calendar 2028 earnings estimate, the stock is “simply too hard to ignore,” Muse said.

The Market Has Doubted Nvidia Before

In 2015, investors priced Nvidia as a gaming company with limited prospects. That discount turned out to be one of the great mispricings in market history.

Today, they are pricing the world’s main AI supplier as if its growth is about to stall.

Whether that doubt proves equally misplaced no longer depends on demand for Nvidia’s chips. It depends on whether its customers can keep paying for them.

headline: 5 Myths And Misunderstandings About Investing In The Stock Market
summary:
Much of what we know about the stock market comes from a mix of theory and empirical evidence.



For example, the idea that earnings drive stock prices is supported by the view that a business’s value is tied to how
content_html:
Much of what we know about the stock market comes from a mix of theory and empirical evidence.

For example, the idea that earnings drive stock prices is supported by the view that a business’s value is tied to how much money it makes. And decades of market data show that stock prices and earnings have exhibited a tight correlation.

There are also ideas that make intuitive sense, but the evidence supporting them is shoddy. In the stock market, this is a big problem because people will trade on these ideas, only to underperform the market.

Especially when it comes to price behavior, if a theory were both sound and reliable, we’d probably hear more about people consistently beating the market with some bulletproof trading strategy. But we don’t.

With that in mind, here are five ideas about the stock market that I’d describe as myths or misunderstandings.

1. Stock market returns revert to a mean

Periods of strong stock market returns should be followed by periods of weak returns, and vice versa. Right?

If you take a long-term chart of the stock market and add a trendline, you’ll see prices above the line for some time and below it most of the time. This makes it tempting to say that the market exhibits mean reversion, or a tendency to gravitate back toward some historical average.

Unfortunately, this behavior is so inconsistent that Professors Paul Marsh, Mike Staunton, and Elroy Dimson concluded that "popular evidence for mean reversion is an ‘optical illusion’ that employs hindsight." They addressed this issue in the 2025 edition of UBS’s "Global Investment Returns Yearbook" and also explored it at length in the 2013 edition, when Credit Suisse published it.

They even went so far as to compare the belief in mean reversion to the Gambler’s Fallacy, the assumption that past outcomes inform future ones.

If mean reversion in the market were consistent and predictable, then there would be a way to trade the phenomenon in such a way as to generate above-average returns. But you don’t really hear about funds or traders consistently beating the market by trading the expectation of mean reversion. (Maybe some secretive hedge fund somewhere has figured it out and they’re not telling us.)

"Market-timing strategies based on mean reversion typically gave lower, not higher, returns," Marsh, Staunton, and Dimson found.

That’s not too surprising when you see the various stats showing periods of strong returns are often followed by more strong returns. Indeed, history shows that investing at all-time highs has produced better returns than investing on all other days.

Keep this in mind the next time someone suggests we’re "due" for weak returns because we just experienced strong returns. What just happened won’t tell you what’s coming next.

2. Valuations revert to a mean

One of the most popular ways to measure value is to divide an asset’s price by its earnings. This is the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. When a stock’s P/E is above its historical average, it’s considered expensive. When it’s below average, it’s considered cheap.

This has led many to assume that expensive stocks tend to get cheaper and cheap stocks tend to get more expensive. In other words, valuations tend to revert to a mean, right?

"We cannot emphasize enough that valuation metrics are NOT historically mean-reverting," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote in January. They’ve characterized it as "an oft-repeated myth."

The firm has advanced this controversial view since 2013 (and again in 2022 and 2025). To make their point, they used a Dickey-Fuller test, a tool statisticians use to analyze time-series data. The test found that P/E ratios lacked stationarity, which means the averages aren’t stable over time.

This conclusion aligns with arguments from some top Wall Street strategists in recent years. They’ve argued that persistent improvements in business performance and capital structures have justified the higher valuations we’ve seen lately, an idea supported by theory.

And so, the mean itself is moving.

The idea that valuations aren’t mean-reverting probably makes a lot of people uncomfortable. Then again, trading based on the assumption of mean reversion hasn’t exactly yielded consistent results for people.

3. Picking a market-beating stock is like calling a coin flip

One of the main reasons to buy the stock of a single company is that you believe the price will outperform the market average over some period of time. Otherwise, you’d just put that money into an index fund tracking the market average.

A lot of people try their hand at stock picking. But most fail to beat the market.

Why? Because most stocks lag the market. And it’s far more than half.

In a study published last year, S&P Dow Jones Indices analysts found that just 19% of S&P 500 companies outperformed the average stock’s return from 2001 to 2025. Most S&P stocks underperformed the index in 13 of the past 24 calendar years.

Even with stock correlations very low and dispersion high — conditions that theoretically favor those looking to beat the market — professional stock pickers have struggled to identify winners!

The truth is that market averages, which have trended higher over the years, are driven by a relatively small number of stocks that generate eye-popping returns. ASU Professor Hendrik Bessembinder has published several studies showing this. Even Warren Buffett has attributed Berkshire Hathaway’s outstanding equity portfolio performance to "a few winners."

4. Holding a market-beating stock is a fun experience

Let’s say you got lucky and managed to buy one of these few stocks that go on to smoke the rest of the market. Buckle up.

In a report published last year, Morgan Stanley’s Michael Mauboussin and Dan Callahan studied the price behavior of 6,500 stocks. They took a closer look at the 20 stocks with the best total shareholder returns over the 40 years from 1985 to 2024.

"The median maximum drawdown was 72% for the best group, and the median maximum drawdown duration, the time from peak to trough, was 2.9 years," they found. "The median time to return to the prior peak was 4.3 years."

Just thinking about one of my positions losing 72% of its value makes me queasy, even knowing full well this is the average behavior of the best stocks.

If you’re a fund manager with picks like this, you may be fired long before you’ve been proven right.

5. The stock market often delivers average returns

The first thing many of us are taught about the stock market is that the average annual return is about 8% to 10%, give or take a point or two.

That gives many people the impression that the market climbs 8% to 10%-ish somewhat frequently.

But that’s far from the truth.

Carson Group’s Ryan Detrick ran the numbers. Since 1950, the S&P 500 returned 8%-10% in just four years.

In reality, the long-term average is the result of many above-average years and many below-average years. Ritholtz Wealth Management’s Ben Carlson observed that in the average up-year, the S&P returned 21%. And in the average down-year, the index lost 13%.

This doesn’t mean you should throw these ideas out the window

Maybe you’d be ill-advised to try to beat the market by trading on one of these myths or misunderstandings.

But that doesn’t mean you should ignore them entirely.

Sometimes, weak returns follow strong returns, valuations move toward the mean, half the stocks you pick beat the market, the outperforming stocks you own never lag, and we get an average year in the market.

In other words, sometimes we do get those brief moments when the market behaves as our gut expects.

Just because the markets can be chaotic and unpredictable doesn’t mean they never make sense. It’s just that they don’t make sense on a predictable schedule.

headline: This Midterm’s Stock-Market Pattern Hasn’t Failed Since 1950, and It Kicks Off This Week
summary: The S&P 500 has risen in the 12 months after every midterm since 1950. Seasonax, BofA and Yardeni weigh in as the Election Day window opens.
content_html:
TradingView data going back to 1950 cover 19 midterm elections. In every case, the index was higher 12 months after the end of October in the election year.

The average gain was 16.6%, and the median was 16.3%. Even the weakest run, from October 2014 to October 2015, delivered about 3%. The strongest, after the 1954 vote, topped 33%.

The short-term picture is messier.

Read Also: The Average Stock Is Beating the S&P 500 by the Most Since April 2009: Is the Rotation Now Over?

From October to year-end, the S&P 500 rose in 13 of those 19 midterm years, with an average gain of 3.6%.

2018 shows the gap. The index slumped 7.6% in the last two months of that year, its worst post-midterm stretch in the sample.

Twelve months after the October close, however, it was up 12%.

Why Traders Start Watching This Week

Americans head to the polls on Election Day, Nov. 3, to elect all 435 House members and about a third of the Senate.

For a historical perspective, Dimitri Speck, founder and chief analyst at seasonal-research firm Seasonax, examined the narrower window around Election Day across 23 midterms since 1934.

From five trading days before the vote to two days after, the S&P 500 rose in 22 of 23 cases, with an average gain of 2.74%.

The only miss came in 1994.

Tuesday’s close is the fifth trading session before Nov. 3. In other words, the window opens today.

Speck links the move to pre-election optimism. He said the rise “is clearly triggered by these elections, as evidenced by the high accuracy rate.”

Bank of America Expects Strong Finish To 2026, But With a Caveat

Paul Ciana, technical strategist at Bank of America Global Research, sees midterm years as the soft spot of the four-year presidential cycle, at least until the fourth quarter.

Since 1940, the S&P 500 has averaged a 4.22% gain in midterm years, compared with 8.85% across all years, according to Ciana.

The fourth quarter flips that.

The index rose in 86% of midterm-year fourth quarters, by an average of 6.6%, against a 78% hit rate and a 3.87% average gain for all years.

Ciana summed up the S&P 500’s midterm profile as “an underdog, but Santa rally outperforms.”

He also flagged the exception that matters most for 2026, the second year of President Donald Trump‘s second term. In 2018, the second year of his first term, the S&P 500 ended the year down more than 6.5%, with no Santa rally.

Read Also: Tech-to-Defensive Rotation, GM Stock Logs Worst Week Since 2023: This Week on Wall Street

Not Everyone Wants to Buy Before the Vote

The S&P 500 — as tracked by the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY) — closed Monday at 7,676.77, up 11.6% this year and about 2.1% below its record high of 7,844.52.

Ed Yardeni, president at Yardeni Research, is in no rush.

He kept a 7,900 year-end target for the S&P 500, about 3% above Monday’s close, and named an escalation of the Middle East war as their main concern.

He said they see some buying opportunities, but “better ones are likely after the November 3 midterm elections.”

The likely outcome also matters for what comes next.

Samuel Tombs, chief U.S. economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, expects divided government to freeze fiscal policy, with President Trump vetoing Democratic spending plans and new tariffs becoming less likely. In his view, less fiscal support should slow growth and give the Federal Reserve room to start easing next summer.

On Polymarket, traders give Democrats a 91.5% chance of winning the House and a 65.5% chance of taking the Senate, the latter up 1 percentage point over the past week.

History offers a tailwind, not a guarantee. Nineteen midterms is a small sample, and 2018 showed how quickly the fourth quarter can break the pattern even when the following year rewards patient investors.

headline: Michael Burry: Today's Market Mirrors the Eve of the Dot-Com Crash
summary: Michael Burry says today’s narrow, overvalued S&P 500 rally mirrors March 2000, explaining the similarities in a detailed analysis.
content_html:
Michael Burry says the stock market’s latest record high resembles the March 2000 dot-com bubble peak more than any other top in modern history.

In an Oct. 24 Substack post, Burry examined all 982 S&P 500 record closes since 1980. He scored each on seven measures of market internals, including the share of stocks near their highs and the share stuck in deep drawdowns.

  • PYPL stock is moving after earnings. Get all the details and data here. 

Two dates ranked at or beyond the 95th percentile of weakness on all seven: March 2000 and Oct. 6, 2026, the most recent record for the index tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:SPY). No other record high in 46 years did. Burry says the pattern first appeared this year on May 27.

A Narrow Rally

Only 19.3% of S&P 500 members traded within 10% of their 10-year highs at the Oct. 6 record, a reading in the 99.5th percentile. Fewer than 100 stocks made up the leadership group, something seen only once before, in March 2000, when the Nasdaq-heavy names behind the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) went vertical.

Those leaders also look tired. Burry found 58% of them sat 5% to 10% below their peaks, the highest share on record. March 2000 came in second at 40%.

At the other end, 23% of index members are what Burry calls "Busted," down more than 40% from their highs. The group sits a median 55% below its peaks.

Read Also: Michael Burry Eyes the Exit on Walmart, Alphabet and Valero

Priced Like 2000

Using his adjusted earnings figures, Burry estimates the S&P 500 trades at about 32 times earnings. The 2000 market traded at roughly 32 to 34 times.

However, the two eras differ. The 10 largest companies traded at 50 times trailing earnings in 2000 against 33 times today. Busted stocks were far cheaper back then, however, with a median of 10.2 times earnings versus 17.2 times now.

See More: Top Value Stocks

The 2000 Playbook

After the 2000 top, leaders posted a median 33% decline over 12 months and 50% over 18 months. Busted stocks rose a median 19% and 18% over the same stretches.

Burry cautions the pattern does not always hold. After the October 2007 peak, every group fell more than 40% over 18 months. Deep discounts offered little protection heading into the 2020 COVID crash either.

Still, he is positioned for a repeat. Burry holds beaten-down names such as Lululemon Athletica Inc. (NASDAQ:LULU), PayPal Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:PYPL) and Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE), set against short positions in AI and semiconductor stocks, a corner of the market tracked by funds like the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH).

Early returns lean his way. From Oct. 6 through Oct. 19, the 114 Busted stocks gained a median 3.2% while the S&P 500 fell 1.6%.

Burry called the move "almost certainly an indication of nothing."

Overall, the company has posted 14 straight double beats through the fourth quarter and is going for its 15th straight double beat on Wednesday.

What Experts Are Saying

With concerns about neocloud financing and capex by big technology companies, Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives sees pressure on the Magnificent Seven stocks like Microsoft ahead of earnings.

“This week will be an important one to gauge the demand trends/GPU building/enterprise capex-driven plans for the Big Tech stalwarts with all the markets watching,” Ives said.

Ives estimates that 800 to 1,000 more data centers will be built in the U.S. over the next few years. The analyst sees hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet as winners from this Fourth Industrial Revolution.

Ives highlights $850 billion of hyperscaler AI spend this year against a cloud backlog of more than $2 trillion, meaning capacity and not demand is the constraint.

“Microsoft is the cleanest expression of that setup. Azure moves the stock, but the read that matters is whether capacity is absorbed as fast as it lands, since backlog compounding ahead of revenue is the demand underwriting the capex.”

Ives maintained an Outperform rating on Microsoft stock with a price target of $615.

Freedom Capital Chief Market Strategist Jay Woods highlights Microsoft’s technicals in a weekly newsletter.

"The technical boundaries are quite clear, but quite wide. The $545-$555 area has become a stubborn ceiling, rejecting shares on three separate occasions, while the $340-$350 zone has repeatedly provided a floor," Woods said.

Woods said the stock has failed to break below its moving averages on several occasions.

"Three strikes, and the bulls are back on defense."

The market expert said a failure to break out could see the stock land closer to $460 or fall to the $350 support level.

"Microsoft remains in a longer-term trading range, and until buyers can convincingly clear that ceiling, history suggests chasing rallies near resistance may be a tough trade."

Investors and analysts will want to see the AI- and cloud-related revenue continue to increase given heavy spending in both areas.

headline: Refiner Stocks Suffer Worst Day Since the Tariff Shock: The Threat Is Not Cheaper Oil
summary: Refiner stocks Valero and Marathon post their worst day since April 2025 as Iran talks and Russian diesel test the crack-spread trade behind CRAK.
content_html:
The most profitable trade in U.S. energy this year just met its first real test. The threat did not come from oil falling. It came from the possibility that a war might end.

Shares of Valero Energy Corp. (NYSE:VLO) fell 8.4% in afternoon trading Tuesday, their steepest decline since early April 2025, when markets were absorbing President Donald Trump‘s “Liberation Day” tariffs.

Marathon Petroleum Corp. (NYSE:MPC) dropped 6.7%, its worst session since April 10, 2025. Phillips 66 (NYSE:PSX) lost 6.5%, the most since Dec. 16.

The VanEck Oil Refiners ETF (NYSE:CRAK) slid 3.3%, cushioned by its international holdings. The fund is still up nearly 65% in 2026, compared with a 12% gain for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY).

Valero Energy daily chart. Source: TradingView

A Margin Repricing, Not an Oil Story

West Texas Intermediate crude fell 1.8% to just under $100 a barrel. Gasoline futures lost 2.2%, and heating oil futures gave up 2.7%.

When refiners fall more than three times harder than the fuels they sell, the market is not repricing the barrel. Instead, it is repricing the crack spread.

The drop also interrupts a rare run. Marathon has risen for 10 straight months, matching the record streak it set between June 2012 and March 2013. October still has three sessions left to decide whether that streak survives.

Read Also: Oil Tops $100 on Iran Fears, Energy ETF XLE Hits New Record: Stock Market Today

Two Signals From Tehran and Moscow

On Tuesday, Iranian state media reported that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei met the country’s top security official after talks in Tehran with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.

Khamenei insisted that Iran’s conditions for ending the war must be met. Even so, the four countries agreed to keep talking.

Meanwhile, Russian diesel is moving west again. A tanker carrying 40,000 tons of Russian diesel left Primorsk on Oct. 22 and is due in New York around Nov. 7, Reuters reported last week.

It would be the first U.S. import of a Russian petroleum product since 2022. The cargo is moving under the sanctions relief tied to Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin.

Neither development adds much physical fuel today. Together, however, they attack the premise of the trade.

The Bet Was on Two Closed Chokepoints

Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz averaged 11.7 million barrels a day in October, according to Kpler data, up from 9.75 million in September but still about 18% below pre-war levels.

Russia banned diesel exports over the summer after Ukrainian drones damaged its refineries. In the U.S., distillate inventories stood about 9% below their five-year seasonal average in the week ended Oct. 16, Energy Information Administration data showed.

That squeeze pushed diesel margins above $100 a barrel at times. It also lifted U.S. retail diesel to $6.32 a gallon, from $3.63 a year ago.

For Valero, it produced a record quarter. Its third-quarter refining margin nearly tripled to $39.24 per barrel. Net income attributable to shareholders reached $6.8 billion, or $23.89 per share.

A refinery in this environment works like a toll bridge over a flooded river. The toll is worth most when every other crossing is under water.

Talks in Tehran and tankers out of Primorsk do not lower the water today. They do, however, give the flood a timeline.

Read Also: Nasdaq 100 Climbs on Chip Rally, Boeing Sinks 10%: Stock Market Today

Valero Saw the Headlines Coming

On last Thursday’s earnings call, Valero Chief Operating Officer Gary Simmons addressed the pressure directly.

“Some of the downward pressure on cracks is really related to more headlines, [but] when you digest the data and you look at how much volume is actually coming out, and then lifting of sanctions is more just a change in trade flows, I think we will see a recovery in cracks moving forward,” Simmons said.

He added that the Russian deal did not represent a “significant volume.”

Wall Street had flagged the same risks a month earlier. On Sept. 22, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne downgraded both Valero and Marathon to Hold from Buy, with price targets of $401 and $413, respectively.

“The current share price implies 2030 midcycle margins near 2025 levels,” Byrne said in the note.

He named diesel demand destruction, an end to the war and political intervention as the key risks. Five weeks later, two of those three surfaced in the same week.

The Squeeze Has Not Gone Away

The physical market is still tight. Brent trades near $110 a barrel, and the first Russian diesel cargo has not yet reached New York.

Bjarne Schieldrop of SEB said, “There is a significant risk premium in crude oil prices.”

For refiners, the question is not whether that premium exists. It is how long it stays inside fuel margins.

The refining trade of 2026 was never just a bet on oil. It was a bet that two of the world’s most important fuel chokepoints would stay shut at the same time. On Tuesday, investors started to price in what happens when one of them begins to open.

headline: S&P 500 Rose 14% In A Year And Got Cheaper
summary: SPY rose 14% in a year and its P/E fell from 28.6x to 24.5x as earnings grew about a third, with the Mag 7 delivering half the growth.
content_html:
On 8 October 2025, JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) Chief Executive Jamie Dimon told the BBC he was “far more worried” than others about a serious market correction. He put the odds near 30%.

A year later, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) is up 14%. It also trades at a lower multiple than it did on the day Dimon spoke.

In a less obvious way, part of the correction he predicted has already happened. SPY’s price-to-earnings multiple fell while its price rose. The reason is that earnings grew more than twice as fast as the price.

Price Up, P/E Down

A year ago, the market was expensive. SPY traded at 28.6x the past year’s earnings of its companies. A few weeks earlier, its P/E had hit its highest level in almost a decade.

Then earnings went on a run. Over the past year, the price alone climbed 13%. Over the same period, the earnings of SPY’s companies climbed about a third. That gap did the correcting: the P/E slid to 24.5x.

That still leaves SPY above its median since 2017. It has come down from the top of its range to just above the middle.

Seven Companies, Half The Growth

Split SPY in two, and the picture sharpens. On one side are the Magnificent 7, or Mag 7: Apple Inc. (AAPL), Microsoft Corp. (MSFT), Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), Alphabet Inc. (GOOGL), Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN), Meta Platforms Inc. (META) and Tesla Inc. (TSLA). On the other side are the remaining 493 companies.

The two groups’ share prices moved in step. Both rose between 12% and 13% over the year. Their earnings went separate ways. Mag 7 earnings rose about two-thirds, while the other 493’s rose about a quarter.

That made the seven companies the engine of the year. They delivered about half of SPY’s earnings growth. Their P/E also fell the most, from 39x to 26x.

The Index Tilted Toward Tech

The tilt started long before this year. In October 2017, the Mag 7 produced about an eighth of SPY’s earnings. Today, they produce about a third. Their weight in the fund has followed the earnings up to about the same share.

They are also far better at turning sales into earnings. The Mag 7 keep about 34% of their sales as earnings, compared with about 11% for the other 493. That mix is one reason SPY can trade above its median since 2017: the index now holds a bigger slice of its most profitable businesses.

What Comes Next

Analysts expect the rest of the market to pick up the pace. Their estimates have the other 493 growing earnings faster than the Mag 7 in the fourth quarter. SPY trades at 18.6x the earnings expected over the next 12 months, a multiple that assumes the run continues.

Big Tech’s third-quarter reports continue this week with Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon.

The biggest tech story of the season is still ahead. Anthropic, the maker of Claude and one of the leaders of the AI market, filed for its long-awaited IPO on Monday. Its Nasdaq debut is expected in mid-November. Investors have talked about a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. If Anthropic raises the $100 billion it is reported to seek, it would be the largest IPO on record.

Anthropic will need time before it can join SPY. The S&P 500 requires a year of trading and positive earnings over the past four quarters. Once Anthropic qualifies, it would be one of the largest additions in the index’s history. It would also tilt SPY further toward tech.

Dimon gave a correction 30% odds. The market took the other 70% and still came out cheaper.

headline: Oct. 28 (Today) is the Best Trading Day of the Year: But 2026 Has a Catch
summary: Oct. 28 is historically the best trading day for the U.S. Here's why 2026 could be different.
content_html:
Based on more than 50 years of stock trading in the U.S., one day has to be the best day for investors. That day happens to be today, Oct. 28, with an average daily gain of 0.50% dating back to 1950.

This year’s best day could be spoiled by a major event.

Best Trading Day of the Year

For many years, Oct. 28 has been known as the historical best trading day for the S&P 500, which is tracked by the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY).

Carson Group Chief Market Strategist Ryan Detrick, who is well-known on social media for his charts and historical trading patterns, highlighted the day earlier this week and why 2026 is different.

"Something has to give, as October 28th is historically the best day of the year. This day falls on this Wednesday and that is also a Fed meeting. Under Kevin Warsh we’ve seen the S&P 500 fall 1.21% in June, 1.52% in July and 0.45% in September. Which history will repeat?" Detrick tweeted.

Those declines refer to the dates of the Federal Reserve meetings, led by Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh in those respective months.

"In other words, when Warsh talks, the market hasn’t liked it, but tomorrow is usually a good day. Time to buckle up!" Detrick said in a blog post.

The Federal Reserve is expected to hold rates steady on Wednesday. A decision to cut or raise rates could create high volatility for a market that has not priced in either of those outcomes. Even without a rate change, the markets could trade uneasily on Wednesday.

While there is no guarantee that Oct. 28 will be the best trading day each year, or have a positive return each year, the 2026 calendar could come with an asterisk due to it also being a Fed day.

A chart shared by Detrick shows that Oct. 28, which is also the market expert’s birthday, is the best date based on average returns since 1950.

The date beats out Dec. 26 and April 9, which have average gains of 0.48% and 0.44%, respectively.

On the other side of the spectrum is Oct. 19, which is the worst day of the year, with an average decline of 0.52% since 1950. This year, Oct. 19 saw a modest 0.4% gain for the S&P 500.

Fighting Against History

The 2026 market may go down as one of the most unusual, with new highs set despite macroeconomic uncertainties and periods of war.

headline: Dot-Com Style Rotation? Strategists Warn Improving Market Breadth Could Be A Bull Trap: 'Be Careful What You Wish For'

content_html:
Market strategists from Carson Research caution that the recent broadening of stock market gains away from technology companies into defensive sectors mirrors the rotation seen during the dot-com bubble, warning investors to “be careful what you wish for.”

Recent Market Divergence

Chief Market Strategist Ryan Detrick and Chief Macro Strategist Sonu Varghese highlighted a recent trading session where the broader index declined while a majority of individual stocks advanced.

Varghese noted that on a recent Thursday, 324 out of 500 S&P 500 stocks gained. However, Varghese stated the S&P 500 fell 1.4%, and technology was down 3.3%.

He stated that the advancing stocks were led by defense, consumer staples, utilities, and healthcare. Addressing the desire for wider market participation beyond technology, Varghese warned, “Be careful what you wish for. You get more breadth, but do you want that to be led by defensives?”

Detrick noted that on the same day, the equal-weight S&P 500 outperformed the capitalization-weighted index by almost 2%. Detrick said it was the “best breadth day on a 1% down day” seen recently.

Emphasizing the necessity of the technology sector, Detrick stated, “You need tech leadership.” Detrick added that technology has been a top-performing sector in almost every bull market over the last 100 years.

Read Also: S&P Changes the Rules – Here's New Value Vs. Growth

Historical Parallels to the Dot-Com Era

Varghese compared the current market conditions to the early 2000s. He stated, “The dot-com bubble… it didn’t end with a bust, right? It ended with rotation.”

According to Varghese, between April 2000 and December 2000, the S&P 500 fell 11%, and technology dropped 48%. During that same period, Varghese noted that utilities were up 46%, financials gained 23%, and consumer staples rose 41%.

Pointing to this historical period, Varghese warned that an increase in market breadth led by defensive stocks could be a negative signal for the market. “That was a rotation,” Varghese said. “I’m not saying we’re in that now, but that’s my ‘be careful what you wish for.'”

How Has the Stock Market Performed?

headline: Forget the Halloween Indicator? 5 ETFs to Consider As ‘Sell in May’ Loses Its Edge
summary: The Halloween indicator is losing its edge as seasonal S&P 500 returns converge. 5 ETFs could help investors hedge a potential summer stock market selloff.
content_html:
The stock market’s famous "Sell in May and Go Away" strategy is losing its edge, raising the question of whether investors should hedge seasonal weakness rather than exit equities altogether.

The Halloween indicator, which favors holding stocks from November through April, has historically delivered stronger returns. But that gap has largely disappeared. According to Yahoo Finance, the S&P 500 averaged gains of 6.8% during November–April and 6.9% during May–October over the past decade. The summer stretch also gained about 23% in 2025.

With the seasonal advantage fading, investors could consider ETFs that seek to reduce equity volatility, provide defensive exposure or diversify portfolio risks.

5 ETFs to Watch If Summer Volatility Returns

1. iShares MSCI USA Min Vol Factor ETF (BATS:USMV)

USMV targets U.S. stocks with lower volatility characteristics than the broader equity market. Its rules-based approach offers investors a way to maintain equity exposure while seeking a smoother ride during market turbulence. However, lower volatility does not guarantee smaller losses in every downturn.

2. iShares MSCI USA Quality Factor ETF (BATS:QUAL)

QUAL focuses on U.S. companies with stronger quality characteristics relative to peers in their respective sectors. Companies with robust profitability and balance sheets may be better positioned to weather economic uncertainty, although quality stocks can still decline sharply during broad market selloffs.

3. State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLP)

XLP provides exposure to consumer staples companies spanning food, beverages, household products and personal care. Demand for these everyday products can be more resilient during economic slowdowns, making the fund a potential defensive allocation. But sector concentration and valuation risks remain.

4. iShares 1-3 Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:SHY)

Investors seeking diversification beyond equities could consider SHY, which tracks short-term U.S. Treasury securities. Its relatively short duration generally makes it less sensitive to interest-rate changes than long-duration bond ETFs, although its price can still fluctuate.

5. AGF U.S. Market Neutral Anti-Beta Fund (NYSE:BTAL)

For a more tactical approach, BTAL seeks to benefit from the relative performance of lower-beta stocks over higher-beta stocks through long and short equity positions. It is not a conventional market hedge and can lose money when its strategy moves against it.

Should Investors Sell in May?

History offers reasons for caution, not a reliable trading signal. The S&P 500 suffered losses of about 15% during May–October 2001, 18% in 2002 and 30% in 2008, according to Yahoo Finance. Yet strong summer rallies have also rewarded investors who remained invested.

Rather than betting on a calendar pattern, investors could compare defensive ETFs with the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) across historical May–October periods, measuring total returns, maximum drawdowns and volatility.

Hedging seasonal weakness may be more practical than abandoning the market. No ETF guarantees protection, and a defensive allocation can underperform when equities rally. Investors should weigh costs, taxes, risk tolerance and time horizons before changing their portfolios.

headline: Tom Lee Sees 'Big Beats' Ahead, Says Kevin Warsh-Led Fed Won't Slow AI Growth Despite Inflation: 'Good News Is Good News'
summary: Tom Lee says the Fed won't slow AI ahead of tech earnings, but FOMC minutes reveal AI investments are actively driving up inflation.
content_html:
Fundstrat’s Tom Lee believes that the Federal Reserve will not attempt to curb artificial intelligence expansion, yet recent Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) minutes indicate that AI investments are actively driving up inflation and tech stocks are positioned to deliver ‘big beats’ during earnings.

Lee’s Bullish Market Outlook

During a CNBC interview on Wednesday, Lee said that the Fed does not view AI as an inflation driver. Lee stated he was “happy to hear him say that he didn’t think AI growth is necessarily inflationary.”

Looking ahead to upcoming tech earnings, Lee argued that the central bank’s stance paves the way for market gains. “I think you’re going to be in a position to say big beats are great because the Fed’s not going to try to slow AI growth,” Lee said.

He added that investors can now evaluate tech performance under the premise that “good news is good news.”

Read Also: 'Wall Street Cares About Free Cash Flow Now': Bloomberg's Ed Ludlow on Buyouts and AI Spending

Fed Records Show Inflation Pressure

Despite Lee’s assertions, the Federal Reserve’s official records present a contrasting economic reality. The FOMC minutes from Sept. 15-16, 2026, explicitly state that “surging AI-related investments were contributing to inflation pressures.”

The minutes further detail that recent consumer price increases were partly driven by “an increase in technology-related consumer goods prices associated with the AI buildout.”

Fed officials also expressed concern that this “AI buildout could cause aggregate demand to outpace aggregate supply over the medium term, putting upward pressure on inflation”.

During his Oct. 28, press conference, Chairman Kevin Warsh noted that “inflation remains elevated.” Warsh highlighted that “high-tech investment is leading the acceleration” in capital expenditures, stating that “these trends bear watching.”

Tech Earnings Anticipation

Trivariate’s Adam Parker supported Lee’s market optimism during the CNBC segment, noting that “the earnings power and cash flows of these businesses are going to be pretty good.”

headline: Top Economist Slams Trump’s $21 Trillion Investment Boast — ‘The Jobs Are American. The Profits Aren’t’
summary: Economist Justin Wolfers says foreign-built factories bring U.S. jobs but not profits, taking aim at Trump’s $21 trillion investment boast.
content_html:
Foreign-built factories bring American jobs but not American profits, economist Justin Wolfers argued, taking aim at President Donald Trump‘s boasts of $21 trillion in investment in the U.S.

Profits Go Abroad

In a post on X Wednesday, Wolfers said the jobs from a foreign-built factory stay in the U.S., but the profits go to the companies abroad.

“When a foreign company builds a factory here, the jobs are American. The profits aren’t.”

“Selling away more of America is a strange thing for a president to brag about,” the University of Michigan professor added.

Trump Links Investment Boast to Tariffs

Earlier this month, Trump said at a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, “We have $21 trillion being invested in our country, more than at any time, for any country anywhere in the world.” The White House’s own investment tracker adds up to $11.3 trillion at face value.

At a rally in Georgia on Saturday, Trump said Audi, the premium unit of Volkswagen AG, will invest about $4 billion in a Georgia assembly plant and create about 4,500 jobs. Audi has no U.S. plant, and tariffs cost it about $1.4 billion last year.

Foreign Investment and Trade Deficit ‘Two Sides of the Same Coin’

Wolfers said foreign investment and trade deficits are linked, since money flowing in from abroad is the flip side of goods flowing in.

“When the president says that what he wants is more foreign investment, it is necessarily the case that that will lead to a larger trade deficit. They’re two sides of the same coin,” he said.

The U.S. goods trade deficit unexpectedly widened 2.1% to $134.9 billion in September, the largest since March 2025, as imports hit a record $344.1 billion, the Commerce Department said Wednesday.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that rising debt yields in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector are not a concern, describing neocloud companies as a minor part of the broader market. This statement follows recent declines in the stock and bond prices of neocloud provider CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV).

No Concern Over Tech Borrowing

Speaking with CNBC’s Brian Sullivan on Wednesday, Bessent addressed questions regarding double-digit yields on AI-related debt. Sullivan asked if the Treasury Secretary was worried about the lower end of the credit spectrum.

“Look, we, we monitor all of this,” Bessent told CNBC. “I don’t think it’s problematic at all because, you know, we’re seeing that the neo-clouds are a small component of the overall ecosystem.”

Bessent further noted that capital continues to flow into the technology sector despite rising borrowing costs. “And we’re still seeing the financing getting done. We’re still seeing the deals get done,” Bessent said. He added that some companies, such as Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), are choosing to “finance with equity.”

headline: US Economy Grew 3.4% in the Third Quarter, Fed's Favorite Inflation Gauge Matches Forecasts (UPDATED)
summary: The US economy grew 3.4% annualized in the third quarter, beating the 3.2% forecast, while September PCE inflation rose 3.6%, matching expectations.
content_html:
Editor’s Note: Article updated with additional content.

The U.S. economy grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis’s advance estimate released Thursday.

The outcome topped economists’ expectations of 3.2% and marked an acceleration from the 2.2% growth in the second quarter.

Real consumer spending grew 3.8%, the same pace as in the second quarter.

In a separate release, September’s personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.6% from a year earlier in September, matching expectations and accelerating from 3.4% in August.

On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.5%, also as expected.

Core PCE rose 3.1% year over year, in line with estimates and up from 3% previously. Month over month, core prices rose 0.3%, matching the consensus.

Personal income rose 0.2% in September, below the 0.3% forecast. Personal spending increased 0.5%, versus expectations of 0.6% and 0.9% in August.

On Wednesday, the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at 3.75%-4.00%, pausing after the September hike.

Businesses Stocked Up as AI Spending Kept Flowing

Investment drove most of the acceleration. Companies built up inventories, led by wholesalers and manufacturers.

Equipment spending also rose, led by computers and peripheral equipment, as the AI buildout continued.

However, much of that equipment came from abroad. Imports rose faster than in the second quarter, led by capital goods.

Because GDP subtracts imports, that weighed on the headline figure. Exports fell, mainly because petroleum shipments dropped.

Fed Hike Bets Hold Steady

Shortly before the release, traders saw an 83% probability of a 25-basis-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

That was little changed from 84.2% a day earlier, but up from 73.3% a week ago and 49.4% a month ago.

Interest rate swaps were little moved after the data.

Treasury Yields Hover Near 5%

The bond market took the report calmly.

The 10-year Treasury yield edged up less than 1 basis point to 5.01%, holding just above the 5% mark. The 2-year yield, which is more sensitive to Fed expectations, rose 1 basis point to 4.70%. Meanwhile, the 30-year yield was flat at 5.33%.

The U.S. dollar index was unchanged at 102.15.

Precious metals came under pressure. Spot gold fell 1.1% to around $4,025 an ounce, while silver dropped 2.8% to $52.45.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) fell 1.5% to roughly $80,040.

Big Tech Earnings Drag Nasdaq Futures

Corporate earnings, rather than macro data, drove stock moves.

Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.2%, and S&P 500 futures slipped 0.4%. Dow futures lost 0.3%. Small caps went the other way, with Russell 2000 futures up 0.3%.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) fell 1.3% in premarket trading. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) declined 0.4%.

Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) was the biggest drag, sliding 11.5% to around $288. Its third-quarter report, released after Wednesday’s close, disappointed investors, even though Google Cloud grew strongly.

Software stocks sold off after earnings. Fortinet Inc. (NASDAQ:FTNT) plunged 27.6%, and ServiceNow Inc. (NYSE:NOW) sank 18.3% after its outlook fell short of expectations.

Caterpillar Inc. (NYSE:CAT) dropped 11% after third-quarter revenue missed forecasts. Higher tariff costs and rising inventories also weighed on the shares. As one of the most heavily weighted stocks in the Dow, Caterpillar pulled the blue-chip index’s futures lower.

Marvell Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MRVL) fell 12.1% on reports that it is in talks to buy Lumentum Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:LITE). Lumentum rose 5.4%.

On the upside, Carvana Co. (NYSE:CVNA) jumped 8.6% after quarterly revenue topped $8 billion for the first time. Chipotle Mexican Grill Inc. (NYSE:CMG) rose 8.4% after reporting its third straight quarter of traffic growth.

The iShares Russell 1000 Value ETF (NYSE:IWD) is up 5% in October and touched a record high of $260.64 on Thursday.

Meanwhile, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) has gained just 0.8% over the same stretch.

That 4.2-percentage-point gap is the widest monthly outperformance for value since February 2001, in data going back to IWD’s launch in 2000.

Against growth, the split is even wider.

The iShares Russell 1000 Growth ETF (NYSE:IWF) is down 3.3% this month. Year to date, IWD is up 23.8%, while IWF has gained only 2.4%.

Wall Street Is Rotating, Not Retreating

Thursday’s session showed the shift in real time.

Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) fell 12% after a disappointing third-quarter report. ServiceNow Inc. (NYSE:NOW) sank 25% on slower contract growth guidance.

On the same day, however, the Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLV) touched an all-time high.

Read Also: ServiceNow Stock Plunges on Worst Day in Company’s History: AI Wins Can’t Hide a Bookings Slowdown

Investors are “increasingly distinguishing between companies successfully monetizing AI and those still incurring significant capital expenditures without a clear revenue or cash flow payoff,” Chris Osmond, chief investment officer at Fifth Third Wealth Advisors, said in emailed comments.

“The resulting environment favors selectivity: current cash flow over distant promises, balance-sheet strength over leverage, and companies that can demonstrate AI monetization rather than simply announce higher AI investment,” Osmond added.

February 2001: When The New Economy Ran Out Of Road

In early 2001, the Federal Reserve had already cut rates twice, and many investors treated the tech selloff as a buying opportunity. February proved them wrong.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) lost 26.2% that month, IWF dropped 17.8% and SPY fell 9.5%. IWD, by contrast, slipped just 2.7%.

Leadership changed hands. Stocks priced for perfection were repriced, while companies with ordinary earnings at ordinary valuations held their ground.

Why 2026 Is Not A Carbon Copy

In February 2001, value won because everything else fell faster. This October, value is rising in absolute terms, and the S&P 500 is still positive for the month.

In other words, money is moving within the market, not leaving it.

The rate backdrop also runs the other way. The Fed held rates at 3.75%-4.00% on Wednesday after raising them in September, and two policymakers dissented in favor of another hike.

As a result, the pressure falls hardest on companies whose value rests on profits far in the future.

“There are mounting signs of markets becoming increasingly unwilling to fund the AI infrastructure build-out,” Sebastian Raedler, investment strategist at Bank of America, said in an Oct. 23 Bank of America Global Research report.

Dennis DeBusschere of 22V Research made a similar point in an Oct. 27 note: “Cash return is scarcer now because of the capital committed to the AI buildout.”

Read Also: Alphabet Stock Set for Worst Day Since March 2020: Search Slowdown Overshadows Cloud Boom

The Question February 2001 Leaves Open

Not everyone sees a broader top forming.

“We don’t believe stocks are about to go into a bear market, despite all of the angst we’ve seen and heard this month about Cap Ex spending,” Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management, said in emailed comments.

Still, in 2001 value stocks’ best month against the market came early in a multiyear leadership change, not at its end.

Whether October 2026 opens a similar cycle depends on one thing Wall Street can’t price yet: how fast AI spending turns into AI revenue.

Why Bitcoin Looks Like It’s Repeating the SpaceX Playbook

Cowen said on the NFA Live podcast that Bitcoin’s current price action looks "almost the exact same" as its drawdown in the 30 days before SpaceX’s IPO, based on a normalized return chart comparing both periods.
