He pointed to the S&P 500’s (NYSE:SPY) roughly 5% drop ahead of the SpaceX IPO as a similar precedent.

Cowen said he expects long-term Treasury yields to spike into the midterms before dropping shortly afterward, drawing a direct parallel to 2018, when the Fed paused rate hikes around that year’s midterms before raising rates again in December despite a falling stock market. 

He noted the Fed’s December 2018 projections pointed to two rate hikes in 2019 that never materialized, and said the market currently prices in two hikes for 2027 that could similarly get priced out if growth concerns take over from inflation concerns.

Why AI-Driven Bank Hacks Are an Underpriced Risk

Panelist Rob pointed to a wave of AI-assisted bank hacks hitting seven countries at once:

  • Latin America: a gang used Claude, Grok and Kimi to steal banking credentials
  • Japan: hackers breached GMO’s currency trading service and demanded $50 million in crypto

He called the scale of these attacks unprecedented compared to anything seen before.

Cowen flagged a more technical risk: recent OpenAI research disproving the exponential time hypothesis, a mathematical assumption underlying much of modern cryptography. 

He said if similar research eventually challenges the broader P versus NP problem, it could theoretically threaten the computational difficulty that blockchain security relies on, though he stressed that outcome remains purely speculative for now.

Why the Panel Expects Midterm Volatility to Fade by 2027

Cowen expects the S&P 500 to stay rangebound until the midterms, followed by a potential final drop before markets rebound heading into 2027. 

Rob cited Polymarket data showing a 68% implied probability that Democrats retake the Senate, noting prediction markets have recently missed high-confidence outcomes in Brazil, Serbia and Israel.

content_html:
Alphabet, Inc’s (NASDAQ:GOOGL) shares plunged nearly 13% on Thursday, wiping out about $482 billion in market value. It was the second-largest one-day loss ever recorded for a U.S.-listed company, behind Nvidia’s $593 billion wipeout in January 2025.

The selloff followed Alphabet’s third-quarter results, which raised concerns about whether its massive artificial intelligence investments are generating sufficient returns.

The concerns extend beyond Alphabet. Amazon.com, Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN) reported 39% growth in AWS revenue, but its trailing 12-month free cash flow fell to a record outflow of more than $42 billion, reflecting increased infrastructure spending.

For ETF investors, the question is whether growing exposure to mega-cap technology companies could amplify losses as investors reassess the returns on AI investments.

Read Also: Alphabet Bulls Dig in After Messy Q3: 'AI Stack Keeps Us Bullish' Cantor Says

QQQ and XLC face concentration risks

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is particularly exposed to this trend. Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT), Alphabet and Amazon are among its largest holdings, making it vulnerable to a broader reassessment of AI valuations and spending.

The Communication Services Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLC) faces even greater direct Alphabet exposure. Its two share classes together account for a substantial portion of the portfolio, alongside Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META).

Thursday’s trading highlighted the impact of these exposures. XLC fell 1.87%, while the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLK) declined 1.18%. The broader SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) lost 0.37%.

Could Equal-Weight ETFs Offer a Buffer?

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP) gained 1.2% on Thursday, even as SPY declined 0.37%.

Unlike traditional market-cap-weighted funds, RSP assigns approximately equal weights to S&P 500 constituents, limiting the influence of individual mega-cap stocks on portfolio performance.

Another alternative is the Invesco NASDAQ 100 Equal Weighted ETF (NASDAQ:QQQE), which provides exposure to Nasdaq-100 companies without allowing the largest constituents to dominate.

However, equal weighting is not necessarily safer. It can increase exposure to smaller, more volatile companies and underperform when mega-cap stocks lead the market.

Market Volatility Becomes Difficult to Ignore

U.S.-listed stocks suffered 18 sessions in 2026 when at least $200 billion in market value was erased—more than the 13 recorded in all of 2025 and more than any year before 2022.

As AI infrastructure spending rises, investors may increasingly distinguish between companies translating AI investments into revenue and those struggling to generate sufficient cash flow.

For ETF investors, portfolio concentration could matter as much as choosing which sector to own.

Trump’s Economic Claims

On Oct. 30, Trump posted on social media that inflation is “way down” under his leadership. In the same publication, Trump stated that income for people and companies is “way up” and declared that “The Golden Age of America Is Upon Us”.

Read Also: Kevin Warsh Views Economy as 'Strong' and 'Pointing in the Right Direction': Crypto Bettors Weigh Recession Odds

Federal Reserve’s Assessment

Trump’s statements contrast with the assessments provided by the Federal Reserve earlier in the week. On Oct. 28, the Federal Open Market Committee released a statement noting that “Inflation remains elevated.”

During a press conference the same day, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh stated that “Americans, of course, are still dealing with inflation that has been running above the Committee’s objective for close to 6 years.”

Warsh added that “inflation is too high” and noted that “Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks”. Warsh also stated that “It’s our responsibility to get inflation down”.

The Sept. 15-16, 2026, Federal Open Market Committee minutes indicated that recent price increases were driven by “the effects of past tariff increases, higher energy and input costs stemming from geopolitical developments, and an increase in technology-related consumer goods prices associated with the AI buildout.”

Monetary Policy Stance

To address economic conditions, the Federal Open Market Committee announced on October 28, 2026, that it “decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4%.”

The committee stated that the “accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2% goal.” The Federal Reserve reaffirmed that “The Committee will deliver price stability.”

content_html:
Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC) is on track to match its worst day on record, and the damage is spreading across chipmakers and the Nasdaq.

The company’s stock fell about 29.6% by midday, matching its 29.6% plunge in July 1974, the steepest one-day drop in its history. The downfall erased about $144 billion of market value by midday. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $15.5 billion and adjusted earnings to 25 cents a share, but Wall Street expected roughly $17 billion and 43 cents.

Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya downgraded Intel to Neutral from Buy and cut his price objective to $100 from $145. He said Intel’s “agentic tide” in data center chips is “more than offset by PC/supply headwinds.”

Read Also: QUICK SPARK: Intel Stock Drops 28%, Eyes Worst Day Since July 1974

The Selloff Did Not Stay With Intel

Aside from Intel, losses from Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD), Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO), Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) and Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM) add up to roughly $631 billion.

Nvidia alone shed about $212 billion as it fell 4.1%, while AMD dropped 11.1% and Qualcomm 11.0%.

The S&P 500 fell 125 points, or 1.6%, to 7,596 by midday.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 386 points, or 0.7%, to 51,957, with Nvidia the heaviest drag.

The Nasdaq 100 dropped 3.2%, on track for its worst session since June 23. All of the Magnificent Seven traded lower, and Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) held up best, down 0.4%.

The Russell 2000 slid 1.8%. The CBOE Volatility Index jumped 15.4% to 19.85.

Treasuries Offer Little Shelter

The 10-year yield rose 2 basis points to 4.95%, while the 2-year yield also rose 2 basis points to 4.62%. The 30-year yield climbed 3 basis points to 5.32%.

Oil extended its rally after reports of a tanker attack near the Strait of Hormuz. West Texas Intermediate crude rose 2.1% to $104.14 a barrel, and Brent gained 2.4% to $113.44.

Precious metals went the other way. Gold fell 3.1% to $3,908.10 an ounce, its lowest level since early October 2025, as traders weighed the risk of another Federal Reserve hike after two officials dissented in favor of an increase this week. Silver lost 5.9% to $49.28, back below $50.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) slipped 0.8% to about $77,280 after reports of a major Binance security breach.

Month-to-date, the Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLV) is up 10.3%, outperforming the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) by 11 percentage points. That’s the widest monthly outperformance of health care stocks over the S&P 500 since the fund’s launch in December 1998.

headline: Alphabet Posts Worst Week Since 2011, Intel Suffers Record Crash as Warsh Sees 'Cracks': This Week on Wall Street
summary: Alphabet logs its worst week since 2011 and Intel its worst day ever as the AI trade cracks, while health care posts a record month against the market.
content_html:
The artificial intelligence trade broke down for a third consecutive week, and the damage this time came straight from the balance sheets of the companies funding the buildout.

Two weeks ago, investors worried about valuations. Last week, they asked who would pay the bill. This week, Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) , Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC) handed them the invoice.

By Friday afternoon, the Nasdaq 100 had slid about 4% on the session to its lowest level since early August and was down roughly 2.5% for the week, its third straight weekly decline. The S&P 500 was off about 2% on the day and close to 1% on the week.

• Alphabet stock is facing resistance. Why are GOOG shares declining?

Alphabet’s Worst Week In 15 Years

Alphabet Inc. lit the fuse on Wednesday night. Revenue came in short of expectations, free cash flow swung to a roughly $9 billion outflow, and management signaled that capital spending will climb again in 2027.

Thursday’s 13% drop was the steepest single-session decline in the stock’s history and erased roughly $482 billion of market value. Shares are down about 13% for the week, the worst weekly showing since August 2011.

The pain spread across the sector. The Communication Services Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLC) is on track for an eighth straight daily loss, its longest losing streak since the fund launched in 2018.

Amazon added to the pressure Thursday night. Earnings of $1.89 per share fell short of the $1.96 consensus, while the company said 2027 capital expenditures will be “meaningfully more” than this year’s roughly $220 billion.

Read Also: Alphabet Sinks 11.8%, Small Caps Rally on Strong GDP Growth: Stock Market Today

Intel’s Worst Day Ever

Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC) delivered the week’s most violent move. The chipmaker guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, well below the $17.07 billion analysts expected, and said it does not expect positive cash flow this year as PC demand weakens.

Shares collapsed about 30% on Friday, the worst session in Intel’s trading history, with no comparable decline in more than 11,700 sessions since 1980.

Bank of America Global Research downgraded the stock to Neutral from Buy, saying in a Friday report that the agentic server CPU tide “is more than offset by PC/supply headwinds.”

Chart: Intel Plunged 30%, Surpassing July 1974’s Drop

Read Also: Chip Stocks Lose $1 Trillion as Intel Sinks 28%

Warsh: ‘Interest Rates Get In The Cracks’

The Federal Reserve left the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday. The decision passed 10-2, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissenting in favor of a quarter-point hike.

Chair Kevin Warsh declined to commit to a December move.

“I don’t believe in forward guidance absent exigent circumstances,” he said.

Asked whether higher borrowing costs could cool the AI boom, he offered a line that aged quickly over the next 48 hours.

“Interest rates get in the cracks. Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything,” Warsh said.

He indicated that investors have grown more selective about where they put money, noting that credit spreads on some assets have blown out while financial conditions have tightened for others.

Thursday’s data gave both camps ammunition.

Third-quarter GDP expanded at a 3.4% annualized pace, ahead of the 3.2% forecast, while the PCE price index accelerated to 3.6% year over year from 3.4%. Weekly jobless claims slipped to 194,000, below the 199,000 expected.

CME FedWatch now prices a 74% probability of a December rate hike, down from 85% right after Wednesday’s meeting.

Treasuries Catch A Bid

Bonds became the safe harbor. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to about 4.92%, after touching 4.89% earlier in the day, the lowest since early September. The 2-year yield dropped to 4.57% and the 30-year held near 5.31%.

Health Care’s Best Month Ever Against the Market

As money fled technology, defensive sectors absorbed it.

The Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLV) is on track for its best month ever relative to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), outperforming by 11% in October, according to data going back to 1998. The previous record was March 2020, at 9.9%.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (NASDAQ:IBB) climbed to an all-time high this week. Regeneron Pharmaceuticals Inc. (NASDAQ:REGN) surged 11% on Friday, its best day since October 2025.

Best and Worst S&P 500 Stocks This Week

The top performers in the S&P 500 this week were Carvana Co. (NYSE:CVNA), up nearly 20%; Pentair plc (NYSE:PNR), up 19.6%, and Vertiv Holdings Co. (NYSE:VRT), up 18%.

At the bottom, Reddit Inc. (NYSE:RDDT) lost about 38% after CEO Steve Huffman warned daily active visitors could fall by a low double-digit percentage in the fourth quarter.

ServiceNow Inc. (NYSE:NOW) dropped nearly 35% after its quarterly report, and Intel fell close to 27%.

Reddit’s 30% plunge on Friday was also the worst day in its history and stretched its losing run to eight sessions, a 41.9% slide.

Records and Streaks

Several stocks are writing history.

Albemarle Corp. (NYSE:ALB) is on track for a 10th straight weekly loss, down 36.9% over the stretch, the longest losing streak in data going back to 1994. The previous record was nine weeks in March 2000.

Interactive Brokers Group Inc. (NASDAQ:IBKR) is heading for a ninth straight weekly drop, a 20.5% decline that doubles as a new record, while SanDisk Corp. (NASDAQ:SNDK) has fallen six weeks in a row, losing 36.6%.

Boeing Co. (NYSE:BA) is down eight weeks in a row, its longest losing stretch since October 2023, and Robinhood Markets Inc. (NASDAQ:HOOD) is on a six-week slide of 30.7%.

On the upside, Marathon Petroleum Corp. (NYSE:MPC) is set for a 10th straight monthly gain, up 171%, matching its record from March 2013. HCA Healthcare Inc. (NYSE:HCA) has risen five months in a row, tying its March 2024 record, and Marriott International Inc. (NASDAQ:MAR) is up seven straight weeks.

Among Friday’s other movers, FedEx Freight Holding Co. (NASDAQ:FDXF) jumped 16%, its best day since May, and Global Payments Inc. (NYSE:GPN) rose 10%. Illumina Inc. (NASDAQ:ILMN) dropped 19%, its worst session since October 2016.

Detroit Rides The Rotation

General Motors Co. (NYSE:GM) gained about 15% this week, its best weekly performance since October 2025. The stock rallied 5.5% on Tuesday after GM announced it will move its listing to Nasdaq on Nov. 17 and invest in its Lansing Delta Township plant to build hybrid vehicles.

Ford Motor Co. (NYSE:F) added about 5% after third-quarter results topped expectations. Revenue reached $49.53 billion against a $46.24 billion estimate, and adjusted EPS of 49 cents beat the 41-cent consensus. Ford also lifted the bottom of its full-year adjusted EBIT guidance to $10.5 billion.

“Ford delivered a strong quarter as we’re entering a defining phase of the company’s transformation,” CEO Jim Farley said.

See More: Top Momentum Stocks

What’s Next: Apple, Midterms and Jobs

Next week brings no Fed meeting, but it does test whether the AI sell-off can find a floor.

Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) report Monday after the close. Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) and Super Micro Computer Inc. (NASDAQ:SMCI) follow on Tuesday, the same day Americans vote in the midterm elections. Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM) and Arm Holdings plc (NASDAQ:ARM) report Wednesday.

The week closes with the October jobs report on Friday, Nov. 6, the last payrolls print before the Fed’s December decision. After September’s 29,000 gain, traders will be watching for any sign the labor market is softening enough to take a December hike off the table.

The S&P 500’s retreat has coincided with a relatively strong earnings season. FactSet (NYSE:FDS) data shows that 60% of companies in the index have reported results, with blended earnings growth of 30%, above the 29% analysts expected.

The strong earnings growth has also coincided with the falling valuation, with its forward price-to-earnings ratio being 18.7, well below the five-year average of 19.8. This multiple is also below the ten-year average of 19.1.

The next important catalyst for the S&P 500 Index and its ETFs like VOO, SPY, and IVV will be more earnings from top companies. Some of the top companies to watch will be Apple, Palantir, AMD, Amgen, Arm Holdings, McDonald’s, and ConocoPhillips.

Amazon and Google dropped after committing to keep their capital spending and after their earnings showed that core revenue was slowing.

The S&P 500, Dow Jones, and Nasdaq 100 have pulled back over the past few weeks as investors rotate out of their artificial intelligence (AI) bets. The Dow has dropped 5.35% from its year-to-date high, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 have fallen 3.27% and 9.57%, respectively. This article looks at the top catalysts to watch this week.

headline: ‘Great For Our Farmers, Great For Our Country’: Trump Says ‘Concept of a Deal’ Reached With Canada
summary: Trump said the U.S. is “very close” to a Canada trade deal and that Ottawa would pay for the Keystone pipeline, days before the midterms.
content_html:
President Donald Trump said Sunday the U.S. is “very close” to a trade deal with Canada, one in which Ottawa would pay for the Keystone pipeline, days before the midterm elections.

US Has Been ‘Losing Money’ With Canada

Trump told reporters, ahead of a rally in Dubuque, Iowa, that he spoke with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and the two sides have “the concept of a deal” that would be “great for our farmers, great for our country and it’ll be fine for Canada, too.”

“We have been losing money for many years with Canada,” Trump said.

He added that “we are now very close to having a deal” after two conversations with his Canadian counterpart last week.

In a post on X, Carney described a “good conversation” with Trump on the future of trade, adding that their teams will now work “in the coming weeks” toward a deal that creates jobs, boosts affordability and respects Canada’s culture and sovereignty.

Read Also: Gavin Newsom Says Trump Delivering ‘Windfall’ Profits For 'Big Oil' Giants XOM, CVX Amid Iran War—Bernie Sanders Says Surge Is ‘Beyond Unacceptable’

Canada to Build Keystone Pipeline

Asked whether the Keystone pipeline is part of the deal, Trump said Canada would “build the Keystone pipeline” and “pay for all of it,” with the U.S. providing the route, which has “largely been determined.”

The President added that the U.S. farmers will pay no tariffs under the deal, noting they had faced duties of as much as 400% on milk products.

Tariff Fight Continues After Trump Exempts Some Canadian Goods

After trade talks broke down in August, the Trump administration imposed 50% duties on $27.6 billion of Canadian goods, and Canada responded with tariffs of 15% to 50% on more than $20 billion of U.S. goods that took effect Sept. 8.

Last month, Trump exempted select Canadian imports from the 50% tariffs, including plywood, paper products and machinery, while adding goods such as carpets, shampoos and air conditioners to the list.

Carney told Politico on Friday that Canada can afford to wait for a new U.S. president rather than accept a deal that does not serve its interests.

Why Bulls Say Bitcoin Won’t Fall Further

Widely-followed market commentator Our Crypto Talk posted on X that Bitcoin bottomed 71 days after the 2014 midterms, 39 days after 2018, and just 13 days after 2022, a shrinking window the account says points to Bitcoin already finding its low this cycle. 

"We don’t see it going below $58K at all, and we’d be very surprised if it did," the post read, citing Bitcoin’s resilience following this week’s Binance hack as further evidence.

Meanwhile, DWF Labs posted on X that Bitcoin gained in the 12 months following each of the last three midterm elections, rising 25%, 45% and 92% respectively, even though the path included drawdowns of 31% and 46% three months into the 2014 and 2018 cycles. 

The post also noted the third year of a presidential term has historically been the strongest for the S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY), gaining in 17 of the last 19 cycles with an 18.9% median return, a pattern Bitcoin has mirrored with gains of 34% in 2015, 92% in 2019 and 155% in 2023.

Why Bears Still Point to $73,000

Widely-followed cryptocurency analyst Ali Martinez posted on X in late September that Bitcoin fell 72%, 65%, 52% and 27% following the 2010, 2014, 2018 and 2022 midterms respectively, calling the pattern worth watching even though it doesn’t prove elections directly cause the declines. 

He flagged Bitcoin’s short-term holder cost basis near $73,000 as the key level to watch, since that zone has historically held through major corrections during confirmed bull markets.

Why $176 Million in Crypto Money Is Riding on Tuesday’s Races

headline: What If China’s AI Crash Was A Feature, Not A Bug?
summary: The great artificial intelligence debate of our time usually focuses on who will win the race for the most powerful model. A far more revealing question sits underneath the surface. Which country is building a
content_html:
The great artificial intelligence debate of our time usually focuses on who will win the race for the most powerful model. A far more revealing question sits underneath the surface. Which country is building a healthier, more durable market structure around this technology? On that front, the evidence points in a surprising direction. China is playing a better long-term game, even though its stock market took a sharp hit first.

Wall Street loves a good American exceptionalism narrative. The story goes that the United States boasts the deepest capital markets, the most advanced chips, and a culture of relentless innovation that China simply cannot match. That story contains real truth, but it misses a crucial nuance. The United States has built a dangerously narrow AI ecosystem that depends on a handful of corporate giants. By contrast, China absorbed a severe financial shock and emerged with a strategy that prioritizes industrial diffusion and global market share over speculative stock prices.

Let us start with the American setup. The U.S. AI boom rests on a concentration of capital and corporate power that is unprecedented in modern financial history. A handful of hyperscalers, led by Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta, are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into data centers and computing infrastructure.

Goldman Sachs estimates that the largest hyperscalers will spend nearly $800 billion on capital expenditures this year alone. Data shows that the “AI Big 10″s now account for roughly 42% of the entire S&P 500 market capitalization. This narrowness creates a fragile loop.

The equity market has become the broader economy’s growth engine. Rising AI profits lift share prices; higher share prices boost wealthy households’ spending power; and that spending keeps demand alive. This works beautifully as long as confidence holds, but it leaves the entire system vulnerable to a single point of failure. The top 10 S&P 500 stocks are the most concentrated they’ve been since 1965. Investors pay roughly 22 times forward earnings for the index, well above its long-term average, and AI-linked names trade at far richer multiples. When an index depends on a tiny group of companies to justify its valuation, the risk of a sudden repricing never disappears. It simply waits.

Now consider China’s path. The Chinese AI stock sector saw a sharp correction that wiped out roughly $480 billion. The STAR50 index, which tracks the country’s leading AI and semiconductor firms, plunged over 40% from its July peak. Even after that sell-off, the index traded at around 100 times trailing earnings, down from nearly 250 times. Retail investors fueled that rally with margin financing and short-term speculation. When sentiment shifted, the unwinding happened quickly. Beijing did not engineer that crash. No government deliberately vaporizes $500 billion in household wealth. The business model that triggered the correction reflects a deliberate and coherent strategic choice.

That choice centers on open-weight artificial intelligence. Labs such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot have released powerful models that anyone can download, modify, and run on their own servers. This approach contrasts with the closed-source, subscription-based models favored by OpenAI and Anthropic. The strategic logic is straightforward. If a developer in Nairobi, Lagos, or Jakarta can access a capable model from China for free, the pricing power of Western AI giants erodes.

Open-weight systems from China accounted for 17.1% of global AI model downloads through August 2025, edging out the U.S. share of 15.86%. On Hugging Face, the world’s leading open-source AI community, architectures from China captured 41% of all downloads by mid-2026. Alibaba’s Qwen ecosystem has birthed over 300,000 derivative models created by developers worldwide. Cumulative downloads of open-source large language models from China crossed 10 billion globally. These are not the metrics of a bubble. They reflect a platform strategy.

The Chinese government actively supports this diffusion. State-backed investors have even sold into domestic rallies to temper speculative excess, favoring long-term industrial utility over short-term financial mania. Beijing wants cheap, efficient AI embedded in manufacturing, logistics, and supply chains, not a bloated software stock bubble that enriches day traders while starving the real economy. China’s manufacturing base gives it an application advantage. The country accounts for roughly 30% of global manufacturing output, and that scale offers a ready testing ground for factory automation, robotics, and logistics software.

The short-term pain is real. Startups in China are bleeding cash as third-party cloud providers capture much of the end-user revenue. Z.ai’s share of its own model’s tokens that a major platform served plunged from 88% to 22% within 20 days of release, as rival hosts undercut its pricing. Financial returns for individual labs remain uncertain. Strategic returns for China’s broader economy and global influence are substantial.

The United States is not standing still on hardware. Washington continues to restrict China’s access to advanced chips, and those restrictions bite. Huawei plans to double production of its top-tier Ascend 910C chip to roughly 600,000 units in 2026, but Nvidia’s best chips still deliver around 4 times the computing power of Huawei’s best offerings. Bernstein estimates that China’s AI computing capacity stood at just 14% of America’s in 2025, and that gap will persist for years. China compensates for hardware weakness with software strength and industrial scale. The country is aggressively replacing foreign chips with domestic alternatives and forcing state-funded data centers to transition to homegrown silicon. DeepSeek’s founder has argued that domestic AI chips lag the U.S. by only about 2 years. The core constraint is production capacity, not fundamental design capability.

The deeper divergence lies in global outreach. The United States ties AI exports, cloud access, and investment to political and security alignment. It builds walls around its technology and expects allies to operate within those walls. China courts the Global South with open-source technology transfers, digital infrastructure, and low-cost AI stacks. It does not demand political loyalty. It offers capability. For a developer in an emerging market who cannot afford an expensive subscription to a Western model, a free Chinese model that runs on local hardware isn’t a compromise. It is a lifeline. This inclusive approach builds grassroots adoption, and adoption creates dependency, standards, and long-term influence.

The American AI trade may not crash tomorrow. Corporate balance sheets are strong, and institutional capital moves more slowly than retail margin debt. The structural vulnerabilities are real, though. The U.S. market depends on a narrow group of companies to justify extraordinary valuations amid rising capital costs and uncertain returns.

China has already taken its medicine. It absorbed a sharp correction, disciplined speculative excess, and doubled down on a strategy that prioritizes widespread adoption over exclusive monetization. That strategy may not produce the strongest quarterly earnings reports. It may not generate the kind of stock market euphoria Silicon Valley celebrates. It builds something more durable. It builds an ecosystem. In the long run, ecosystems outlast bubbles.

headline: Ed Yardeni's Midterms Prediction: Democratic Sweep Could Be a 'Cold Shower' for Stock Market
summary: Ed Yardeni says a Democratic sweep could deliver a “cold shower” for stocks as deeper gridlock raises risks around debt and shutdowns
content_html:
Wall Street usually welcomes divided government. But veteran market strategist Ed Yardeni warns that a Democratic sweep in Tuesday’s midterm elections could deliver a “very cold shower” for stocks, even with Republicans retaining the White House.

Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, told Bloomberg that growing political divisions could make it harder for Congress to respond to future economic crises.

Traders on Polymarket put the probability of Democrats capturing both the House and Senate at approximately 73%, with more than $52 million traded across the election market.

But Yardeni believes stock investors may not have fully priced in that possibility, noting that some remain skeptical of polls showing strong Democratic support.

Why Gridlock Could Hurt Stocks

“Usually the market loves gridlock, but in this situation we’re talking about much more partisanship,” Yardeni said.

Investors traditionally welcome divided government because it makes major policy changes harder to pass, reducing the risk of sudden changes to taxes and regulations.

Yardeni worries, however, that Washington could become so divided that lawmakers struggle to agree even when action is urgently needed.

He warned that future government shutdowns and disputes over the national debt could last considerably longer, potentially causing greater economic damage.

For Yardeni, the bigger concern is what happens if bond investors lose confidence in Washington’s ability to manage its finances.

Yardeni coined the term “bond vigilantes” in 1983 to describe investors who push back against excessive government borrowing by selling bonds.

If those investors demand higher yields, borrowing costs for businesses could rise, putting pressure on stocks. Congress might then need to agree on deficit reduction precisely when political divisions make compromise most difficult.

Yardeni Still Sees Buying Opportunities

Despite his warning, Yardeni isn’t predicting the end of the bull market.

In an October 29 Financial Times column, he argued that stock-market declines following the midterms could offer buying opportunities, supported by resilient economic growth and corporate earnings.

His view contrasts with that of Morgan Stanley strategist Mike Wilson, who sees the election as a potential clearing event for stocks, with the removal of political uncertainty potentially supporting a rally.

For investors in the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), Yardeni’s warning is that even an election result widely anticipated by traders could introduce fresh risks if political gridlock fuels another fiscal confrontation.

Oil prices plunged nearly 7% Monday—and Peter Schiff says insiders traded ahead of the flip.

Why Schiff Calls This Market Manipulation

"Once oil short positions are covered and new longs are established, expect another reversal of the official position," Schiff wrote, adding he expects the pattern to repeat "until markets no longer react to anything his administration says."

headline: EXCLUSIVE: AI Bubble Risk Is Low, but SMH Faces a Bigger Threat Than QQQ, Expert Warns
summary: Ai Funds founder Tal Schwartz's AI Bubble Pop Index puts AI bubble risk at just 3/20, but flags risks in chip ETFs, with SMH more vulnerable than QQQ.
content_html:
The risk of an artificial intelligence bubble bursting remains relatively low, but investors could be overlooking significant concentration risks in some of the most popular semiconductor ETFs, according to Tal Schwartz, founder of Ai Funds.

The firm’s recently unveiled AI Bubble Pop Index currently scores the risk at just 3 out of 20, based on Oct. 2 readings. However, Schwartz cautions that the index measures the broader market, not individual sectors.

“It doesn’t score sectors, so a low reading isn’t a clean bill of health for any of them,” he told Benzinga.

Read Also: Semiconductor Stocks Are Cheaper Than the S&P 500: Is It Time to Buy SOXX and SMH ETFs?

Nvidia Exposure Separates the Riskiest AI ETFs

Among major AI-related ETFs, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH) appears particularly vulnerable. When asked which, among the major ETFs investors use to play the AI theme, has the greatest vulnerability to an AI spending slowdown, Schwartz opined that it was SMH, due to its concentration.

Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) accounts for approximately 21% of its portfolio, while its top 10 holdings represent 69% of assets, according to Morningstar data.

By comparison, the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF (NASDAQ:AIQ) holds approximately 90 stocks, with its top 10 accounting for around 33% and Nvidia representing less than 3%.

“The more a fund depends on one group of customers’ spending, the more a capex slowdown could hurt it,” Schwartz said.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) also carries semiconductor exposure but is more evenly distributed, with Nvidia accounting for approximately 8%.

AI Spending Slowdown Could Hit Chipmakers Hard

A hypothetical 20% reduction in hyperscaler AI infrastructure spending over the next 12 months could put chip equipment makers, memory manufacturers, AI accelerators and networking suppliers under pressure.

“The suppliers whose revenue is that spending: chip equipment makers, memory, AI accelerators and networking, plus the optical and power names common in thematic funds. These companies carry high fixed costs, so a revenue dip tends to hit earnings harder, and their valuations assume years of growth," Schwartz explained.

“In the 2022 chip downturn, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 45% from its January high to its October low. The twist is that the hyperscalers themselves could hold up better, because spending less lifts their free cash flow,” he added, illustrating the sector’s vulnerability to spending cycles.

QQQ and SPY Also Carry Hidden AI Risks

At September-end, the top 10 stocks represented approximately 47% of the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) and 39% of the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY).

“The risk runs deeper than the weights. Nvidia sells to Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon.com, Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Meta Platforms, Inc (NASDAQ:META), which sit in the same funds, so one capex decision hits both sides,” Schwartz explained.

He added, “A cap-weighted index is static by design. It owns the most of whatever has already risen the most, and it rides every decline.”

Investors seeking to reduce concentration could consider the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP), where technology accounts for approximately 16% of assets, compared with roughly 40% in SPY. However, equal weighting introduces greater exposure to banks, cyclicals and rate-sensitive stocks, Schwartz cautioned.

Why a Low Bubble Score Doesn’t Eliminate AI Risks

Three of the index’s 10 indicators currently carry yellow readings: AI-linked layoffs, China’s cheaper AI models and the yield curve. Big Tech capital expenditure already consumes approximately 80% of operating cash flow, with spending above 100% triggering a warning.

Schwartz also sees cheaper Chinese AI models threatening U.S. companies’ pricing power.

“In my view, it’s the chance that AI monetization disappoints because of Chinese ‘AI dumping,’ landing on a highly concentrated system,” he said.

Drawing parallels with Cisco Systems Inc (NASDAQ:CSCO) during the dot-com boom, Schwartz noted that even dominant technology suppliers can experience severe corrections.

“Cisco sold the routers that built the internet, Nvidia sells the chips that power AI, and both became the world’s most valuable company,” Schwartz said.

“On its way up, Cisco fell 38% in early 1997 on slowing sales and 37% in 1998 during the Russia/LTCM crisis. Yet it gained about 590% in the two years before its March 2000 peak. Nvidia lost $589 billion in one day on the DeepSeek scare in January 2025, then regained nearly all of it within weeks. Scares like these are swings. Cisco fell 89% by October 2002 only after its customers stopped buying,” he explained, noting that what ends a boom remained the same — customers reducing spending.

For ETF investors, his warning is particularly relevant: “Segments can swing hard inside a calm market. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed 20% below its June record in July, then fell 6.7% on October 22 alone.”

summary: Bitcoin and gold have “blown their tops,” Mike McGlone warns, as a stock correction threatens a historic market reset.
content_html:
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) and gold have "blown their tops," Bloomberg Intelligence strategist Mike McGlone said Monday, pointing to a stock market correction as the trigger that could drag both lower heading into Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Why McGlone Sees All Risk Assets Rolling Over Together

McGlone said on The Wolf Of All Streets podcast that Bitcoin, gold and silver have all pulled back to key support levels alongside a broader equity correction, calling it a Faustian bargain starting to unwind. 

A chart overlaying Bitcoin, gold and the S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY) on 50-week moving averages shows gold just beginning to roll over while Bitcoin already has, he said.

The real signal to watch, McGlone argued, is whether the S&P 500 closes lower this week, calling that outcome "the beginning of potentially the biggest reset of a lifetime." 

Correlations between gold, copper and the S&P 500 are running at record highs on a 50-week basis, he noted, meaning a stock pullback would likely drag commodities down rather than lift them as a safe haven.

Why McGlone Doesn’t Buy the ‘Markets Always Rally After Midterms’ Thesis

McGlone pushed back on the popular narrative that stocks reliably rise after midterm elections, warning that widespread consensus on any single outcome usually signals danger. 

He pointed to Bitcoin’s drop toward its 50-week moving average, a rolling housing market, and a sharp pullback in natural gas as signs a broader deflationary shift is underway.

Fellow guest Mario Nawfal pushed back on the crypto reaction specifically, noting Bitcoin only fell 4% to 5% during the week of the Binance hack, even as Intel dropped 30% and Alphabet fell 12%. 

He called that relative strength, not confirmation Bitcoin is rolling over.

Why the Debt Ceiling Could Hit Sooner Than Expected

Nawfal flagged the debt ceiling, set at $41.1 trillion against a national debt already above $40.5 trillion, as an underappreciated risk that could surface before year-end rather than its usual March timing. 

He compared the setup to 2011, when a debt ceiling standoff triggered a US credit downgrade from S&P and sent gold from $1,400 to $1,900.

Central banks have been accumulating gold at a record pace since 2022, Nawfal said, framing the metal as an emerging reserve asset rather than a traditional inflation hedge:

  • 2021 purchases: $26 billion
  • 2025 purchases: $96 billion

He also pointed to a Bank of England consultation paper exploring whether gold should be tokenized for financial market liquidity, calling it a sign institutional interest extends well beyond retail demand.

McGlone and Nawfal agreed the Fed faces a difficult choice heading into December, caught between inflation still above its 2% target and a stock market already showing signs of fatigue.

Fundstrat’s Tom Lee believes the stock market has hit a bottom following the recent decline in tech stocks, maintaining his target for the market to finish the year above 8,200 amid resilient artificial intelligence demand.

Tech Sell-Off and AI Demand

Addressing the recent tech sell-off, Lee indicated that the downward trend has concluded. “I think we are at the bottom,” he said. Lee emphasized that the underlying fundamentals remain strong for the tech sector, specifically noting that “the market for AI is still very tight.”

Climbing a Wall of Worry

headline: $80 Billion Hedge Fund Braces for Bear Market
summary: Paul Singer's Elliott warns a massive bear market looms. See how the $80B fund is hedging against AI hype and market excess.
content_html:
Elliott Investment Management warned that investors could flip abruptly from the fear of missing out (FOMO) to FOGO, the “fear of getting obliterated.”

In its latest investor letter, as reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, the $80 billion hedge fund led by Paul Singer and Jonathan Pollock compared today’s debt-fueled, tech-heavy markets to the Roaring ’20s before the Great Depression.

“At present, virtually every alarm bell warning of a substantial bear market ahead is ringing,” the letter said.

A Stack of Tail Risks

Elliott flagged widening U.S. budget deficits, persistent inflation, private-credit portfolios and AI hype – including circular investments between tech firms and infrastructure makers, plus debt-financed capital spending.

It also called out zero-day options and meme-stock betting, which it said were more like gambling than investing.

“So many factors have lined up to cause this great boom that it might take disruption in only one or two of them to shift this momentum into reverse,” the firm wrote, warning of “a cascading, self-reinforcing unwind of this bull market.”

The Price of Protection

Elliot’s performance reflects these concerns. It went flat in the third quarter and up a little under 2% through September. In contrast, the S&P 500 returned nearly 13% over the same period.

Distressed debt and hedges tied to gold, currencies, stocks and interest rates lost money. Commodities, arbitrage and credit hedges made money.

“Over Elliott’s five-decade existence, fallow periods have existed, but these have historically been accompanied by market turbulence and followed by periods of rare opportunities,” the letter said.

“Our goal is to be well positioned—protected on the downside, and with capital to deploy into the bargains—when the tide turns again.”

The firm sees opportunities in healthcare activism, producing energy properties and, eventually, forced sellers in dislocated credit markets.

Inside the Defensive Wall

Elliott’s latest 13F filing dated August 14 shows the firm’s lean on hard assets. Triple Flag Precious Metals Corp. (NYSE:TFPM) led at $3.99 billion, 18% of the total.

Phillips 66 (NYSE:PSX) followed at $3.25 billion, then Suncor Energy Inc. (NYSE:SU) at $1.58 billion and Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. (NYSE:HPE) at $1.46 billion.

Southwest Airlines Co. (NYSE:LUV), where Elliott won a board overhaul in 2024, remains a $1.25 billion position. PepsiCo Inc. (NASDAQ:PEP) and Synopsys Inc. (NASDAQ:SNPS) are small stakes, at $173 million and $101 million.

headline: SPY Vs. IWM: Why 3.4% GDP Growth Leaves Two Different Tests For Investors
summary: The U.S. expansion reached 78 months through October as third-quarter GDP grew 3.4%, while September real spending stalled. SPY investors face a test of earnings breadth and investment returns; IWM investors must also
content_html:
The U.S. expansion reached 78 months through October as third-quarter GDP grew 3.4%, while September real spending stalled. SPY investors face a test of earnings breadth and investment returns; IWM investors must also examine domestic demand, debt repricing and interest coverage.

The Print

The U.S. economic expansion has run for 78 months through October 2026, measured from May 2020, the month after the National Bureau of Economic Research’s last designated trough. NBER has not announced a subsequent peak, although its determinations are retrospective.

Real gross domestic product grew 3.4% annualized in the third quarter, accelerating from 2.2% in the second. September was less convincing: real consumer spending was nearly flat, real disposable income fell 0.3%, and payrolls increased by 29,000.

Those contrasting figures set different tests for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and the iShares Russell 2000 ETF (NYSE:IWM). For SPY, the question is whether investment and output growth translate into earnings across large companies. For IWM, investors must also assess whether smaller businesses can cover borrowing costs when domestic demand softens.

What The GDP Numbers Establish

The 11 U.S. expansions completed since the October 1949 trough averaged 66.6 months. Four lasted longer than 78 months, reaching 92, 106, 120 and 128 months. A historical average is not an expiration date for the current cycle.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported that real final sales to private domestic purchasers increased 4.9% annualized in the third quarter, versus 4.6% in the second. This measure includes consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, but excludes inventories, government spending and net exports.

Overall investment growth reflected both private inventory investment and equipment spending, including information-processing equipment. Inventory accumulation can change subsequent production needs, while equipment investment raises the question of whether capital expenditures eventually generate revenue and cash flow.

For the capitalization-weighted S&P 500, stronger aggregate GDP does not establish that earnings gains are broad across constituents. SPY investors can compare growth in sales and operating cash flow with capital spending, and check whether earnings gains are concentrated among a limited group of companies.

September consumer data complicate the picture. Nominal personal consumption expenditures rose 0.5%, but the PCE price index also rose 0.5%. Inflation-adjusted spending increased less than 0.1%, rounded to 0.0%. Higher nominal sales need not signal stronger real demand.

Why IWM Faces A Different Test

IWM tracks the Russell 2000, where borrowing structures add another variable. Wells Fargo Investment Institute reported on October 27 that floating-rate borrowing represented 40.07% of the Russell 2000’s debt classified by interest-rate type, compared with 8.50% for the S&P 500, using data as of October 13.

These percentages concern debt for which interest-rate type could be classified, not all debt outstanding across either index. They are not measurements of ETF-level interest expense.

The gap nevertheless identifies a financing channel worth examining. Floating-rate debt can reprice as short-term rates change, while fixed-rate debt generally reflects prevailing market conditions when refinanced. If demand weakens while borrowing costs remain high, interest expense can absorb more operating income at affected companies.

September payrolls rose 29,000 following revised changes of minus 10,000 in July and plus 133,000 in August. Their sum implies a third-quarter gain of 152,000. August and September estimates remain preliminary.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the approximate 90% confidence interval for a monthly payroll change at plus or minus 122,000. September’s gain is not statistically distinguishable from zero at that level; this does not establish that employment was unchanged.

What Investors Should Watch Next

For SPY, the next test is whether stronger investment translates into broader earnings, margins and cash-flow growth. Investors can examine capital expenditures against operating cash flow and look beyond index-level earnings totals to their concentration.

For IWM, the parallel test combines sales demand and debt service. Quarterly results can show changes in interest expense relative to EBITDA, refinancing rates, interest coverage and free cash flow. Index-level debt exposure alone cannot establish how each company will fare.

September PCE inflation was 3.6% year over year, while core PCE inflation, excluding food and energy, was 3.1%. On October 28, the Federal Reserve held its policy target at 3.75% to 4.00%, with two dissenters preferring an increase.

October employment is scheduled for November 6, while updated third-quarter GDP and October personal income and spending are scheduled for November 25. Both could change the assessment.

The distinction is in what investors need to verify. SPY raises questions about the breadth and returns of investment-led growth. IWM adds a more immediate test of domestic demand, debt repricing and interest coverage. Neither follows from the expansion’s age alone.

headline: 'Marking Their Calendar': Tom Lee Says Investors Don't Have 'Conviction' to Buy the Dip Until After Midterms
summary: Tech stocks have taken a beating, and Fundstrat’s Tom Lee says investors who want to buy the dip are waiting until after the midterms.
content_html:
Technology stocks have taken a beating over the past month, and Fundstrat head of research Tom Lee said many investors who want to buy the dip have decided to wait until after the midterm elections.

Voters head to the polls Tuesday.

Buyers Are ‘Marking Their Calendar‘

Lee told CNBC on Friday that institutional investors “just don’t have conviction until after midterms,” and that retail traders are waiting on the sidelines too, with a lot of doom saying about the election.

With so much riding on the outcome, many people are hesitant to buy the dip right now, he said, and “as strange as it sounds,” they are “marking their calendar until Nov. 3.”

Until then, he expects stocks to fall.

Read Also: Nasdaq Dips Over 1% as Tech Stocks Fall: Investor Sentiment Weakens, Fear & Greed Index Moves to ‘Extreme Fear’ Zone

Plenty of Money

Lee said “someone” looks like they are getting liquidated, though he does not know whether it is an institution, and the drops are causing forced selling.

The equal-weight market is still rising, he said, so “there still is plenty of money sloshing around.”

Gridlock Worries Meet a ‘Clearing Event‘

Market commentator The Kobeissi Letter said Monday that October’s selloff is “more than just a correction in tech stocks,” and that investors are “pricing in two years of political gridlock.”

Polymarket traders give Democrats a 95% chance of winning the House and 78% of winning the Senate.

Last month, Lee said that a Democratic Congress “would be viewed as gridlock,” which markets tend to like, and that the midterms would be a “clearing event” ahead of the S&P 500 reaching 8,400 by year-end.

Since 1938, the S&P 500 has gained in about 95% of the 12-month periods after midterms, according to Fidelity Investments.

headline: Bitcoin Could Face Third and Final 2026 Low in Q4 if S&P500 Drops, Analyst Cautions
summary: Bitcoin could form a third low as Benjamin Cowen warns the S&P 500 remains one of the last major indexes left to fall.
content_html:
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) could see a third low this year, according to analyst Benjamin Cowen, who is pointing to the S&P 500 as one of the last major indexes still due for a bigger drop.

Why Cowen Says the S&P 500 Hasn’t Fallen Enough Yet

Cowen said Tuesday that the Nasdaq has already dropped more than 10% this quarter, while the Russell 2000 fell 11% to 12% and the Dow dropped about 7%, closely mirroring 2018’s midterm-year correction. 

The S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY), by contrast, is down only about 4%, which Cowen called a sign it’s "one of the last things to fall" before any policy response from the administration.

Cowen pointed to the S&P’s return path during President Donald Trump’s current term closely tracking his first term, with a correction early in both 2018 and 2026 followed by a similar drop emerging late in both years. 

He said the index has already broken below its 50-day moving average and entered its bull market support band, and expects it to test the 200-day moving average near 7,300 before the correction runs its course.

Why Cowen Sees This Fitting the Midterm Playbook

Cowen pointed to the last three midterm years, 2014, 2018 and 2022, which each produced a correction early in the year followed by a second drop late in the year, and 2026 has followed the same script with a roughly 13% decline already completed earlier this year. 

He argued that widespread predictions the Q4 correction wouldn’t happen simply because everyone expected it mirror similar false comfort around Bitcoin’s own seasonal Q4 weakness.

"We’ve talked about the Q4 dump for Bitcoin and people say, well, it’s not going to happen because everyone’s expecting it," Cowen noted.

"But we said the same thing back in February and the same thing back in the summer for Bitcoin, and every single time it happens anyways," he added.

Why Oil and the Iran War Remain the Bigger Wildcard

Cowen sees WTI crude climbing toward the top of its trading range after the midterms unless a ceasefire holds in Iran.

He said markets have repeatedly priced in an Iran deal this year, only for those expectations to fade within weeks. Over the next 12 to 18 months, he thinks investors could start brushing off similar reports.

Cowen expects stocks to bottom within the next couple of months and then rebound. He sees a potential OpenAI IPO in early 2027 as the next major event for investors.

headline: This Midterm Nightmare Scenario Puts S&P 500 Down 10% by Year-End, Evercore Warns
summary: Evercore warns a disputed Democratic sweep plus deeper Iran involvement could send the S&P 500 down 10% to 6,800, erasing 2026 gains.
content_html:
A Democratic sweep resulting in a disputed midterm election combined with deeper U.S. military involvement in Iran could erase nearly all of the S&P 500’s gains for 2026, according to Evercore ISI research cited by CNBC.

Evercore released its midterm election analysis Sunday that mapped out several possible election outcomes and the likely market response to each one, giving investors a framework for what could follow once ballots are counted.

How the Worst Case Unfolds

Its bleakest projection begins with a Democratic sweep and a contested result. From there, Evercore sees the S&P 500 sliding more than 10% to 6,800 by year-end if President Donald Trump expands military action in Iran before the new Congress takes office in January. The firm described such a move as "kinetic escalation," CNBC reported.

Timing matters here. The stretch between Election Day and the January swearing-in leaves roughly two months in which political uncertainty at home could collide with conflict abroad.

A drop to 6,800 would cancel out almost all of the index’s roughly 11% advance so far this year. Holders of broad index funds such as the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSE:VOO) would see most of a strong year evaporate in its final weeks.

Read Also: Trump Celebrates Republican Victory in Guam — 'Wow, Hopefully an Indication for Things to Come!'

Oil, Credit and Growth Risks

"This would be a ‘dip not to be bought,’" analysts led by Julian Emanuel, Evercore’s chief equity and quantitative strategist, wrote in the report, according to CNBC.

Emanuel pointed to several forces capable of turning an initial decline into a drawn-out sell-off. Among them: a surge in oil prices, widening credit spreads and a slowing economy.

Each would land differently across the market. Higher crude prices typically benefit energy producers such as ExxonMobil Holdings Corp. (NYSE:XOM) and Chevron Corp. (NYSE:CVX).

Airlines, including Delta Air Lines Inc. (NYSE:DAL) and United Airlines Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:UAL), tend to feel the pain through rising fuel costs.

Wider credit spreads would pressure high-yield debt, a corner of the market tracked by the iShares iBoxx $ High Yield Corporate Bond ETF (NYSE:HYG).

Taken together, the pressures Emanuel outlined could weigh on stocks for months and set up a difficult start to 2027, he cautioned.

See More: Top Growth Stocks

Not the Base Case

Emanuel does not view the scenario as his most likely outcome, but he does count it among the risks he fears most.

His broader advice to investors remains intact. Evercore ISI still recommends buying any weakness tied to the election, as long as the worst-case scenario does not play out. Investors following the firm’s lead would treat election-driven pullbacks in benchmarks such as the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) as potential entry points.

The Bottom Line

A disputed count alone carries its own set of risks. Escalation in Iran before the new Congress is seated would add another, and Evercore sees that combination potentially pushing stocks sharply lower.

headline: S&P 500 Could Win No Matter Who Wins the Midterms: 5 ETFs to Watch Under JPMorgan's 4 Scenarios
summary: JPMorgan sees the S&P 500 holding firm across all four midterm scenarios. Here are five ETFs to watch for potential policy-driven gains.
content_html:
The 2026 U.S. midterm elections could create political uncertainty, but JPMorgan sees limited downside for equities regardless of which party controls Congress.

According to a scenario analysis by JPMorgan Market Intelligence, based on Bloomberg prediction market data as of Nov. 1, the S&P 500 could gain between 0.25% and 1.25% across three of the four possible congressional outcomes. Even a Democratic sweep, the most likely outcome, carries a projected reaction ranging from a 0.25% decline to a 0.50% gain.

Read Also: QUICK SPARK: Trump Celebrates Republican Victory in Guam — 'Wow, Hopefully an Indication for Things to Come!'

The analysis assigns a 66% probability to Democrats winning both chambers (Blue Wave), a 26% probability to a Democratic House and Republican Senate (Split Congress), a 7% probability to a Republican sweep (Red Wave) and just 1% to a Republican House and Democratic Senate (The Other Split).

The findings suggest investors may want to focus less on predicting the election winner and more on positioning their portfolios for the potential policy and sector implications.

Five ETFs to Watch

1. State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY)

The broad-market benchmark is the most direct way to position for JPMorgan’s relatively benign outlook. With projected S&P 500 moves confined to a narrow range, investors may prefer diversified exposure over concentrated political bets.

2. Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ)

A Democratic sweep could revive concerns about AI regulation and scrutiny of mega-cap technology companies. JPMorgan, however, argues that legislative restrictions face significant hurdles, making any AI-related pullback a potential buying opportunity for AI bulls. QQQ offers exposure to major technology and AI beneficiaries.

3. State Street Health Care Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE:XLV)

Health care could emerge as a beneficiary of a Democratic victory, with policy priorities potentially shifting toward health care affordability and funding. Reuters identifies health care stocks as one of the sectors that could benefit from a strong Democratic showing.

4. iShares Global Clean Energy ETF (NASDAQ:ICLN)

Clean energy stocks could attract renewed attention under a Democratic-controlled Congress. Potential changes to renewable energy incentives and environmental policies could influence the sector’s outlook.

5. iShares U.S. Aerospace & Defense ETF (BATS:ITA)

A Republican sweep could support defense stocks if the administration maintains its spending priorities. Reuters notes that increased defense spending is among the potential implications of continued Republican control.

Read Also: $1 Billion Flows Out of Bitcoin ETFs as Midterm Elections Put Trump's Crypto Agenda to the Test

The election may matter more for sector leadership than for the S&P 500’s overall direction. JPMorgan’s projections suggest that investors should watch policy-sensitive industries while keeping broad-market exposure.

However, these are illustrative ETF examples, not specific fund recommendations from JPMorgan. The actual market reaction will also depend on corporate earnings, interest rates and Treasury yields.

While prediction markets and polls heavily favored a Democratic sweep, early results confirming Democratic Senate victories in Georgia, North Carolina, and Virginia align with those expectations. Lee noted that resolving this political uncertainty often helps sidelined cash re-enter the market, allowing equities to climb the proverbial “wall of worry” into a strong year-end finish.

headline: 'Worst Possible Combination:' Top Analyst Warns of Trump White House With Democratic Congress — Here's What the S&P 500 Has Historically Averaged
summary: S&P 500 data shows gridlock is the market's best scenario at 15.1%, while a GOP president and Dem Congress is the worst at 4.9%.
content_html:
Historical market data shows a divided congressional government produces the highest average returns for the S&P 500. At the same time, a Republican president paired with a Democratic Congress results in the lowest historical market gains.

The ‘Worst Possible Combination’

When factoring in the political affiliation of the sitting president, the dynamic shifts significantly. According to Ryan Detrick‘s historical data, “The worst possible combination is a Republican President and a Democratic Congress.”

This specific political makeup—a scenario that would apply to Donald Trump assuming the presidency alongside a Democratic-majority Congress—historically yields an average annual S&P 500 return of just 4.9%.

Detrick observed that markets were actively pricing in this data, adding, “Futures seem to agree so far.” Responding to a question about whether this 4.9% figure was primarily driven by the Global Financial Crisis, Detrick stated, “It is the most likely scenario at 22 times. So it is somewhat, but some other bad years in there for sure.”

Read Also: Tom Lee Says 'We Are at the Bottom' as Tech Sell-Off Rocks Markets — But He Still Sees S&P 500 Above 8,200 By Year-End

The ‘Best Scenario’ for Stocks

A split Congress yields an average S&P 500 annual return of 15.1%, based on historical data spanning 1951 to 2025. Sharing the data on X, Detrick, stated, “Good reminder that the best scenario for stocks is a split Congress.”

When looking strictly at congressional makeup without factoring in the executive branch, Detrick noted that “A Democrat controlled Congress is the worst scenario historically,” as that setup averages a 6.7% return compared to 11.3% for a Republican-controlled Congress.

Historical Market Context

The data, sourced from Carson Investment Research and FactSet, tracks market performance starting with the 82nd Congress. Under a Republican president with a Republican Congress, the index averages a 7.6% return, while a Republican president with a split Congress averages 13.7%.

Conversely, a Democratic president paired with a split Congress yields the highest specific combination return at 17.0%, while a Democratic president with a Republican Congress averages 16.3%. A Democratic president paired with a Democratic Congress averages an 8.6% return.

How Has the Stock Market Performed?

The S&P 500 index has advanced 10.36% year-to-date. Similarly, the Nasdaq Composite index was up 9.19%, and the Dow Jones gained 7.04% YTD.

On Tuesday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (NASDAQ:QQQ), which track the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, respectively, closed mixed. SPY rose 0.30% to $754.35, while QQQ advanced 0.62% to $685.28. Meanwhile, the Dow tracker, State Street SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (NYSE:DIA), ended 0.44% lower at $517.06.

headline: Dan Ives Says Democratic Sweep Will Slow AI Buildout, Estimates 10% Of Planned US Data Centers ‘Will Not Happen Now’
summary: Dan Ives says Democrats’ sweep could slow U.S. AI infrastructure growth, with 10% of planned data centers now at risk.
content_html:
Dan Ives, technology analyst and Yorkville Ives & Co. partner and senior managing director, said Democratic control of Congress could slow the U.S. artificial-intelligence (AI) infrastructure buildout, estimating that 10% of planned data centers "will not happen now."

Ives Sees Slower Data Center Expansion

Ives said Wednesday that the "Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House" represented a "seismic shift" for the AI infrastructure story.

He said the election result "will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years" and could slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 data centers across the country.

"We estimate 10% of datacenters will not happen now," Ives wrote on X, adding that some investors may favor a slower construction pace while others could view it as additional risk.

Democrats secured control of both the House and Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections, according to the Associated Press. The party also scored gubernatorial victories, including Gina Hinojosa’s defeat of Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas.

Read Also: 'Worst Possible Combination:' Top Analyst Warns of Trump White House With Democratic Congress — Here's What the S&P 500 Has Historically Averaged

Thorne Rejects End Of AI Trade, Schiff Points To Economy

James E. Thorne, chief market strategist at Wellington-Altus, pushed back against expectations that slower construction would end the AI investment cycle.

"Expect the doomer narrative to shift: America won’t build the data centers, and the AI trade is over. Wrong on both counts," Thorne wrote on X.

He added that slowing data-center construction and ending the Iran war would be positive for bringing inflation down.

Economist Peter Schiff, meanwhile, characterized the Democratic victory as a judgment on President Donald Trump’s economic record.

Schiff called the election a "referendum on Trump," saying voters experienced economic hardship while Trump had been "boasting of a booming economy."

Gerstner Also Flags Capacity Risk

The comments followed a warning from Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, who said on the All-In Podcast election-night livestream that 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected data-center capacity could fail to come online.

"I think it’s going to be really challenging for the AI infra," Gerstner said.

Still, Gerstner said he did not expect America to retreat from AI, calling it a global race.

How Has the Stock Market Performed?

The S&P 500 index has advanced 10.36% year-to-date. Similarly, the Nasdaq Composite index was up 9.19%, and the Dow Jones gained 7.04% YTD.

content_html:
When discussing the stock market, most people tend to focus on what happens during regular Wall Street trading hours. After all, that is when most trading takes place.

Yet one often overlooked aspect is that prices can also change between one session’s close and the next session’s open. How much do these moves actually contribute to overall returns?

In this article, we will explore that question by comparing the historical performance of the regular trading session, also known as the cash session, with overnight performance in SPY, the ETF that tracks the S&P 500 Index. We will then break down overnight results by day of the week and examine how profits and drawdowns change when we limit trading to Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday nights.

Why Use the SPY ETF to Analyze the S&P 500?

For our analysis, we will use SPY, one of the world’s most liquid ETFs. Because it tracks the S&P 500 Index, it provides a useful reference for studying the behavior of the U.S. stock market.

We chose this instrument for a reason. Rather than using instruments commonly employed in systematic trading, such as S&P 500 futures, we are focusing on an ETF, which has a simpler structure and does not require us to manage contract expirations. Futures are more complex instruments, and rolling from one contract to the next can introduce price discontinuities known as rollover gaps. If not handled properly, these gaps can distort the results of the analysis.

The goal of this article is less about developing a trading system ready for live trading and more about analyzing market behavior and identifying potential recurring patterns.

Each trader can then assess whether and how to capitalize on any edge identified in the analysis, choosing the instrument that best suits their needs while considering factors such as accessibility, trading costs, and capital efficiency.

Cash vs. Overnight Sessions: Comparing Returns in SPY

Let’s begin with Figure 1, which compares the performance of two strategies: one that trades exclusively during the cash session and another that holds positions only overnight.

By cash session, we mean the period from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. The strategy buys $10,000 worth of SPY at the market open and closes the position at the end of the same session, holding no position overnight.

The overnight session, by contrast, runs from one trading session’s close to the next session’s open. In this case, the strategy buys SPY at 4:00 p.m. and sells it at 9:30 a.m. on the next trading day, capturing price changes between the two sessions, including any opening gaps.

Figure 1. Comparison of cash-session and overnight trading results in the SPY ETF.

At first glance, the results appear clear: the overnight session substantially outperformed the cash session, generating a total profit of approximately $15,000, compared with roughly $5,900 during regular trading hours.

A closer look at the two curves, however, reveals two quite different periods.

Before 2010, the gap between the two equity curves gradually widened. In other words, while the overnight session contributed positively to market gains, the cash session delivered much weaker results, at times accumulating substantial losses.

From 2010 onward, that difference appears less pronounced. Both sessions contributed positively to stock market gains, and the cash session performed considerably better than it had during the previous decade. Another interesting observation emerges during two specific downturns: the pandemic-related crash in 2020 and the market decline in 2022. In both cases, the cash session held up relatively better than the overnight component, which experienced sharper declines.

Based on the overall results, however, the overnight session offers the more promising starting point for further analysis. Let’s focus exclusively on this component and examine how its returns are distributed across the days of the week.

The goal is to determine whether the observed edge is spread evenly across the week or tends to be concentrated on particular days.

Overnight Trading in SPY: Results by Day of the Week

In Figure 2, we have broken down the overnight strategy’s results by day of the week, producing five separate equity curves.

The strategy works as described above, except that each curve includes only trades initiated on a specific day. For example, the Monday curve shows the results of buying SPY at Monday’s close and selling it at Tuesday’s open. Similarly, the Friday curve includes trades opened at Friday’s close and closed at the following Monday’s open, covering the weekend as well.

The results reveal clear differences across the days of the week. Monday’s overnight session stands out as the most profitable historically, generating a total profit of more than $7,300, well above the results for any other day.

The Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday overnight sessions also produced positive overall results, although their profits were considerably smaller, at approximately $3,400, $2,500, and $2,700, respectively.

Thursday is the clear exception: it is the only day of the week with a negative overall result, recording a loss of approximately $900.

These results show that the edge observed in the overnight session is not evenly distributed throughout the week but varies by day.

At this point, a natural question arises: what would happen if we traded only on the days that delivered the most promising results?

For example, we could limit trading to the Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday overnight sessions. We would exclude Thursday because of its negative results, and Friday, despite its positive performance, to avoid the additional risks associated with holding a position over the weekend.

Figure 2. Cumulative results of the overnight strategy in SPY, broken down by day of the week.

Monday Through Wednesday Overnight Trading: Effects on Profits and Drawdowns

In Figure 3, we compare the original overnight strategy with a more selective version that trades only on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday nights, excluding the Thursday and Friday sessions.

The results are particularly interesting. Despite taking fewer trades, the modified strategy retains most of the original strategy’s total profit, with approximately $13,300 versus $15,000.

The most significant improvement, however, concerns risk. Looking at the two equity curves, we can see that the more selective version follows a much smoother path, with substantially smaller drawdowns.

This is reflected in the ratio of net profit to maximum drawdown, which rises from 3.7 for the original strategy to 9.6 for the modified version, more than two and a half times the original value.

In other words, trading less frequently allows us to achieve nearly the same profit with considerably less risk exposure. This result highlights the importance of identifying a statistical edge and understanding when to put it to work.

Figure 3. Comparison of the overnight strategy in SPY without a day-of-week filter and the version with entries limited to Monday through Wednesday.

The Overnight Risk Premium: One Possible Explanation for the Results

Our analysis shows that a substantial share of historical U.S. stock market returns has occurred during the overnight session, with marked differences across the days of the week.

But why does this happen? One possible explanation is the so-called overnight risk premium. Investors who hold positions overnight remain exposed to economic news, geopolitical events, and potential opening gaps, without always being able to respond promptly. The positive returns observed could therefore represent compensation for taking on this additional risk.

If that were the main explanation, however, we might also expect particularly strong results from the Friday overnight session, which spans the entire weekend and involves longer exposure to unexpected events. Instead, although this session was profitable, its performance fell well short of the Monday overnight session.

The risk premium therefore remains one possible interpretation, but it is unlikely to explain all the differences observed, particularly those between individual days of the week.

What we can say, however, is that simply filtering trades by day of the week preserved most of the historical profits while significantly reducing drawdown.

Once again, we have seen how even a straightforward analysis of market behavior can provide a useful starting point for identifying new systematic trading opportunities.

Until next time, happy trading!
